name: Arm Circles
instructions: Stand with your feet shoulder-width apart and extend both arms straight out to your sides at shoulder height, forming a T-shape with your body.
Begin making small, controlled circles with both arms simultaneously, moving forward. Keep your core lightly engaged and your shoulders relaxed — do not shrug them up toward your ears.
Gradually increase the size of the circles over 8 reps until you are making large, sweeping circles that challenge your shoulder range of motion.
After completing 15 forward circles, reverse direction and perform 15 backward circles, again starting small and gradually getting larger.
Keep your breathing steady throughout. If you feel tension in your neck, drop your chin slightly and relax your jaw.
cues: Keep your arms as straight as possible throughout — avoid bending the elbows
Stand tall: chest lifted, core lightly braced, feet grounded
Start small and build bigger — do not start with large swings
modification: If shoulder discomfort occurs, reduce the circle size or bend your elbows slightly to reduce lever length.

sensation.feelHere: A mild, warming ache around the shoulder joint and across the upper back.
sensation.notHere: A pinch at the very front point of the shoulder — that's the joint catching, not warming up.
sensation.stopIf: Any sharp catch or clicking with pain, or tingling down either arm.

name: Hip Circles
instructions: Stand with feet shoulder-width apart and place both hands on your hips. Slightly bend your knees to soften the joints.
Begin rotating your hips in a large, slow circle — push them forward, then to the right, then back, then to the left, creating a smooth circular motion.
Think of drawing a big oval on the floor with your hips. Keep your upper body as still as possible — the movement comes purely from the hips and pelvis.
Complete 10 full circles in one direction, then reverse and perform 10 circles in the opposite direction.
Breathe normally throughout and move at a pace that lets you feel the full range of motion in each direction.
cues: Let your hips drive the movement — your shoulders should barely move
Move slowly and deliberately to warm up the hip joint fully
Relax your belly — gripping your abs tightly will restrict the range of motion
modification: Hold onto a wall or chair with one hand for balance if needed.

sensation.feelHere: A loosening, oiling sensation around the hip socket as it moves through the circle.
sensation.notHere: A pinch at the front of the hip crease at the top of the circle — that's a range problem, not warming up.
sensation.backNote: Keep the motion in your hips, not your low back. If your low back is doing the swaying, shrink the circle.
sensation.stopIf: Sharp pinching in the front of the hip, or any pain shooting into the leg.

name: Leg Swings
instructions: Stand sideways next to a wall or sturdy surface. Place your right hand lightly on the wall for balance. Shift your weight onto your right foot.
Swing your left leg forward and backward in a controlled pendulum motion. Start with a small range of motion and gradually increase the swing height over the first few reps.
Your leg should swing naturally — do not force it higher than your comfortable range. Your standing leg stays slightly soft, not locked.
After 12 front-to-back swings, turn to face the wall and swing your leg side to side (across your body and out to the side) for 12 more reps.
Switch legs and repeat both directions on the right leg.
cues: Let momentum do the work — do not muscle the leg higher than it naturally goes
Keep your torso upright and avoid leaning to compensate for the swing
This is a mobility drill, not a stretch — do not hold at the top
modification: Hold the wall with both hands and reduce the swing height if balance is challenging.

sensation.feelHere: A light, springy stretch-and-release feeling at the front and back of the swinging hip.
sensation.notHere: A sharp tug in the groin at the top of the swing — that means you're forcing height, not letting momentum swing you.
sensation.backNote: Keep your torso upright through the swing. Leaning to compensate loads the low back for no reason.
sensation.stopIf: Any pinch that lingers after the swing stops, or tingling down the leg.

name: Cat-Cow Stretch
instructions: Start on all fours on your mat — hands directly under your shoulders and knees directly under your hips. Your spine is in a neutral, flat position (tabletop).
For Cow: Inhale slowly. As you breathe in, let your belly drop toward the floor, lift your chest and chin gently upward, and allow your tailbone to rise slightly. Your back arches gently downward.
For Cat: Exhale slowly. As you breathe out, round your spine up toward the ceiling like an angry cat. Tuck your chin toward your chest and tuck your tailbone under. Your back arches upward.
Flow between these two positions smoothly and continuously, letting your breath guide the movement — inhale into Cow, exhale into Cat.
Move through 10 full breath cycles. This is about spinal mobility, not stretching hard — find a comfortable range and breathe into it.
cues: Let your breath lead the movement — each position should be timed with an inhale or exhale
Move through your entire spine from tailbone to neck, not just one spot
Keep your arms straight and weight evenly distributed between hands and knees
modification: If wrist discomfort occurs, make fists or use forearms on the mat instead of flat hands.

sensation.feelHere: A gentle wave of movement rolling up and down your whole spine, rib by rib.
sensation.notHere: A pinch concentrated in one spot of the low back — the motion should spread evenly, not hinge at one point.
sensation.backNote: This is gentle, controlled spinal motion, not a loaded stretch — both directions should feel easy and free.
sensation.stopIf: Any sharp catch in the low back, or tingling or numbness anywhere in the legs.

name: Thoracic Rotation (Thread the Needle)
instructions: Start on all fours on your mat — hands under shoulders, knees under hips, spine neutral.
Place your right hand behind your head, elbow pointing out to the side. Keep your left hand firmly planted on the mat for support.
Inhale to prepare. As you exhale, rotate your right elbow downward, threading it under your left arm across your body. Let your right shoulder drop toward the mat as far as comfortable.
Inhale and reverse the movement, rotating your right elbow up toward the ceiling, opening your chest and following it with your eyes. This is the full rotation — feel it in your mid and upper back.
Complete all reps on the right side, then switch: left hand behind head, right hand planted, repeat the threading motion on the left side.
cues: The rotation comes from your upper back (thoracic spine), not your lower back or hips
Keep your hips level and square — do not let them rotate or shift
Follow your elbow with your eyes to encourage the full rotational range
modification: Reduce the rotation range if you feel tightness — even a small range of motion is beneficial for warm-up purposes.

sensation.feelHere: A twisting, opening feeling through your mid and upper back as you thread the arm through.
sensation.notHere: Rotation happening in your low back or hips instead — your hips should stay square and still throughout.
sensation.backNote: Keep the rotation above your waist. If your low back is twisting to make up range, shrink the movement.
sensation.stopIf: Any sharp low-back pain, or tingling down either arm or leg.

name: Push-Up
instructions: Start in a high plank position — hands slightly wider than shoulder-width apart, arms straight, core tight, body in a straight line from head to heels. Do not let your hips sag or pike up.
Take a breath in. Begin lowering your body toward the floor by bending your elbows at roughly a 45-degree angle away from your torso (not flared wide, not pinned to your sides).
Lower until your chest is approximately 1–2 inches from the floor or as low as you can control. Your whole body should move as one unit — do not lead with your hips.
Press through your palms to push back up to the starting position, fully extending your arms. Exhale as you press up.
Reset your form at the top before the next rep — check that your hips are neither sagging nor raised and your core is still engaged.
cues: Keep your body in a rigid plank — imagine a broomstick resting along your spine, hips, and head
Elbows at roughly 45 degrees — not straight out like a T or pressed tight to your ribs
Full range of motion: lower with control, press with power
modification: Drop to your knees for a kneeling push-up, keeping the same straight line from knees to head. This reduces the load significantly while maintaining the movement pattern.

sensation.feelHere: The middle of your chest and the back of your upper arms.
sensation.notHere: The front of your shoulders or your lower back. Those mean the wrong area is working.
sensation.firstCue: Keep elbows at 45 degrees, not flared to a T. Lower for a slow 3 count.

wrongSpot.fix: Elbows are flaring out to a T. Bring them to about 45 degrees from your ribs and re-set your shoulder blades before each rep.
Your hips are sagging. Squeeze your glutes and brace your core so your body stays a straight line.
Spread your fingers wide and stack your wrists directly under your shoulders instead of angled forward.
You're craning your head up. Keep your gaze slightly ahead of your hands and let your neck stay neutral.

sensation.nextDay: A dull ache across the chest and backs of arms for 1-2 days is normal. Sharp pain is not.
sensation.backNote: If your hips sag, your low back arches to compensate. Keep your core braced and stop the set once you can't hold a straight line.
sensation.stopIf: Any shooting pain, numbness, or tingling down an arm.

mistakes.right: Brace your core and squeeze your glutes to keep a straight line from head to heels.
Keep elbows at roughly 45 degrees from your torso, not straight out to the sides.
Lower until your chest is 1-2 inches from the floor, then press to full extension.

name: Glute Bridge
instructions: Lie on your back on the mat with your knees bent and feet flat on the floor, hip-width apart. Your feet should be close enough that you can just graze your heels with your fingertips when arms are at your sides.
Press your lower back gently into the mat to engage your core. Take a breath in to prepare.
As you exhale, press through both heels and squeeze your glutes to lift your hips off the floor. Drive your hips upward until your body forms a straight line from your knees to your shoulders.
Squeeze your glutes firmly at the top — hold for 1–2 seconds. Do not overextend by pushing your lower back into an arch; the movement should end when your hips are in line with your torso.
Inhale and slowly lower your hips back to the floor with control. Lightly touch the floor and immediately begin the next rep without relaxing fully.
cues: Drive through your heels, not your toes — if you wiggle your toes, you should still be able to lift
Squeeze your glutes hard at the top — the hip height is secondary to the glute contraction
Do not arch your lower back at the top: the goal is a straight line, not a big curve
modification: Place a folded blanket or pillow under your hips and use a smaller range of motion if you feel any discomfort.

sensation.feelHere: The glutes — the meat of your backside. It should feel like a squeeze, then a burn.
sensation.notHere: Your low back, and not mainly your hamstrings.
sensation.firstCue: Heels close to your butt, tuck your pelvis slightly, then squeeze the glutes to lift.

wrongSpot.fix: Your feet are too far away. Walk your heels in until your fingertips can just graze them; shins vertical at the top.
You are lifting too high and arching. Stop when your body forms a straight line from shoulders to knees, no further.
Tuck your pelvis and press your ribs down before you lift, and hold that all the way up.
You are pushing through your toes. Drive through your heels instead.

sensation.nextDay: A deep ache in the glutes for a day or two is exactly right.
sensation.backNote: One of the safest hip exercises for you, but only if the lift comes from the hips rather than an arched back. Height is not the goal — the squeeze is.
sensation.stopIf: You feel anything travel down your leg, or your low back pinches at the top.

name: Bodyweight Squat
instructions: Stand with your feet shoulder-width apart (or slightly wider), toes turned out 15–30 degrees. Arms can be extended in front of you for balance or crossed at your chest.
Take a breath in. Begin the squat by pushing your hips back first (as if reaching for a chair behind you), then bend your knees to lower down.

Descend until your thighs are as close to parallel to the floor as comfortable — or lower if mobility allows. Keep your chest tall, spine neutral, and knees tracking over your second toe (not caving inward).
At the bottom, pause briefly. Then press through your full foot — heel, mid-foot, and ball — to drive back up to standing.
Exhale on the way up. Fully extend your hips and knees at the top before beginning the next rep.
cues: Hips back first, then knees bend — this keeps your weight back over your heels
Chest stays tall throughout — if you are rounding forward, squat to a shallower depth
Knees track over your toes — actively push them out if they tend to collapse inward
modification: Squat to a chair or box behind you — touch the surface lightly and stand back up. This limits depth and gives you a target.

sensation.feelHere: The front of your thighs and your glutes, especially as you stand back up.
sensation.notHere: Your low back, or a pinching feeling in the front of your knees.
sensation.firstCue: Sit your hips back like reaching for a chair. Lower for a slow 3 count.

wrongSpot.fix: You're pitching forward. Sit back rather than straight down, brace before descending, and stop a few inches short of full depth.
Your shins are sliding too far forward. Sit back more and let your hips lead the movement, not your knees.
Turn your toes out slightly more and actively push your knees out over your toes as you descend.
You're leaning to one side. Check your weight is even between both feet before each rep.

sensation.nextDay: Front-of-thigh and glute soreness for 1–3 days is normal. Low back soreness the next day is not.
sensation.backNote: If your torso pitches forward, load shifts onto your spine. Sit back, reduce depth to what you control, and elevate your heels slightly if needed.
sensation.stopIf: Any shooting pain, numbness, or tingling down your leg. Stop the set immediately if that happens.

mistakes.right: Actively push your knees out over your toes throughout the descent and the ascent.
If you're rounding forward, reduce your depth until you can keep your chest tall.
Keep weight through your full foot, heel included, as you drive back up.

name: Forward Lunge
instructions: Stand tall with feet together and hands on your hips or hanging at your sides.
Take a large step forward with your right foot — roughly 2–3 feet, depending on your height. Your right foot should land flat on the floor.

Lower your back (left) knee toward the floor by bending both knees simultaneously. Your right thigh should reach parallel to the floor and your right knee should be directly over your right ankle, not shooting forward past your toes.
Push through your right heel to drive yourself back up to the starting standing position. Bring your right foot back next to your left.
Repeat on the left side. Alternate legs for each rep, counting each side as one rep.
cues: Stay tall through your torso — avoid leaning forward over your front thigh
Front knee stays behind or directly above your front ankle — do not let it drift forward
Control the descent — do not let your back knee crash into the floor
modification: Perform a shorter step and reduce the depth of the lunge. Hold onto a wall or chair for balance support.

sensation.feelHere: Front thigh and glute of your stepping leg, plus a stretch in the back leg's hip.
sensation.notHere: The front knee of your leading leg — sharp or pinching pain there is not the target.
sensation.firstCue: Keep your torso tall over your hips. Lower for a slow 2 count.

wrongSpot.fix: Your knee is traveling past your toes. Take a longer step forward so your shin stays closer to vertical.
You're leaning forward over the front thigh. Stay upright — try step-back lunges instead, they're kinder to your back.
Control the descent instead of dropping; stop an inch or two above the floor.
Land with your whole front foot flat rather than on your toes.

sensation.nextDay: Front thigh and glute soreness for 1–3 days is normal. Front knee soreness the next day is not.
sensation.backNote: Leaning forward over the front thigh shifts load onto your low back. Stay upright, and if it keeps happening, swap to step-back lunges instead.
sensation.stopIf: Any shooting pain, numbness, or tingling down a leg, or sharp knee pain.

mistakes.right: Take a bigger step forward so your front knee doesn't drift past your toes.
Keep your chest up and stacked over your hips throughout the movement.
Lower under control and stop just short of the floor instead of dropping.

name: Wall Sit
instructions: Find a flat, clear wall. Stand with your back flat against the wall, feet about 2 feet in front of you and shoulder-width apart.

Slide your back down the wall by bending your knees until your thighs are parallel to the floor — as if sitting in an invisible chair. Your knees should be directly above your ankles, not pushed forward past your feet.
Keep your entire back flat against the wall throughout — do not let your lower back peel away from the wall or arch. Your head, shoulders, and entire back should maintain contact.
Hold this position for the full 30 seconds. Breathe steadily — do not hold your breath. Keep your core lightly engaged.
To come out of the position, simply slide back up the wall to standing. Do not push off your thighs with your hands.
cues: Keep your back fully flat on the wall — this is what makes it back-safe
90-degree angle at the knees is ideal, but go shallower (less bend) if needed
Breathe steadily and keep your hands resting on your thighs, not pushing
modification: Slide down to only a 45-degree knee bend instead of 90 degrees — this significantly reduces the quad load.

sensation.feelHere: A deep burn in the front of your thighs, building through the hold.
sensation.notHere: Your knees themselves, or your low back — both should stay quiet and flat against the wall.
sensation.firstCue: Keep your entire back flat on the wall. Breathe steadily through the hold.

wrongSpot.fix: You're too low or too far from the wall. Slide up slightly and bring your feet closer until it's your thighs that burn.
Your back is arching off the wall. Press it flat and shorten the hold time until you can maintain that.
Check your feet are evenly spaced and your weight is centered, not shifted to one side.
Move your feet slightly further from the wall so your shins aren't overly angled.

sensation.nextDay: Quad soreness for 1–2 days is normal. Knee soreness the next day is not.
sensation.stopIf: Any sharp knee pain, or numbness or tingling in your legs.

mistakes.right: Walk your feet further from the wall until your knees stack directly over your ankles.
Keep your entire back, including your low back, pressed flat against the wall.
Breathe steadily throughout the hold instead of bracing and holding your breath.

name: Step-Back Lunge
instructions: Stand tall with feet together and hands on your hips. This is the safer alternative to a forward lunge for the lower back because the torso stays more upright.
Take a large step backward with your right foot. Land on the ball of your right foot, keeping your right heel off the floor throughout the movement.
Bend both knees to lower yourself toward the floor. Your left (front) thigh should approach parallel to the floor and your left knee should stay directly above your left ankle.
Keep your torso completely upright — the step-back lunge naturally encourages this. Your chest should face forward, not tilt down.
Drive through your left heel to step your right foot back to the starting position. Repeat on the other side. Alternate for each rep.
cues: Step back far enough that your front knee stays over your ankle — not pushed forward
Keep your torso completely vertical throughout — this is the key advantage of step-back lunges
Control the lowering phase — 2 seconds down, 1 second up
modification: Hold onto a wall or countertop for balance support, or reduce the depth of the lunge.

sensation.feelHere: Glute and front thigh of your front leg, plus a stretch through the back leg's hip.
sensation.notHere: The front knee — this variation is designed to keep pressure off it compared to forward lunges.
sensation.firstCue: Keep your torso upright. Lower for a slow 2 count, 1 up.

wrongSpot.fix: Step back further so your front shin stays more vertical and your knee stays above your ankle.
You're tilting your chest down. Keep it facing forward and upright the whole rep.
Keep your back heel lifted and land softly on the ball of your back foot.
Check your step length is equal on both sides; a short step overloads that leg's knee.

sensation.nextDay: Glute and front thigh soreness for 1–3 days is normal. Front knee soreness the next day is not.
sensation.backNote: This version keeps your torso upright by design, so it's easier on your spine than forward lunges. Still, don't let your chest tip forward as you fatigue.
sensation.stopIf: Any shooting pain, numbness, or tingling down a leg, or sharp knee pain.

mistakes.right: Keep your chest facing forward and vertical throughout the step-back and return.
Step back far enough that your front knee doesn't drift past your toes.
Take 2 seconds lowering and 1 second driving back up instead of rushing.

name: Bird Dog
instructions: Start on all fours on your mat — hands directly under your shoulders, knees directly under your hips, spine in a neutral flat position (not arched or rounded). This is your tabletop position.
Take a breath in. As you exhale, simultaneously extend your right arm straight forward (thumb pointing up) and your left leg straight back behind you. Keep both limbs parallel to the floor.
Hold this extended position for 2 seconds. Your hips must stay perfectly level — do not let the side with the raised leg tilt or rotate. Think of balancing a cup of water on your lower back.
Inhale and return both limbs slowly to the starting position. Your hand and knee should hover just above the floor before the next rep.
Repeat on the opposite side (left arm + right leg). Each pair of extensions counts as one rep.
cues: Keep your hips perfectly square and level — this is the hardest and most important part
Extend long through your fingertips and heel, not just lifting the limbs
Brace your core before you move — pretend you're about to be poked in the belly
modification: Instead of extending the arm and leg simultaneously, extend only the leg while keeping both hands on the floor. Master leg-only first, then add the arm.

sensation.feelHere: A steady brace across your stomach and the glute of your standing-leg side.
sensation.notHere: A pinch or ache in the low back itself, especially on the extended-leg side.
sensation.firstCue: Brace like you're about to be poked in the belly. Move for a slow 3 count.

wrongSpot.fix: You're lifting the leg too high. Only go as high as your hips stay level — imagine balancing water on your low back.
Slow down and lift the leg less. Square your hips to the floor before you extend the arm.
Stack your hand directly under your shoulder, not out in front, and spread your fingers wide.
Keep your gaze down at the floor, not forward — your neck should stay in line with your spine.

sensation.nextDay: A mild deep-core ache for a day is normal. Low back soreness the next day is not.
sensation.backNote: This is a core rehab staple, not a spine risk. The only failure mode is the hips rotating or the back arching — if that happens, lift the leg less, not more.
sensation.stopIf: Any shooting or electric pain, or numbness or tingling in a leg.

mistakes.right: Stop the moment your hips start to tilt or the low back arches — height doesn't matter, level hips do.
Extend and return slowly, holding the top position for a full 2 seconds each time.
Brace your core before each extension, like you're about to be poked in the stomach.

name: Dead Bug
instructions: Lie flat on your back on the mat with arms pointing straight up toward the ceiling and knees bent at 90 degrees directly above your hips (tabletop position).
Take a deep breath in. As you exhale, slowly lower your right arm overhead toward the floor while simultaneously straightening and lowering your left leg toward the floor.
Lower both limbs until they are just above the floor — do not let your lower back arch away from the mat. If it arches, don't go as low.
Inhale and return both limbs to the starting position in a controlled manner.
Repeat on the opposite side (left arm + right leg) — that is one full rep.
cues: Press your lower back firmly into the mat throughout the entire movement
Move slowly — this is not a speed exercise, it is a control exercise
Breathe out as you lower, breathe in as you return
modification: Instead of fully extending your leg, only lower it halfway down and keep a slight bend in the knee.

sensation.feelHere: A deep, constant brace low across your stomach, below the belly button.
sensation.notHere: Your low back lifting or arching away from the floor — that means the core let go.
sensation.firstCue: Press your low back flat into the mat. Lower for a slow 3 count.

wrongSpot.fix: Stop lowering the arm and leg sooner. Only go as far as your low back stays flat on the mat.
Lower the leg only halfway instead of toward the floor, and keep a slight bend in the knee.
Let your head rest heavy on the mat — you shouldn't be lifting it to help.
Exhale as you lower the limbs, inhale as you return — breath-holding spikes belly pressure.

sensation.nextDay: A deep central-ab ache for a day or two is normal. Low back soreness the next day is not.
sensation.backNote: One of the safest exercises in this program. The only failure mode is the low back arching off the mat — if it lifts even slightly, shorten the range.
sensation.stopIf: Any shooting or electric pain, or numbness or tingling in a leg.

mistakes.right: Only lower the arm and leg as far as your low back stays pressed flat into the mat.
Slow down — this is a control exercise, not a speed one.
Keep the opposite arm and leg steady while only the moving side lowers.

name: Bicep Curl
instructions: Stand tall with feet shoulder-width apart, holding a dumbbell in each hand at your sides, palms facing forward. Keep your shoulders back and down — do not let them round forward.
Keeping your elbows pinned close to your sides and your upper arms completely still, exhale and curl both dumbbells upward by bending at the elbow.
Curl until the dumbbells are at shoulder height and you feel a strong contraction in your biceps. Your elbows should not drift forward past your torso.
Pause at the top for one second, then inhale and slowly lower the dumbbells back to the starting position over 2–3 seconds. Control the descent — do not let gravity drop them.
Repeat for all reps. If you cannot keep your upper arms still, the weight is too heavy — switch to the 10lb dumbbells.
cues: Upper arms stay pinned to your sides — only your forearms should move
Squeeze the bicep hard at the top before lowering
Lower slowly — the downward phase builds as much strength as the upward phase
modification: Curl one arm at a time (alternating curls) to reduce total load and focus on each arm individually.

sensation.feelHere: The front of your upper arm, between your shoulder and elbow, building to a burn.
sensation.notHere: Your forearm or wrist. That means grip or wrist motion is taking over the work.
sensation.firstCue: Keep elbows pinned to your sides. Lower slow — 2–3 seconds down.

wrongSpot.fix: You're gripping the dumbbells too hard. Hold them lightly — a firm hold is enough, a death grip is not.
Your wrist is bending back at the top. Keep it straight, in line with your forearm, throughout the curl.
Your elbows are drifting forward or you're swinging the weight up. Pin your elbows to your sides and slow down.
You're leaning back to help swing the weight up. Stand tall and keep your torso still.

sensation.nextDay: A burn in the front of the upper arm for 1–2 days is normal and expected.
sensation.stopIf: Numbness or tingling in your hand, or sharp pain at the elbow or wrist.

mistakes.right: Keep your upper arms completely still and let only your forearms move through the full rep.
Keep your elbows pinned close to your sides throughout — drifting forward shifts work to the shoulders.

mistakes.wrong: Dropping the weight on the way down
mistakes.right: Lower over 2–3 seconds with control — the descent builds as much strength as the lift.

name: Dumbbell Shoulder Press
instructions: Stand or sit tall. Hold a 15lb dumbbell in each hand at shoulder height with palms facing forward. Your elbows should be at roughly 90 degrees, just below or at ear level.

Take a breath in. As you exhale, press both dumbbells straight up overhead until your arms are fully extended but not locked. The dumbbells should travel in a slight inward arc as they meet near the top.
At the top, your arms should be directly overhead (not leaning forward). Pause briefly.
Inhale and lower the dumbbells slowly back to the starting position at shoulder height. Control the weight — do not let it fall.
Keep your core braced throughout and avoid arching your lower back by tucking your pelvis slightly. If you feel lower back strain, sit on a bench or switch to 10lb dumbbells.
cues: Keep your core braced — do not arch your lower back to get the weight up
Press the weights straight up — avoid pressing forward in front of your head
Control the lowering phase — 2 seconds down keeps the muscles working
modification: Use 10lb dumbbells and perform seated with your back supported against a wall for extra spinal support.

sensation.feelHere: The top and side of your shoulders, with the back of your upper arms finishing the press.
sensation.notHere: Your neck or the top of your traps taking over, or a pinch in your lower back.
sensation.firstCue: Press straight up, not forward. Lower for a slow 3 count to shoulder height.

wrongSpot.fix: You're shrugging to finish the press. Stop a few inches before full lockout and keep your shoulders down away from your ears.
You're pressing forward instead of straight up. Keep the dumbbells stacked directly over your elbows the whole way.
You're arching to get the weight up. Tuck your pelvis slightly and brace your core, or sit on a bench for support.
You're locking out hard at the top. Stop just short of full extension.

sensation.nextDay: A dull ache across the shoulders for 1-2 days is normal. Sharp pain in the joint or neck is not.
sensation.backNote: Overhead pressing is where the low back tends to arch to help finish the lift. Tuck your pelvis slightly, brace your core, and sit down if you feel any strain.
sensation.stopIf: Anything shoots down your arm, or your hand goes numb or tingly.

mistakes.right: Keep the dumbbells stacked directly above your shoulders, not out in front.
Tuck your pelvis slightly and brace your core, or sit down and switch to lighter dumbbells.
Keep your shoulders pulled down away from your ears through the whole press.

name: Lateral Raise
instructions: Stand tall with feet shoulder-width apart. Hold a 10lb dumbbell in each hand at your sides, palms facing inward. Keep a very slight bend in your elbows throughout the movement.
Take a breath in. As you exhale, raise both arms out to your sides simultaneously, leading with your elbows (not your hands). Think of pouring water out of a jug — your pinky side leads slightly.
Raise until your arms are at shoulder height — parallel to the floor. Do not raise above shoulder level, as this adds unnecessary shoulder impingement risk.
Pause for one second at the top, then inhale and slowly lower the dumbbells back to your sides over 2 seconds.
Do not use momentum or shrug your shoulders to help the weight up. If you cannot maintain control, use lighter weight or perform one arm at a time.
cues: Lead with your elbows, not your hands — this targets the lateral deltoid more effectively
Stop at shoulder height — higher is not better and can stress the shoulder joint
No swinging — if you are swinging your body to get the weight up, go lighter
modification: Perform one arm at a time while bracing the other hand against your thigh for control. Reduce to lighter resistance if 10lb is too heavy.

sensation.feelHere: The side of your shoulder, right at the cap of the arm.
sensation.notHere: The top of your traps, between your neck and shoulder. That's a shrug, not a raise.
sensation.firstCue: Push the dumbbells out toward the walls. Raise for a slow 2 count.

wrongSpot.felt: Top of the traps or neck
wrongSpot.fix: You're shrugging the weight up. Keep your shoulders pulled down away from your ears and go lighter if needed.
You're raising above shoulder height. Stop the arms once they're parallel to the floor.
You're leading with your hands instead of your elbows. Think of pouring water from a jug as you lift.
You're using body swing to move the weight. Go lighter and keep your torso still throughout.

sensation.nextDay: A light ache on the side of the shoulder for 1-2 days is normal. Trap or neck soreness usually means shrugging happened.
sensation.stopIf: Any sharp pinch in the shoulder joint, or numbness or tingling in the hand.

mistakes.right: Stop once your arms are parallel to the floor — higher adds impingement risk, not benefit.
Keep your shoulders down and let the raise come from the side of the shoulder, not the traps.
Stand tall and still; go lighter if you need momentum to move the weight.

name: Bent-Over Dumbbell Row
instructions: Stand with feet hip-width apart. Hinge at your hips (push them back, not down) to bring your torso to roughly 45 degrees — keep your spine completely neutral, not rounded. Hold a 15lb dumbbell in each hand with arms hanging straight down.
Take a breath in and brace your core firmly. As you exhale, drive both elbows back and up, rowing the dumbbells toward your lower ribcage.
At the top of the row, your elbows should be close to your torso and pulled behind your back. Squeeze your shoulder blades together firmly.
Inhale and lower the dumbbells with control back to the starting hanging position. Do not let them drop.
Maintain your hip-hinge position for all reps — do not stand up between reps. If you feel your lower back, re-brace your core and ensure your hips are truly hinged, not squatting.
cues: Spine must stay neutral — round back under load is the risk to avoid; brace hard before each rep
Drive elbows back, not up — think of putting your elbows in your back pockets
Keep the dumbbells close to your body, not swinging wide away from your torso
modification: Perform a single-arm row with your free hand resting on a table or chair for spinal support. This allows you to keep a more neutral spine more easily.

sensation.feelHere: The middle of your back and the sides under your armpits, on both sides at once.
sensation.notHere: Your lower back or your biceps. Both mean the back muscles are being bypassed.
sensation.firstCue: Pull your shoulder blades back first, then bend the elbows. Slow 2-count up.

wrongSpot.fix: Your hips are rising or your torso is rounding. Reset the hinge, brace your core, and lower the weight until your spine stays still.
You're curling, not rowing. Start each rep by squeezing the shoulder blades back before the elbows bend.
You're gripping too hard. Loosen your hold — the hand is just a hook, not the mover.
You're rounding forward at the bottom. Keep your chest lifted and shoulder blades set before you start pulling.

sensation.nextDay: A dull ache across the upper and mid back for 1–2 days is expected. Sharp low-back pain is not.
sensation.backNote: This exercise loads a bent-over spine directly. If your torso twists, sags, or your low back strains, stop the set — that's the hinge breaking down, not weakness.
sensation.stopIf: Any pain shooting down a leg, numbness, tingling, or a sharp pull in the low back.

mistakes.right: Hold the hinge position for the entire set. Standing up and re-hinging each rep repeatedly strains the low back.
Keep your spine neutral by pushing your hips back, not down, and bracing your core before the first pull.
Drive the elbows back with control instead of jerking the torso to help — that shifts load into the spine.

name: Goblet Squat
instructions: Stand with feet slightly wider than shoulder-width, toes turned out 30–45 degrees. Hold a 10lb dumbbell vertically at your chest with both hands cupped around one end, elbows pointing down.
Take a breath in and brace your core. Begin the squat by pushing your hips back and out, then bend your knees to lower yourself between your legs.
Descend as deep as comfortable — aiming for thighs parallel to the floor or lower. Your elbows should track inside your knees as you descend; use them to gently push your knees outward.
Keep your chest tall and the dumbbell close to your body throughout the entire movement. Your heels must stay flat on the floor.
Drive through your heels to press back up to standing, exhaling on the way up. Squeeze your glutes at the top.
cues: Use your elbows to push your knees out — this opens the hips and protects the knees
Keep the dumbbell close to your chest — letting it drift forward pulls you forward
Heels stay down — if they rise, you need to work on ankle mobility or widen your stance
modification: Reduce the squat depth and hold the dumbbell at your chest with two hands close to your body, squatting to a chair for reference.

sensation.feelHere: Front of your thighs and glutes, with a light brace through your midsection and upper back.
sensation.notHere: Your low back, wrists, or the front of your shoulders holding the weight.
sensation.firstCue: Keep the weight tight to your chest. Lower for a slow 3 count.

wrongSpot.fix: The weight is drifting away from your chest, pulling you forward. Keep it pinned to your sternum the whole descent.
Sit back more before bending your knees, letting your hips travel back and down, not just down.
Cup the dumbbell from underneath rather than gripping it tightly; let your palms support the weight.
Use your elbows to gently push your knees outward as you descend.

sensation.nextDay: Thighs and glutes ache for 1–3 days. Wrist or low back soreness the next day is not expected.
sensation.backNote: Letting the weight drift forward pulls your torso and spine forward with it. Keep it tight to your chest and stop the descent once your back starts rounding.
sensation.stopIf: Sharp or shooting pain, or any numbness or tingling down a leg.

mistakes.right: Widen your stance slightly or work on ankle mobility so your heels stay flat.
Keep the dumbbell pinned close to your chest through the entire rep.
Pause briefly at the bottom before driving back up, instead of springing out of the hole.

name: Tricep Kickback
instructions: Stand next to a sturdy surface (chair or table) for support. Hinge at the hips to bring your torso to roughly 45 degrees, keeping your spine neutral and core braced. Place your free hand on the support surface.
Hold a 10lb dumbbell in your working hand. Bring your upper arm up until it is parallel to the floor and pinned close to your side. Your elbow is bent at 90 degrees — this is the starting position.
Take a breath in. As you exhale, extend your forearm backward by straightening your elbow until your entire arm is parallel to the floor and straight.
Squeeze your tricep hard at the fully extended position for one second. Do not let your upper arm drop — it stays parallel to the floor throughout.
Inhale and slowly return your forearm to the 90-degree bent starting position. Complete all reps on one side, then switch arms.
cues: Upper arm stays parallel to the floor and does not swing — only your forearm moves
Squeeze the tricep hard at full extension before returning
Keep your core braced to protect your spine in the hinge position
modification: Use a lighter resistance band or perform with no weight first to learn the movement pattern.

sensation.feelHere: The back of your upper arm, right above the elbow, as you straighten it.
sensation.notHere: Your shoulder swinging the weight, or your lower back rounding under load.
sensation.firstCue: Pin your upper arm to your side. Extend for a slow 2 count.

wrongSpot.fix: Your upper arm is swinging to help. Pin it against your side and only move your forearm.
You're locking out hard at the end. Stop just short of full extension and squeeze the muscle instead.
Your hinge is too deep or your core isn't braced. Stand a bit taller and brace before each rep.
Keep your wrist straight in line with your forearm instead of letting it bend under the weight.

sensation.nextDay: A focused ache on the back of the upper arm for 1-2 days is normal. Elbow joint pain is not.
sensation.backNote: The hinged position loads your spine under tension. Keep your core braced and your back flat — stop if you feel it in your low back instead of your arm.
sensation.stopIf: Sharp elbow pain, or any numbness or tingling in the hand.

mistakes.right: Keep your upper arm pinned parallel to the floor; only the forearm should move.

mistakes.wrong: Rounding the back in the hinge
mistakes.right: Keep your spine neutral and core braced throughout the hinge position.

mistakes.wrong: Rushing the squeeze at the top
mistakes.right: Pause and squeeze the triceps for one full second at full extension.

name: Floor Chest Press
instructions: Lie on your back on the mat. Hold a 15lb dumbbell in each hand at chest level, elbows bent at 90 degrees and resting on the floor. Feet are flat on the floor, knees bent. The floor limits how far your elbows can drop, which actually protects your shoulders.
Take a breath in. As you exhale, press both dumbbells straight up toward the ceiling, extending your arms fully. The dumbbells should travel on a slight inward arc and nearly touch at the top.
Hold briefly at the top — arms extended, dumbbells over your chest.
Inhale and lower the dumbbells slowly back down until your elbows touch the floor lightly. Control this descent — do not let the weights drop with gravity.
Touch the floor briefly and immediately begin the next press without relaxing your chest. That contact point is just a depth reference.
cues: Press up and slightly inward — imagine pushing the dumbbells together at the top
Lower until elbows touch the floor — this is your natural stopping point on the floor
Keep your shoulder blades pressed into the mat throughout
modification: Use 10lb dumbbells and a narrower grip width if shoulder discomfort occurs.

sensation.feelHere: The middle and outer part of your chest, plus the back of your upper arms.
sensation.notHere: The front, bony point of your shoulder. That means the wrong muscle is taking over.
sensation.firstCue: Press up and slightly inward. Lower for a slow 3 count until elbows touch the floor.

wrongSpot.fix: Your shoulder blades are rolling forward. Press them into the mat and hold that position for the whole set.
Bring your elbows closer to your ribs, roughly 45 degrees, not flared straight out to the sides.
That's the joint, not the muscle. Stop the set, drop the weight, and shorten the range.
Keep your wrists stacked directly above your elbows instead of letting them bend backward under load.

sensation.nextDay: A broad ache across the chest for 1-3 days is normal. Sharp pinpoint pain is not.
sensation.backNote: This one is spine-friendly — lying on the floor removes the ability to arch. Keep your low back lightly touching the mat throughout.
sensation.stopIf: Anything shoots down your arm, or your hand goes numb or tingly.

mistakes.right: Keep them closer to your ribs, around 45 degrees, to protect the shoulder joint.
Lower with control and let your elbows touch the floor lightly, not drop with gravity.
Keep your shoulder blades pressed into the mat for the entire set, not just at setup.

name: Single-Leg Romanian Deadlift (Light)
instructions: Stand tall holding a 10lb dumbbell in your right hand at your side. Shift your weight onto your left foot. Soften your left knee slightly — do not lock it.

Take a breath in and brace your core. Hinge forward at the hips — push your hips straight back as you lower the dumbbell down your left shin. Your right leg lifts behind you as a counterbalance, staying in line with your torso.
Lower until you feel a stretch in your left hamstring or your torso is parallel to the floor — whichever comes first. Keep your spine completely neutral throughout; do not round your back.
Exhale and drive through your left heel to return to standing, squeezing your left glute at the top. Bring your right foot back to the floor for balance.
Complete all reps on the left side, then switch — hold the dumbbell in your left hand and balance on your right foot.
cues: Hinge at the hip, not the waist — your spine stays long and neutral as your hips push back
Think of your torso and raised leg as a seesaw — they should move in sync
This is a balance exercise too — slow down if you are wobbling
modification: Hold onto a wall lightly with your free hand for balance, or keep both feet on the ground and hinge to a moderate depth (not a full single-leg RDL).

sensation.feelHere: A deep stretch through the hamstring of your standing leg, then a glute squeeze as you rise.
sensation.notHere: Your low back. Wobbling in the standing ankle is normal balance work, not the target.
sensation.firstCue: Push hips straight back, not down. Lower for a slow 3 count.

wrongSpot.fix: Hips dropped down instead of back, or you descended past your hamstring's limit. Push hips toward a wall and stop when the hamstring feels tight.
You're squatting the knee instead of hinging. Keep the standing knee softly bent and push the hips back, not down.

wrongSpot.felt: Can't feel the hamstring at all
wrongSpot.fix: You're not going deep enough. Lower until you feel a real stretch before returning, staying within a neutral spine.
That's stability, not target. Touch a wall lightly with your free hand and focus only on the hip hinge.

sensation.nextDay: A stretch-type ache in the hamstring of the working leg for 1–2 days is expected.
sensation.backNote: This is a hinge, not a bend — hips travel back toward a wall, not down. Stop the descent the instant your hamstring feels tight, not when the weight nears the floor.
sensation.stopIf: Anything shoots or tingles down the back of your leg, or your low back sharply pinches.

mistakes.wrong: Rounding the back to reach lower
mistakes.right: Stop the descent where your spine stays neutral, even if that means a shorter range than you'd like.
Keep the standing knee soft but not bending much; push the hips straight back instead of down.

mistakes.wrong: Torso and raised leg moving separately
mistakes.right: Move them together like a seesaw — as the torso tips forward, the back leg rises in line with it.

name: Dumbbell Reverse Fly
instructions: Stand with feet hip-width apart. Hinge at your hips to bring your torso to roughly 45 degrees — spine neutral, core braced. Hold a 10lb dumbbell in each hand hanging straight down with palms facing each other.
Take a breath in. As you exhale, raise both arms out to your sides simultaneously, leading with your elbows. Keep a slight bend in your elbows throughout.
Raise until your arms are parallel to the floor or as high as you can comfortably go. Squeeze your shoulder blades together at the top.
Inhale and slowly lower the dumbbells back to the starting hanging position with full control.
Maintain your hinge position throughout all reps. If you feel your lower back fatiguing, reduce your torso angle (stand more upright) or rest between reps.
cues: Lead with your elbows, not your hands — this better targets the rear deltoids
Squeeze your shoulder blades together at the top of each rep
Keep the movement smooth and controlled — do not swing or use momentum
modification: Perform seated, leaning forward with chest resting on thighs — this removes the hip-hinge hold and allows you to focus purely on the arm movement.

sensation.feelHere: The back of your shoulders and between your shoulder blades as your arms rise out to the sides.
sensation.notHere: Your traps shrugging up near your neck. That means the weight is too heavy for this move.
sensation.firstCue: Lead with your elbows, not your hands. Raise slow, squeeze blades together at the top.

wrongSpot.fix: You're shrugging to lift the weight. Go lighter and keep shoulders pulled down away from your ears.
Your hinge is breaking down or you're using momentum. Stand more upright or rest between reps.
You're gripping hard or bending the elbows too much. Loosen your grip and keep elbows only slightly bent.
You're swinging the weight up. Slow the raise and stop lifting your arms above shoulder height.

sensation.nextDay: A light ache across the shoulders for a day is normal — go lighter if it's more than that.
sensation.backNote: Holding the hip hinge loads your low back over time. If it fatigues or aches, stand more upright or rest between reps rather than pushing through.
sensation.stopIf: Any pain shooting down a leg, or sharp low-back pain during the hinge. Stop and stand up.

mistakes.right: Keep your torso at roughly 45 degrees throughout — standing tall shifts the work off the rear delts.
Raise and lower slowly and smoothly — momentum means the muscle isn't doing the work.
Stop the raise once your arms are parallel to the floor — higher recruits the traps instead.

name: Dumbbell Plank Pull-Through
instructions: Get into a high plank position with hands directly under your shoulders and body in a straight line from head to heels. Place a 10 lb dumbbell on the floor just outside your left wrist.
Brace your core firmly and squeeze your glutes. Your hips must stay square and level to the floor throughout — this is the anti-rotation challenge.
Keeping your right hand planted on the floor, reach your left hand across and under your body, grip the dumbbell, and drag it across to the right side. Place your left hand back on the floor.
Now reach your right hand across, grip the dumbbell, and drag it back to the left side. Left and right together equals one rep.
The moment one hand leaves the floor, your core is fighting rotation — resist it completely. Move slowly and with control, not speed.
cues: Hips must stay square — if yours are rocking or twisting, slow down or switch to a lighter dumbbell
Squeeze your glutes and brace your abs before you reach — build full-body tension first
Look straight down at the floor to keep your neck neutral
modification: Do the pull-through without a dumbbell — just drag your open hand across the floor. This removes load while you build the movement pattern and core stability.

sensation.feelHere: A bracing squeeze through your whole midsection resisting the twist, plus shoulders.
sensation.notHere: Your low back, or one hip dropping lower than the other as you reach.
sensation.firstCue: Squeeze your glutes and brace before you reach. Drag the weight for a slow 3 count.

wrongSpot.fix: That means the exercise isn't being done. Slow way down or switch to no weight until hips stay square.
Squeeze your glutes and brace your abs before you reach, not after.
Keep that hand stacked directly under your shoulder and push the floor away.
Look straight down at the floor instead of watching your hand move.

sensation.nextDay: A deep ache across the stomach and sides for a day is normal. Low back soreness is not.
sensation.backNote: This is an anti-rotation drill — the goal is hips staying dead square. If they rock or twist, slow down or drop the weight rather than pushing through.
sensation.stopIf: Any shooting or electric pain, or numbness or tingling anywhere.

mistakes.right: Slow the reach down and, if needed, use a lighter dumbbell or no weight until hips stay level.
Move slowly and with control — speed is what lets the hips twist.
Brace your core and squeeze your glutes before each reach, and hold that tension the whole set.

name: Banded Glute Bridge
instructions: Place a resistance loop band just above your knees. Lie on your back with knees bent, feet flat on the floor hip-width apart, and arms at your sides.
Press your knees gently outward against the band so they track directly over your ankles (not caving inward). Maintain this outward pressure throughout the entire exercise.
Press your lower back gently into the mat, then drive through both heels and squeeze your glutes to lift your hips off the floor.
Rise until your hips form a straight line with your knees and shoulders. Squeeze your glutes hard at the top and keep pressing your knees out against the band.
Hold for 1–2 seconds at the top, then slowly lower your hips back to the mat with control. The band adds continuous hip abductor activation throughout the movement.
cues: Push your knees outward against the band throughout — this activates your glute medius
Squeeze your glutes hard at the top, not just lift your hips
Drive through your heels — wiggling your toes should not affect your ability to lift
modification: Use a lighter resistance band or remove the band and perform a standard glute bridge if the abductor demand is too high.

sensation.feelHere: The glutes, plus a burn on the outer hip from pushing your knees out against the band.
sensation.notHere: Your low back, and not mainly your hamstrings or the front of your thighs.
sensation.firstCue: Push knees out against the band the whole time, then squeeze glutes to lift. Go slow.

wrongSpot.fix: Your feet are too far away. Walk your heels in until your fingertips can just graze them.
You lifted too high and arched. Stop at a straight line from shoulders to knees, no higher.

wrongSpot.felt: Front of the hip or knees cave in
wrongSpot.fix: You relaxed the outward knee pressure. Keep pushing your knees out against the band for the entire rep, not just at the top.
You're pushing through your toes. Drive through your heels instead and let the band do the abduction work.

sensation.nextDay: A deep glute ache plus soreness on the outer hip for 1–2 days is expected.
sensation.backNote: Same hip-extension exercise as the plain bridge, just with outer-hip work added. Lift from the hips, not an arched back; height is not the goal.
sensation.stopIf: Anything travels down your leg, or your low back pinches at the top of the lift.

mistakes.wrong: Knees caving inward against the band
mistakes.right: Actively push the knees outward against the band for the entire set, not just the lift.

mistakes.wrong: Arching the low back at the top
mistakes.right: Stop at a straight line from shoulders to knees; tuck the pelvis before you lift.

mistakes.wrong: Feet too far from the hips
mistakes.right: Walk the heels in until your fingertips can just graze them, shins vertical at the top.

name: Clamshell
instructions: Place a resistance loop band just above your knees. Lie on your side on the mat with your hips stacked, knees bent to about 45 degrees, feet together. Support your head with your lower arm.
Keep your feet together throughout the movement. Take a breath in. As you exhale, lift your top knee upward toward the ceiling, rotating from the hip — like a clamshell opening.
Open as far as you can without your hips rolling backward. Your pelvis should stay completely still — place your top hand on your hip to monitor for rocking.
Pause at the top for one second, feeling the outer glute working. Then inhale and slowly lower your knee back to the starting position.
Complete all reps on one side, then switch sides.
cues: Keep your feet together — the rotation comes from the hip, not the foot separating
Pelvis stays still — if your hips rock back, you have gone too far
You should feel this in the outer glute, not your hip flexors or lower back
modification: Remove the resistance band and perform with bodyweight only, focusing on perfect form before adding resistance.

sensation.feelHere: A burn on the side of your hip, a hand's width below the top of the hip bone.
sensation.notHere: The front of your hip crease, or your low back from the pelvis rocking backward.
sensation.firstCue: Keep your hips stacked and still; lift the knee only from the hip. Go slow.

wrongSpot.fix: You're rocking your pelvis backward to fake more range. Keep a hand on your hip to catch any rocking and stop the lift there.
Same pelvis-rocking issue, just felt higher up. Shrink the range until your hips stay completely stacked and still.

wrongSpot.felt: Front of the thigh, like a hip flexor
wrongSpot.fix: You're leading with the knee bending forward instead of rotating from the hip. Keep feet together and rotate only.
Your range is too small or the band too loose. Open further, right up to where the hip starts to rock, and add tension.

sensation.nextDay: A burn deep on the side of the hip for 1–2 days; this muscle is often under-trained.
sensation.stopIf: Sharp pinching pain deep in the front of the hip joint itself, not a muscle burn.

mistakes.wrong: Rocking the pelvis backward to open wider
mistakes.right: Keep a hand on your hip to monitor rocking; stop the lift the instant it starts.

mistakes.wrong: Feet separating instead of staying together
mistakes.right: Keep feet together throughout — the rotation should come entirely from the hip, not the foot.
Slow down and pause a full second at the top to let the outer glute do the work.

name: Banded Lateral Walk
instructions: Place a resistance loop band just above your ankles. Stand with feet shoulder-width apart with slight tension already in the band. Soften your knees into a mini-squat position — about a quarter-squat depth.
Keep your chest up and core braced. Take a step to the right with your right foot — about shoulder-width plus a few inches. Maintain the quarter-squat position throughout.
Bring your left foot in to follow, but do not let it come all the way in — keep enough distance to maintain band tension. Never let your feet come together.
Continue stepping right for the full set (12 steps right = one set), then reverse direction and walk left for another 12 steps.
Stay low in the squat position for the entire set. The moment you stand tall, the exercise becomes much easier and less effective.
cues: Stay low throughout — do not stand up and re-squat with each step
Keep toes pointing forward — do not let your feet angle outward as you tire
Control each step — do not snap the band by stepping too fast
modification: Use a lighter band or place the band above the knees instead of above the ankles to reduce resistance.

sensation.feelHere: A burn on the outer hip, a hand's width below the hip bone, on the leading leg.
sensation.notHere: The front of your hip, your low back, or your knees from the mini-squat position.
sensation.firstCue: Stay low in the mini-squat and step wide against band tension. Move slow and controlled.

wrongSpot.felt: Front of the hip or thigh
wrongSpot.fix: You're rotating your pelvis or letting your toes turn out instead of isolating the hip. Keep toes forward and hips square.
You stood up out of the squat, or you're leaning your torso to help step. Stay low and keep your chest tall and still.
Your knees are caving inward as you step. Keep pressing them outward against the band the entire time.

wrongSpot.felt: Barely feel it in the hip
wrongSpot.fix: You stood too tall, which removes the band tension and the effort. Sink deeper into the mini-squat and stay there the whole set.

sensation.nextDay: A burn on the outer hip and glute for 1–2 days; the front thigh may ache lightly too.
sensation.stopIf: Sharp pinching in the hip joint itself, or any knee pain that doesn't ease with a wider stance.

mistakes.right: Stay in the mini-squat for the entire set; standing up removes the tension and the point of the exercise.
Keep constant band tension — never let your feet touch or fully close the gap.

mistakes.wrong: Toes turning outward as you tire
mistakes.right: Keep toes pointing forward throughout to keep the work in the outer hip, not the front of the hip.

name: Banded Pull-Apart
instructions: Stand tall with feet shoulder-width apart. Hold a resistance band in front of you at chest height with both hands, palms facing down. Your hands should be shoulder-width apart with slight tension already in the band.
Keep your arms straight. Take a breath in. As you exhale, pull the band apart by moving your hands outward and backward, squeezing your shoulder blades together.
Pull until the band touches your chest (or as far as your range of motion allows) and your arms are out to your sides. Squeeze your shoulder blades together firmly at this end position.
Hold for one second, feeling the contraction in your upper back and rear delts. Then inhale and slowly return to the starting position with control.
Keep your arms as straight as possible throughout — avoid bending the elbows to compensate.
cues: Keep arms straight and initiate the pull from your shoulder blades, not your biceps
Squeeze your shoulder blades together at the end range — that is where the benefit is
Stand tall — do not lean back or shrug your shoulders to pull the band
modification: Use a lighter band or widen your grip (hands further apart) to reduce resistance.

sensation.feelHere: Between your shoulder blades and the back of your shoulders as your hands pull apart.
sensation.notHere: Your biceps or the top of your traps. Those mean the arms or shoulders are compensating.
sensation.firstCue: Pull from your shoulder blades first, arms stay straight. Hold one second at the end.

wrongSpot.fix: You're bending your elbows to help. Keep your arms straight and start the pull by squeezing the shoulder blades.
You're shrugging or leaning back to pull. Stand tall and keep your shoulders down away from your ears.
You're gripping the band too hard. Relax your hands — they only need to hold the ends.
You're pulling the band too high, near your face. Keep it at chest height throughout the movement.

sensation.nextDay: A light ache between the shoulder blades for a day, if any at all — this is a light exercise.
sensation.stopIf: Sharp pinching in the shoulder joint, or numbness or tingling anywhere in the arm.

mistakes.right: Keep your arms straight throughout — the movement should come entirely from your shoulder blades.
Stand tall and stationary. Let your upper back muscles do the pulling, not body lean.
Slow down and hold the squeeze for a full second at the end of each pull.

name: Dumbbell Rear Delt Fly
instructions: Stand with feet hip-width apart, holding a 10 lb dumbbell in each hand. Hinge at the hips until your torso is at roughly a 45-degree angle — back flat, neutral spine, knees soft.
Let the dumbbells hang directly below your chest, palms facing each other. This is your starting position. Take a breath here and reset your brace.
As you exhale, raise both arms out to the sides in a wide arc, leading with your elbows rather than your hands. Stop when your arms are parallel to the floor.
At the top of the movement, turn your thumbs slightly upward — this external rotation fully engages the rear delts and rotator cuff. Pause for one second.
Inhale and slowly lower the dumbbells back to the starting position over 2 seconds. Control the descent — the lowering phase is where the rear delts do the most work.
cues: Lead with your elbows, not your hands — this keeps the rear delts doing the work instead of the traps
Do not shrug your shoulders or hike them toward your ears at the top
If you cannot control the weight on the way down, the dumbbell is too heavy — these should feel light
modification: Perform seated at the edge of a chair with your torso folded forward over your thighs — this removes the hip hinge demand and makes it easier to isolate the rear delts.

sensation.feelHere: The back of your shoulders, with a light burn at the top as your thumbs turn up.
sensation.notHere: Your upper traps near the base of your neck. That's a sign of shrugging, not lifting.
sensation.firstCue: Lead with your elbows in a wide arc. Lower slow — 2 seconds down.

wrongSpot.fix: You're shrugging your shoulders up. Keep them pressed down and go lighter if you can't stop it.
You're leading with your hands instead of your elbows. Widen the arc and think elbows first.
You're gripping the dumbbells too hard. Hold them loosely — the hand is just along for the ride.
Your hinge is sagging under fatigue. Try the seated version, which removes the hip-hinge demand entirely.

sensation.nextDay: A light ache across the back of the shoulders for a day. This exercise should feel light, not heavy.
sensation.backNote: Holding a hip hinge for high reps can fatigue the low back. Switch to the seated version if it starts to ache.
sensation.stopIf: Any pain shooting down a leg or arm, or sharp low-back pain during the set.

mistakes.right: Lead every rep with your elbows moving out wide — the hands should trail behind them.
Keep your shoulders pulled down throughout. Turn thumbs up only at the very top for external rotation.

mistakes.wrong: Using a weight too heavy to control on the way down
mistakes.right: Go lighter — the slow lowering phase is where this exercise works the rear delts most.

name: Side Plank
instructions: Lie on your right side with your legs straight and stacked on top of each other. Place your right forearm on the mat, elbow directly under your right shoulder.

Engage your core and lift your hips off the floor, creating a straight diagonal line from your head through your hips to your feet. Your body should form a plank — do not let your hips sag toward the floor.
Stack your feet or place the top foot slightly in front of the bottom foot for balance. Your top arm can rest on your hip or extend toward the ceiling.
Hold this position for 20 seconds. Breathe steadily — do not hold your breath. Keep your hips up and your core braced throughout.
Lower with control and repeat on the left side. Each side counts as one set.
cues: Keep hips lifted — hip sag removes the anti-lateral flexion challenge
Press your forearm into the mat and think of pushing the floor away to engage your shoulder
Breathe normally — holding your breath increases internal pressure unnecessarily
modification: Perform with knees bent and stacked — the bottom knee acts as a kickstand reducing the load significantly.

sensation.feelHere: A burning squeeze along the side of your torso, from ribs to hip, on the down side.
sensation.notHere: The point of your bottom shoulder, or your low back.
sensation.firstCue: Push the floor away through your forearm. Lift your hips for a slow 3 count.

wrongSpot.fix: You're sagging into the joint. Actively push your forearm into the mat to lift through the shoulder, not rest on it.
Your hips have dropped or rotated. Stack hips and shoulders vertically and lift them higher before holding.
Keep your head in line with your spine — don't let it drop toward the floor or crane up.
Your hips are likely sagging toward the floor, taking the load off. Lift them until your body forms a straight line.

sensation.nextDay: A burn along the side of the torso for a day or two is normal. Shoulder or low-back soreness is not.
sensation.backNote: Hips dropping or rotating shifts load into the low back. If you can't keep a straight line, drop to the bent-knee version rather than holding a sagging shape.
sensation.stopIf: Any shooting or electric pain, or numbness or tingling in an arm or leg.

mistakes.right: Lift your hips until head, hips, and feet form one straight diagonal line.
Push your forearm into the mat to actively lift, rather than letting your shoulder collapse.
Breathe steadily throughout the hold instead of bracing by holding air in.

name: Forearm Plank
instructions: Start by kneeling on the mat. Place your forearms on the mat shoulder-width apart, elbows directly under your shoulders. Clasp your hands together or keep forearms parallel.
Step your feet back, one at a time, until your body forms a straight line from head to heels. Your toes are curled under on the mat.
Brace your core by drawing your belly button in slightly and squeezing your glutes. Your hips should be level — not raised into the air or sagging toward the floor.
Hold this position for 25 seconds, breathing steadily through your nose. Keep your head neutral — do not look up or drop your chin into your chest.
Lower to your knees with control when the time is up. Rest and repeat.
cues: Squeeze your glutes — this protects your lower back and stabilizes your pelvis
Straight line from head to heels — use a mirror or ask someone to check your form
Push your forearms into the floor — this activates your shoulder stabilizers and prevents sagging
modification: Drop to your knees for a forearm plank from knees. Keep your hips in line with your knees and shoulders.

sensation.feelHere: A deep bracing burn across your stomach, plus your shoulders and glutes working.
sensation.notHere: An ache across your low back — that means your hips have sagged.
sensation.firstCue: Squeeze your glutes and tuck your hips slightly. Breathe steadily through your nose.

wrongSpot.fix: Your hips are sagging. Tuck your pelvis slightly, squeeze your glutes, and pull your ribs down.
Shorten the hold to whatever time you can keep that tucked shape — 10–20 seconds done well beats 60 seconds sagging.
Push your forearms into the floor rather than letting your chest sink between them.
Keep your head neutral, eyes down at the floor — don't look up or tuck your chin.

sensation.nextDay: A deep ab burn or mild shoulder fatigue for a day is normal. Low back soreness is not.
sensation.backNote: Sagging hips let the spine hang instead of the abs holding, loading the low back. Tuck the pelvis and squeeze the glutes, or hold for less time with the right shape.
sensation.stopIf: Any shooting or electric pain, or numbness or tingling in an arm or leg.

mistakes.right: Tuck your pelvis slightly and squeeze your glutes to keep hips level, even if that shortens your hold time.
Lower your hips until your body forms one straight line from head to heels.
Hold only as long as you can keep the tucked, level shape — a short good hold beats a long sagging one.

name: Single-Leg Glute Bridge
instructions: Lie on your back with knees bent and feet flat on the floor, hip-width apart. Extend your right leg straight up toward the ceiling (or keep a slight bend in the knee).
Press your lower back into the mat and brace your core. Drive through your left heel and squeeze your left glute to lift your hips off the floor.
Rise until your body forms a straight line from your left knee through your hips to your shoulders. Your hips should stay level — resist the temptation to let the right side drop lower.
Hold at the top for 2 seconds, squeezing your glute. Then lower your hips slowly back to the mat with control.
Complete all reps on the left side, then switch: right foot drives, left leg extends. Count each side separately.
cues: Keep your hips level — the raised-leg side will want to dip, so consciously push both hips to the same height
Drive through the planted heel, not the ball of the foot
This is much harder than a standard bridge — reduce reps if needed to maintain perfect form
modification: Keep the extended leg bent at 90 degrees (foot toward ceiling) rather than straight to reduce the balance challenge.

sensation.feelHere: The glute of your planted leg, working much harder than the two-leg version, plus core bracing.
sensation.notHere: Your low back, or the hamstring of the planted leg cramping.
sensation.firstCue: Press through the planted heel and keep both hips level. Move slow, no rushing.

wrongSpot.fix: You lifted too high, arching to compensate for the missing second leg. Stop at a straight line from shoulders to knee, no higher.

wrongSpot.felt: Hip of the raised leg dips or drops
wrongSpot.fix: You're letting that side sag instead of holding it level. Consciously push both hips to the same height throughout.

wrongSpot.felt: Hamstring cramping on the planted leg
wrongSpot.fix: Your planted foot is too far from your hips. Walk it in closer until shins are near vertical at the top.
You're rotating the pelvis to help lift. Keep your hips square to the ceiling and slow the rep down.

sensation.nextDay: A stronger glute ache than the two-leg bridge, one side more than the other, is expected.
sensation.backNote: The single-leg version tempts you to arch or twist to make up for the lost support. Lift from the hip only; stop at a straight line, don't overreach for height.
sensation.stopIf: Anything travels down either leg, or your low back pinches or twists sharply.

mistakes.wrong: Hips sagging on the raised-leg side
mistakes.right: Push both hips to the same height the entire rep — check by feel, not a mirror.

mistakes.wrong: Arching the back to gain height
mistakes.right: Stop at a straight line from shoulders to knee; do not push higher by arching.
Slow down — a controlled tempo is what keeps the pelvis from rotating or dropping.

name: Glute Bridge Isometric Hold
instructions: Lie on your back with knees bent and feet flat on the floor, hip-width apart. Arms rest at your sides.
Press your lower back gently into the mat. Drive through both heels and squeeze your glutes to lift your hips off the floor until you form a straight line from knees to shoulders.
Hold this top position for the full 30 seconds. Keep squeezing your glutes continuously — do not relax them mid-hold. Breathe steadily.
Keep your hips level throughout — do not let one side drop. Your core should be actively engaged.
Lower slowly after the hold. Rest and repeat.
cues: Keep squeezing your glutes for the entire hold — this is an active contraction, not a passive hang
Breathe — inhale through your nose, exhale through your mouth, do not hold your breath
If your hips start to shake or drop, you have reached your limit — lower with control
modification: Reduce the hold to 15 seconds and build up over time.

sensation.feelHere: A building, steady burn in the glutes that intensifies the longer you hold the top position.
sensation.notHere: Your low back, and not a shaking, cramping feeling in your hamstrings.
sensation.firstCue: Keep actively squeezing the glutes the whole hold — don't just hang there. Breathe steadily.

wrongSpot.fix: Your feet are too far from your hips. Walk your heels in until your fingertips can just graze them.
You're holding too high and arching instead of extending the hip. Drop to a straight line from shoulders to knees and stay there.
You stopped actively squeezing. Keep the glutes contracted hard for the entire hold, not just at the start.
You're pressing weight into your toes instead of your heels. Shift your weight back onto your heels.

sensation.nextDay: A deep, fatigued glute ache — like the end of a hard set — for 1–2 days.
sensation.backNote: An isometric hold is spine-friendly, but only if the hip stays where it started. Do not let fatigue pull you into an arch — end the hold before that happens.
sensation.stopIf: Anything travels down your leg, or your low back pinches or arches involuntarily as you fatigue.

mistakes.right: Keep actively squeezing the glutes for the entire duration, not just the first few seconds.

mistakes.wrong: Holding too high with an arched back
mistakes.right: Settle at a straight line from shoulders to knees and stop there for the whole hold.
Breathe steadily throughout — inhale through the nose, exhale through the mouth, do not brace by holding air.

name: Modified Pigeon Pose
instructions: Lie on your back with both knees bent and feet flat on the floor. This is the supine (lying-down) version of pigeon, which is safer for the lower back than the traditional floor version.
Cross your right ankle over your left thigh, just above the knee. Flex your right foot (point toes toward your shin) to protect your knee joint.
Reach both hands behind your left thigh and gently draw your left leg toward your chest. You will feel a deep stretch in the outer right hip and glute.
Hold this position for 40 seconds, breathing slowly and deeply. With each exhale, allow your body to relax into the stretch a little more — do not force it.
Lower both feet back to the floor slowly and repeat on the other side (left ankle over right thigh).
cues: Keep your right foot flexed throughout to protect the knee joint — do not let the foot go limp
Breathe into the stretch — tension in your breath creates tension in the muscle
If you cannot reach your thigh comfortably, loop a towel or strap around it
modification: Keep the bottom foot on the floor (without pulling the leg in) to reduce the intensity of the stretch.

sensation.feelHere: A broad, deep pulling stretch across the outer hip and glute of the crossed leg.
sensation.notHere: Tingling, electric, or burning sensations travelling down the back of the leg — that's nerve tension, not a stretch.
sensation.backNote: Your low back stays flat on the floor throughout. If it's arching to compensate, pull the leg in less.
sensation.stopIf: Any tingling, numbness, or shooting sensation down the leg. Should feel like a firm pull, never a sharp one.

name: Supine Figure-4 Stretch
instructions: Lie on your back with both knees bent, feet flat on the floor. Cross your right ankle over your left knee to form a figure-4 shape. Flex your right foot.
Let your right knee fall gently to the right — you should feel an immediate stretch in the outer right hip. If this is already deep enough, stay here.

For a deeper stretch: Reach your right hand through the gap between your legs and your left hand around the outside of your left thigh. Clasp your hands behind your left thigh and gently pull it toward your chest.
Hold for 40 seconds, breathing deeply. Your entire back stays flat on the mat throughout — do not let your hips rock to one side.
Release and switch sides: left ankle over right knee.
cues: Flex your top foot (toes toward shin) to protect the knee joint
Your back stays flat on the mat — do not let your hips twist
This targets the piriformis — a small muscle deep in the glute that can contribute to sciatic irritation
modification: Keep the bottom foot on the floor without pulling in and just let the crossed-knee drop open passively.

sensation.feelHere: A broad, deep pulling stretch in the outer hip and glute of the crossed leg.
sensation.notHere: Tingling or electric sensations running down the back of the leg — this stretch sits close to the sciatic nerve, so back off if you feel it.
sensation.backNote: Keep your back flat on the mat and hips square. If your hips rock to one side, pull the leg in less.
sensation.stopIf: Any tingling, numbness, or shooting pain down the leg. This is not a 'push through it' sensation — ease off immediately.

name: Child's Pose
instructions: Kneel on your mat with your big toes touching and knees apart (wider for a hip-opening variation, together for a lower back focus). Sit back onto your heels.
Walk your hands forward as far as you can, lowering your chest toward the floor between your thighs. Let your forehead rest on the mat.
Extend your arms as far forward as comfortable, feeling a lengthening through your spine and a gentle opening through your hips and lower back.
