Hold for 40 seconds, breathing deeply. Each exhale, allow your hips to sink a little heavier toward your heels and your chest a little lower toward the floor.
To come out, walk your hands back and slowly rise up, supporting yourself with your hands.
cues: Allow gravity to do the work — this is a passive, restful stretch, not an active effort
Breathe into your back body — try to feel your back ribs expand with each inhale
Wider knees gives more hip opening; narrower knees focuses the stretch more on the spine
modification: Place a folded blanket or pillow between your thighs and calves if sitting back onto heels is uncomfortable.

sensation.feelHere: A gentle lengthening across your low back and a light opening through your hips and shoulders.
sensation.notHere: Sharp pinching pain in the low back — this pose should feel restful, not straining.
sensation.backNote: This is a passive, supported position — let gravity do the work rather than actively pushing into it.
sensation.stopIf: Any sharp back pain, or tingling or numbness in the legs.

name: Doorway Chest Stretch
instructions: Stand in a doorway. Raise both arms to shoulder height and bend your elbows to 90 degrees, placing your forearms vertically against the door frame on each side.
Step one foot forward through the doorway so you are in a staggered stance. Keep your core lightly engaged and spine tall.
Gently lean your body forward through the doorway until you feel a stretch across your chest and the front of your shoulders. Do not push aggressively — let the stretch come gradually.
Hold for 30 seconds. Breathe steadily and relax into the stretch with each exhale. Your forearms stay on the door frame throughout.
Step back to release. You can also perform this one arm at a time for a unilateral variation.
cues: Keep your elbows at shoulder height — lower elbows target the lower pec, higher elbows target the upper pec
Lean forward gently — this is not a stretch you force; let gravity and your lean do the work
Stand tall — do not let your lower back arch excessively as you lean
modification: Perform with one arm at a time using a wall corner if a full doorway is not available.

sensation.feelHere: A broad pulling stretch across the chest and the front of the shoulders.
sensation.notHere: A pinch deep inside the shoulder joint — that means you're leaning too far or too fast, not stretching the muscle.
sensation.backNote: Stand tall as you lean. Don't let your low back arch to reach further into the doorway.
sensation.stopIf: Sharp shoulder pain, or tingling or numbness down the arm. Should feel like a firm pull, never a sharp one.

name: Seated Hamstring Stretch
instructions: Sit on the floor on your mat with both legs extended straight out in front of you. Sit up as tall as possible — if your back rounds heavily, sit on a folded blanket or towel to tilt your pelvis forward.
Flex both feet so your toes point toward the ceiling. Take a breath in and sit even taller through your spine.
As you exhale, hinge forward from your hips (not by rounding your back) to reach your hands toward your feet. Reach as far as comfortable — your shins, ankles, or feet.
Hold this position for 40 seconds, keeping a long spine. Breathe steadily — with each exhale, try to hinge a little further forward from the hip.
To come out, press your hands into the floor beside you and sit up slowly.
cues: Hinge from your hips, not your back — think of your torso tilting forward as a unit, spine long
If you can barely reach your shins, that is perfectly fine — hamstring flexibility takes weeks to build
Flex your feet actively — pointing toes reduces the hamstring stretch
modification: Loop a towel or resistance band around your feet and hold the ends to bridge the gap if you cannot reach your feet.

sensation.feelHere: A broad pulling stretch along the back of the thigh, from behind the knee up toward the sit bone.
sensation.notHere: Tingling, electric, or burning sensation running down the back of the leg — that's the sciatic nerve, not a hamstring stretch, and it means back off immediately.
sensation.backNote: Hinge from your hips with a long spine rather than rounding your low back to reach further.
sensation.stopIf: Any tingling, numbness, or shooting sensation down the leg. Should feel like a firm pull, never a sharp one.

name: Kneeling Hip Flexor Stretch
instructions: Kneel on your mat with your right knee on the floor directly under your right hip. Step your left foot forward so your left knee is at 90 degrees directly over your left ankle — a half-kneeling position. Use a folded blanket under your right knee if it is uncomfortable.

Sit tall, lengthen your spine, and gently tuck your pelvis slightly under (posterior pelvic tilt) — this is the key step that actually creates the hip flexor stretch. Without the tuck, the stretch is minimal.
Shift your hips slightly forward (not by leaning your torso, but by sliding your hips) until you feel a stretch in the front of your right hip.
Hold for 40 seconds. Breathe steadily and try to deepen the pelvic tuck slightly with each exhale to intensify the stretch.
Switch sides: left knee on floor, right foot forward.
cues: Tuck your pelvis under (flatten your lower back) — this is what creates the stretch, not just leaning forward
Keep your torso upright — do not lean your chest toward your front knee
The stretch should be felt in the front of the back-leg hip, not in the front knee
modification: Place a folded towel under your kneeling knee for cushioning. Reduce the forward shift if the stretch is too intense.

sensation.feelHere: A broad pulling stretch across the front of the hip and upper thigh of the back leg.
sensation.notHere: Pain in the front of the kneeling knee — that's the joint being loaded, not the hip flexor stretching.
sensation.backNote: Tuck your pelvis under and keep your torso upright. Don't arch your low back to lean forward.
sensation.stopIf: Sharp knee or back pain, or any tingling down the leg. Should feel like a firm pull, never a sharp one.

name: Standing Quad Stretch
instructions: Stand tall near a wall or chair for balance support. Shift your weight onto your left foot.

Bend your right knee and bring your right heel toward your right glute. Reach back with your right hand and hold your right ankle or the top of your foot. If you cannot reach, loop a towel around your ankle.
Keep your knees together — your right knee should point straight down toward the floor, not out to the side. Keep your torso upright and core lightly engaged.
Hold for 30 seconds. You should feel a stretch along the front of your right thigh. Avoid pulling so hard that your knee lifts or your foot pulls away from center.
Lower your foot and switch sides.
cues: Keep both knees side by side — pulling your knee out to the side changes the stretch target
Stand tall — do not lean forward or arch your lower back
Use a wall for balance; wobbling reduces the quality of the stretch
modification: Lie face-down on the mat and bend one knee, reaching back to hold the ankle — this removes the balance challenge entirely.

sensation.feelHere: A broad pulling stretch down the front of the thigh from hip to knee.
sensation.notHere: Sharp pain at the front of the knee — that means you're pulling the heel too hard, not lengthening the thigh.
sensation.backNote: Stand tall. Don't arch your low back to compensate for a tight hip.
sensation.stopIf: Sharp knee pain, or any tingling down the leg. Should feel like a firm pull, never a sharp one.

name: Dumbbell Single-Arm Row
instructions: Stand in a staggered stance — left foot forward, right foot back. Hinge forward from the hips until your torso is roughly parallel to the floor. Rest your left hand on your left knee for support. Hold a 15 lb dumbbell in your right hand, arm hanging straight down.
Brace your core and keep your back flat. At the bottom, let the dumbbell pull your shoulder blade slightly forward — this is the full stretch position.
As you exhale, drive your right elbow up and back toward the ceiling. Think 'elbow to the sky,' not 'hand to my hip.' Keep the dumbbell close to your body.
Pull until your elbow is level with or just above your torso and your shoulder blade is fully retracted — squeezed in toward your spine. Pause briefly.
Inhale and slowly lower the dumbbell back to the full stretch over 2 seconds. Complete all reps on the right side, then switch your stance and repeat on the left.
cues: Drive the elbow, not the hand — your forearm is just a hook connecting you to the weight
Keep the non-working shoulder square and level — do not rotate your torso to help the lift
Full stretch at the bottom is as important as the squeeze at the top
modification: Use the 10 lb dumbbell or reduce reps to 8 per side while your back strength builds.

sensation.feelHere: The side and middle of your back, under and behind the armpit on the working side.
sensation.notHere: Your biceps, your forearm, or your low back. All three mean the back is being bypassed.
sensation.firstCue: Pull your shoulder blade back first. Let the elbow follow, not lead.

wrongSpot.fix: You are curling. Start each rep by sliding the shoulder blade toward your spine, then bend the elbow.
You are gripping too hard, or the weight is too heavy. Loosen the hand and go lighter.
Your torso is twisting or rounding. Set your ribs down, square your shoulders, and lower the weight.
You are letting the shoulder roll forward at the bottom. Stop the lowering a little earlier.

sensation.nextDay: Soreness under the armpit and along the side of the back for 1–2 days is a good sign.
sensation.backNote: Keep your spine still — the arm moves, the back does not. If your torso twists to finish a rep, that rep was too heavy.
sensation.stopIf: You get pain travelling down your leg, or any electric or burning sensation in the back.

name: Prone Y-T-W
instructions: Lie face down on your mat with your forehead resting on a folded towel or your hands. Engage your core lightly to protect your lower back throughout all three positions.
Y position: Raise both arms overhead in a wide V shape with thumbs pointing toward the ceiling. Lift just your arms off the mat 2–3 inches, hold 2 seconds, lower. This targets the lower trapezius.

T position: Bring your arms straight out to your sides at shoulder height, forming a T shape with thumbs up. Lift both arms 2–3 inches, hold 2 seconds, lower. This targets the middle trapezius and rear deltoids.

W position: Bend your elbows to 90 degrees and raise them beside your head in a W shape with elbows wide. Squeeze your shoulder blades together as you lift. Hold 2 seconds, lower. This targets the rotator cuff and lower trap.

Complete 8 reps of each shape (Y then T then W) in sequence — that is one full set. Move slowly and with control. The range of motion is small; only lift as high as you can without straining your neck.
cues: Thumbs point toward the ceiling in each position — this externally rotates the shoulder
Only lift your arms — do not arch your lower back or lift your chest off the mat
Movements are small and controlled — this is shoulder activation work, not a power exercise
modification: Perform one arm at a time, resting the other at your side. Reduce the hold time to 1 second if your shoulder fatigues quickly.

sensation.feelHere: A light, targeted burn between your shoulder blades and along the back of your shoulders.
sensation.notHere: Your neck or lower back straining. Those mean you're lifting your head or arching too much.
sensation.firstCue: Lift only 2–3 inches, thumbs up. Hold 2 seconds — smaller and slower beats bigger.

wrongSpot.fix: You're moving too big or too fast. Shrink the range to 2–3 inches and hold each position for a full 2 seconds.
You're lifting your head to help. Keep your forehead down and let only your arms lift.
You're arching to lift your chest off the mat. Keep your core lightly braced and your chest down.
Your thumbs aren't turned up. Rotate them toward the ceiling in each of the three positions.

sensation.nextDay: Little to no soreness is normal — this is light activation work, not a strength builder.
sensation.backNote: Light core bracing protects your low back here, but the risk is arching to lift higher. Keep the lift small and let your chest stay on the mat.
sensation.stopIf: Any pinching in the shoulder joint, or numbness or tingling in your hands or arms.

mistakes.wrong: Moving too fast through all three shapes
mistakes.right: Slow down. Hold each of the Y, T, and W positions for a full 2 seconds before lowering.

mistakes.wrong: Lifting the chest or head off the mat
mistakes.right: Keep your forehead and chest down — only your arms should lift a few inches.
A small 2–3 inch range is enough. Higher just recruits your low back instead of your upper back.

name: Supine Spinal Twist
instructions: Lie on your back on the mat with both legs straight. Draw your right knee in toward your chest and hold it briefly.
Cross your right knee over your body to the left side, guiding it gently with your left hand. Aim to bring your right knee toward the floor on the left side — it does not need to touch the floor.
Extend your right arm straight out to the right at shoulder height, palm facing up. Turn your head to look toward your right hand. This is the full twist position.

Hold for 40 seconds, breathing slowly and deeply. With each exhale, allow the twist to deepen slightly. Your right shoulder should remain in contact with the mat — if it lifts, reduce how far the knee crosses.
Release slowly and switch sides: left knee crosses to the right, left arm extends, head turns left.
cues: Keep both shoulders flat on the mat — if one lifts, reduce the depth of the twist
Breathe into the twist — tension in your breath creates tension in the muscle
Let gravity do the work — do not force the knee down with your hand
modification: Place a pillow or folded blanket under your crossed knee to reduce the depth of the twist if it feels too intense in the lower back.

sensation.feelHere: A broad, gentle stretch through the side of your torso and outer hip as the knee crosses over.
sensation.notHere: Sharp pinching pain in the low back — that means the twist has gone deeper than your spine is ready for today.
sensation.backNote: Keep both shoulders flat on the mat. If one lifts, you've twisted further than your back is ready for — let it settle less.
sensation.stopIf: Any sharp low-back pain, or tingling or numbness down either leg.

name: 90/90 Hip Stretch
instructions: Sit on the floor on your mat. Bend your right leg in front of you with your shin roughly at a 90-degree angle to your thigh. Bend your left leg to the side with your shin also at 90 degrees behind you. Both hips should be on or close to the floor.
Sit as tall as possible. You will feel a stretch in the outside of your front hip (right glute and external rotators) and across the inside of your back hip (left hip flexor and internal rotators).

Place your hands on the floor beside you for support. Take a breath in and sit even taller through your spine. As you exhale, hinge slightly forward at the hip over your front leg — lean from your hip, not by rounding your back.
Hold for 40 seconds, breathing steadily. Focus on sitting tall and gradually relaxing into the stretch rather than forcing a deep fold.
To switch sides, lift both knees, pivot, and place your left shin in front and your right shin behind. Repeat on the other side.
cues: Keep both sit bones in contact with the floor — if one hip floats up, reduce the angle of the back leg
Sit tall before folding — rounding your lower back early takes the stretch away from the hips
This stretch targets both internal and external hip rotation simultaneously — normal to feel it in different spots
modification: Sit with your back against a wall for posture support. Place folded blankets under both thighs if your hips are very tight.

sensation.feelHere: A broad stretch across the outer hip of the front leg and the inner hip of the back leg.
sensation.notHere: Sharp pinching pain deep in either hip joint — that's a range problem, not a muscle stretching.
sensation.backNote: Sit tall before you fold forward. Rounding your low back early pulls the stretch away from the hips.
sensation.stopIf: Sharp hip joint pain, or any tingling down either leg.

name: Single-Leg Balance Hold
instructions: Stand tall near a wall or stable surface within arm's reach for safety. Shift your weight onto your right foot and stand with your right knee very slightly soft — never fully locked.

Lift your left foot off the floor, bending the left knee to about 90 degrees so your left thigh is roughly parallel to the floor. Keep your hips level — resist the urge to let your left hip drop lower than your right.
Fix your gaze on a single stationary point at eye level. This focal point dramatically improves balance. Keep your arms relaxed at your sides.
Hold for 30 seconds without touching the wall. If you feel yourself tipping, allow a brief fingertip touch — the goal is to need it less and less over time. Breathe normally throughout.
Switch feet and repeat on the left leg. Both sides count as one set.
cues: Pick a focal point and do not look down — eyes down is the most common cause of wobbling
Keep your hips level — the raised-leg hip wants to drop, actively hold it even
Small ankle adjustments are normal and healthy — your ankle is supposed to be working
modification: Keep your fingertips lightly on the wall throughout. Progress to fingertip touch only, then no contact. For an advanced challenge, close your eyes.

sensation.feelHere: Small, constant corrections in your standing foot and ankle — not a burn.
sensation.notHere: A muscle burn anywhere, or your standing knee aching.
sensation.firstCue: Pick one still point at eye level and fix your gaze there. Keep hips level.

wrongSpot.fix: Your knee is locked out. Keep it very slightly soft, never fully straight.
Actively hold that hip level with the other one — don't let it sink lower.
You're likely looking down. Fix your gaze on one still spot at eye level instead.
It's too easy. Close your eyes, or bring fingertip support away from the wall.

sensation.nextDay: No real soreness expected — maybe mild ankle fatigue. Knee or hip pain the next day is not normal.
sensation.stopIf: Sharp pain in the standing knee or ankle, or true dizziness rather than normal wobble.

mistakes.right: Keep a very slight, soft bend in the standing knee throughout the hold.
Fix your eyes on one still point at eye level — looking down is the top cause of wobbling.
Actively keep both hips level, resisting the raised-leg side sinking lower.

name: Bodyweight Calf Raise
instructions: Stand with your feet hip-width apart near a wall or stable surface for light balance support. Place your fingertips lightly on the surface — do not hold or press, just use it for balance.
Press through the balls of both feet to rise onto your toes as high as possible. Pause at the top for one full second, feeling the contraction in your calves.
Slowly lower your heels back to the floor over 2–3 seconds. This slow lowering is the most important part — eccentric loading of the Achilles tendon is the primary strengthening stimulus.
Your heels should fully return to the floor between reps — do not bounce or spring from the bottom. A brief pause at the floor before each rep ensures full range of motion.
Complete 15 reps per set. As this becomes easy, progress to single-leg calf raises: same movement on one foot at a time with the other foot lightly resting against your ankle.
cues: Rise as high as you can — maximum height engages the full calf and Achilles range
Lower slowly — 2–3 seconds on the way down is where the real strengthening happens
Keep your knees straight throughout — bending them shifts the load from gastrocnemius to soleus
modification: Reduce to 10 reps per set. For greater range of motion, stand on the edge of a step with heels hanging slightly off.

sensation.feelHere: A burn in the meat of your calf, both the upper bulge and lower toward the ankle.
sensation.notHere: Your Achilles tendon or the arch of your foot — sharp pain there is a tendon signal, not muscle work.
sensation.firstCue: Rise as high as you can. Lower over a slow 3 count.

wrongSpot.fix: Reduce your range slightly and rise less explosively; sharp tendon pain means back off, not push through.
Press through the ball of your foot evenly rather than rolling onto your big toe.
You may be leaning too far forward. Keep your weight stacked over the balls of your feet.
Keep your knees straight but not locked, and make sure you're not bending them to assist.

sensation.nextDay: A deep calf ache for 1–2 days is normal, especially after the slow lowering. Achilles soreness is not.
sensation.stopIf: Sharp Achilles pain, or any pain that feels like a pull rather than a burn.

mistakes.right: Pause briefly with heels down before each rep instead of springing up.
Rise as high onto your toes as you can to get the full range.
Keep your knees straight throughout so the calf, not the knee, does the work.

name: TRX Row
instructions: Set TRX straps to mid-length. Stand facing the anchor point and hold both handles with an overhand grip, palms facing down. Walk your feet toward the anchor until your body is at about 45 degrees to the floor — the more horizontal, the harder the row.
Hang with arms fully extended, body in a straight line from heels to shoulders. Your heels are on the floor. Brace your core and squeeze your glutes to keep your body rigid like a plank.
Take a breath in. As you exhale, drive both elbows back toward your hips, rowing your chest up toward the handles. Keep your body in a straight plank throughout — do not let your hips sag or pike.
Pull until your chest reaches the handles and your elbows are behind your torso. Squeeze your shoulder blades together firmly at this top position and hold for one second.
Inhale and lower yourself back to the fully extended starting position with control. Your body stays rigid throughout — only your arms and shoulder blades should move.
cues: Keep your body in a rigid plank — if your hips drop, you lose the core challenge and reduce back activation
Drive your elbows toward your back pockets, not straight up toward the ceiling
Walk your feet in (more horizontal) to make it harder; walk feet back (more upright) to make it easier
modification: Walk your feet back toward vertical to reduce difficulty. Beginners should start at a 60-70 degree angle from the floor.

sensation.feelHere: Your mid and upper back, between the shoulder blades, plus your core holding the plank.
sensation.notHere: Your low back aching. That means the plank is breaking down, not the back working.
sensation.firstCue: Squeeze shoulder blades together first, then pull. Keep hips locked in a straight line.

wrongSpot.fix: Your hips are sagging. Brace your core and squeeze your glutes to keep a straight line from heels to shoulders.
You're pulling with the arms first. Initiate by drawing the shoulder blades back before bending the elbows.
You've walked too close to the anchor for your current strength. Step back toward vertical to lighten the load.
You're shrugging up as you pull. Keep your shoulders pulled down away from your ears.

sensation.nextDay: A broad ache across the upper back and core for 1–2 days is normal after this one.
sensation.backNote: If your hips sag or pike, your low back takes the strain instead of your core. Walk your feet toward vertical until you can hold a straight line.
sensation.stopIf: Sharp low-back pain, or any pain shooting down a leg. Stop and reset your plank.

mistakes.right: Brace your core and squeeze your glutes hard to keep a rigid plank throughout every rep.
Drive the elbows back toward your hips and lead the pull with your shoulder blades.

mistakes.wrong: Feet too close to anchor for your level
mistakes.right: Walk your feet back toward vertical until you can complete all reps with good form.

name: TRX Push-Up
instructions: Set TRX straps to mid-length with handles at about knee height. Face away from the anchor. Place both hands in the TRX handles, arms extended, and step back until you are in a high plank position at roughly 45 degrees to the floor.

Hands directly below shoulders, wrists neutral, core braced, body in a rigid line from head to heels. The handles will swing slightly — actively resist this instability with your core and shoulder stabilizers.
Take a breath in. Bend your elbows at roughly 45 degrees and lower your chest toward the handles in a controlled push-up. The straps will oscillate — resist this throughout.
Lower until your chest is level with the handles or your elbows reach 90 degrees. Do not let your hips sag or elbows flare wide.
Press forcefully back to the starting position, exhaling as you push. Fully extend your arms without locking your elbows. Reset your form before the next rep.
cues: Keep your body rigid throughout — TRX push-ups immediately expose any form breakdown
Elbows at 45 degrees, not flared wide — same mechanics as a floor push-up
Walk your feet further from the anchor (more upright) to make it easier if the instability is too great
modification: Walk your feet back away from the anchor to a more upright position, reducing the load significantly. Master floor push-ups first and use TRX as a progression.

sensation.feelHere: The middle of your chest, the back of your upper arms, and a deep core burn from stabilizing.
sensation.notHere: The front of your shoulder, or a sharp catch in the shoulder joint as the straps swing.
sensation.firstCue: Keep elbows at 45 degrees and resist the strap sway. Lower for a slow 3 count.

wrongSpot.fix: Elbows are flaring wide. Bring them to about 45 degrees from your torso, same as a floor push-up.
The swing is too much to control. Walk your feet back to a more upright angle to reduce the load and the sway.
Your hips are sagging as the straps move. Brace your core harder and squeeze your glutes throughout.
Keep your wrists neutral in the handles instead of letting them bend under the swinging load.

sensation.nextDay: A broad ache across the chest and a deep core soreness for 1-2 days is normal. Sharp joint pain is not.
sensation.backNote: If your hips sag while resisting the sway, your low back arches to compensate. Keep your core braced and go more upright if you lose that line.
sensation.stopIf: Anything shoots down your arm, or your hand goes numb or tingly.

mistakes.right: Brace your core harder and keep a straight line from head to heels throughout.
Keep them at roughly 45 degrees from your torso, same as a standard push-up.

mistakes.wrong: Fighting the strap swing with speed
mistakes.right: Slow down. A controlled tempo lets your core and shoulders manage the instability.

name: Dumbbell Floor Press
instructions: Lie on your back on the floor with knees bent and feet flat. Hold a 15 lb dumbbell in each hand at chest level, elbows resting on the floor. Your upper arms should form roughly a 45-degree angle to your torso — not splayed straight out to the sides.

Press your lower back gently into the floor and brace your core. Your elbows — not the dumbbells — should be what contacts the floor at the bottom. This natural range-of-motion limit protects your shoulders.
Take a breath in. As you exhale, press both dumbbells up and slightly inward on a slight arc, bringing them closer together as they rise. Stop just before your elbows lock out.
Pause briefly at the top, feeling the contraction across your chest. Then inhale and lower slowly, allowing your elbows to come to rest on the floor.
Pause fully at the bottom before each rep — do not bounce. Each rep starts from a dead stop, which removes momentum and makes the exercise more effective.
cues: Elbows at 45 degrees from your body — not flared to 90 — to protect your shoulder joints
Press up and slightly inward — bring the dumbbells toward each other as they rise to activate the chest
Pause fully at the bottom before each rep — do not bounce off the floor
modification: Use 10 lb dumbbells or reduce reps to 8 while building pressing strength. Focus on the pause at the bottom.

sensation.feelHere: The middle and outer part of your chest, plus the back of your upper arms.
sensation.notHere: The bony front point of your shoulder. That means the wrong muscle is doing the work.
sensation.firstCue: Pin your shoulder blades down into the floor. Lower for a slow 3 count.

wrongSpot.fix: Your shoulder blades are rolling forward. Squeeze them back and down into the floor and hold them there the whole set.
Bring your elbows closer to your ribs — roughly 45 degrees, not straight out sideways.

wrongSpot.felt: Sharp or pinching at the shoulder
wrongSpot.fix: That is the joint, not the muscle. Stop the set. Drop the weight and shorten the range.
Turn your palms to face each other and keep your wrists stacked straight over your elbows.

sensation.nextDay: A broad ache across the chest is normal for 1–3 days. Sharp pinpoint pain is not.
sensation.backNote: This one is deliberately spine-friendly — the floor stops you arching. Keep your low back lightly touching the floor; do not arch to press more weight.
sensation.stopIf: Anything shoots down your arm, or your hand goes numb or tingly.

name: Resistance Band Overhead Press
instructions: Stand on the middle of your resistance band with feet shoulder-width apart. Hold the band ends at shoulder height, palms facing forward, elbows at 90 degrees just below ear level.
Take a breath in and brace your core. Tuck your pelvis slightly to prevent your lower back from arching when you press overhead — this is the most important cue.
As you exhale, press both hands straight up overhead until your arms are nearly fully extended. The band increases resistance as you press — control the movement throughout.
Your arms should finish directly overhead, not angled forward. Pause briefly without locking your elbows.
Inhale and slowly lower the band back to shoulder height over 2-3 seconds. This controlled descent works the shoulders equally to the press.
cues: Core braced and pelvis slightly tucked — do not arch your lower back to complete the press
Press directly overhead, not forward — your arms should finish directly above your ears
Stand on more of the band (feet wider apart) for more resistance; less for a lighter load
modification: Spread your feet wider on the band to reduce working length and resistance. Perform seated to remove lower back stability demands.

sensation.feelHere: The top and side of your shoulders, with the back of your upper arms finishing the press.
sensation.notHere: Your neck or traps taking over, or a pull in your lower back as you press.
sensation.firstCue: Tuck your pelvis before you press. Move for a slow 3 count on the way down.

wrongSpot.fix: You're shrugging to finish. Stop a few inches short of full extension and keep your shoulders down.
You're pressing forward instead of straight up. Finish with your arms directly above your ears.
The band's resistance is pulling you into an arch. Tuck your pelvis and brace your core before you press.
Keep your wrists straight in line with your forearms instead of letting the band bend them backward.

sensation.nextDay: A dull ache across the shoulders for 1-2 days is normal. Sharp joint or lower back pain is not.
sensation.backNote: The band's resistance increases as your arms rise, which tempts your low back into an arch. Tuck your pelvis and brace your core the whole rep.
sensation.stopIf: Anything shoots down your arm, or your hand goes numb or tingly.

mistakes.right: Finish each rep with your arms directly overhead, not angled ahead of you.

mistakes.wrong: Letting the band snap you down
mistakes.right: Control the lowering phase over 2-3 seconds instead of letting the band pull your arms.

mistakes.wrong: Standing too narrow for the load
mistakes.right: Adjust your foot width on the band to match a resistance you can control with good form.

name: Resistance Band Lateral Raise
instructions: Stand on the middle of your resistance band with feet shoulder-width apart. Hold both ends at your sides, palms facing inward. Keep a very slight bend in your elbows throughout.
Take a breath in. Your starting position has your hands at your sides with light tension already in the band.

As you exhale, raise both arms out to your sides simultaneously, leading with your elbows. Think of pouring water from a jug — your pinky side leads slightly, which targets the lateral deltoid most effectively.
Raise until your arms are at shoulder height — parallel to the floor. Do not raise above this level.
Pause for one second at the top, then inhale and slowly lower your arms back to your sides over 2 seconds.
cues: Lead with your elbows, not your hands — this targets the lateral deltoid correctly
Stop at shoulder height — higher adds impingement risk without extra benefit
No shrugging or swinging; if you cannot control the movement, shorten the band length
modification: Stand on less of the band (near one end) to reduce resistance. Perform one arm at a time if needed for control.

sensation.feelHere: The side of your shoulder, right at the cap of the arm.
sensation.notHere: The top of your traps, between your neck and shoulder. That's a shrug, not a raise.
sensation.firstCue: Push the band out toward the walls. Raise for a slow 2 count.

wrongSpot.felt: Top of the traps or neck
wrongSpot.fix: You're shrugging to move the band. Keep your shoulders down and shorten your stance on the band if it's too heavy.
You're raising above shoulder height. Stop the arms once they're parallel to the floor.
You're leading with your hands. Lead with your elbows, like pouring water from a jug.
You're moving too fast through the band's slack. Slow the whole rep down to keep tension even.

sensation.nextDay: A light ache on the side of the shoulder for 1-2 days is normal. Trap or neck soreness usually means shrugging happened.
sensation.stopIf: Any sharp pinch in the shoulder joint, or numbness or tingling in the hand.

mistakes.right: Stop once your arms are parallel to the floor.
Keep your shoulders pulled down; shorten the band if it's pulling you into a shrug.
Stand tall and still; shorten the band length rather than swinging to move it.

name: Resistance Band Bicep Curl
instructions: Stand on the middle of your resistance band with feet shoulder-width apart. Hold the band ends at your sides with palms facing forward, upper arms close to your sides.
Keep your upper arms completely still throughout — the movement comes only from your forearms rotating upward. Shoulders back and down before starting.
Take a breath in. As you exhale, curl both hands upward toward your shoulders by bending at the elbows. The band resistance increases as you curl — maintain control through the full range.
Curl until you feel a strong bicep contraction with forearms roughly vertical. Pause and squeeze for one second at the top.
Inhale and slowly lower the band back to the starting position over 2-3 seconds. The controlled lowering builds as much strength as the curl itself.
cues: Upper arms stay pinned to your sides throughout — only your forearms should move
Squeeze the bicep hard at the top before lowering
Slow on the way down — 2-3 seconds on the descent builds serious strength
modification: Stand on less of the band for lighter resistance. Perform one arm at a time to focus on each side individually.

sensation.feelHere: The front of your upper arm, with the burn increasing as your hands rise higher.
sensation.notHere: Your forearm or wrist strain. That means you're gripping too hard or bending the wrist.
sensation.firstCue: Elbows pinned at your sides. Lower slow against the band, 2–3 seconds.

wrongSpot.fix: You're squeezing the band handles too hard. Loosen your grip — hold firmly, not tightly.
Your wrist is bending back as you curl. Keep it straight and let the elbow do the bending.
Your elbows are drifting forward or up. Keep them pinned to your sides for the entire rep.
You're leaning back to help pull against the band. Stand tall and keep your torso still.

sensation.nextDay: A burn in the front of the upper arm for 1–2 days, more noticeable near the top of the range.
sensation.stopIf: Numbness or tingling in your hand, or sharp pain at the elbow or wrist.

mistakes.wrong: Leaning back against the band tension
mistakes.right: Keep your torso upright and stationary — let your arms fight the band, not your body weight.

mistakes.wrong: Letting the band snap back down
mistakes.right: Control the return over 2–3 seconds — the band fights hardest at the top, use that.
Keep your feet centered on the band so both sides feel even resistance throughout.

name: Resistance Band Squat
instructions: Stand on the middle of your resistance band with feet shoulder-width apart, toes turned out 15-30 degrees. Hold the band ends at shoulder height with elbows pointing forward — a front-rack position. There should be light tension in the band when standing.
Take a breath in and brace your core. Begin the squat by pushing your hips back first, then bend your knees to lower yourself. Keep your elbows up and chest tall throughout.
Descend until your thighs reach parallel to the floor or as deep as comfortable. Your knees should track over your second toe. The band adds peak resistance as you stand back up.
Pause briefly at the bottom, then press through your full foot to drive back up to standing, exhaling on the way up.
Fully extend your hips and knees at the top before the next rep. The band provides increasing resistance through the standing phase, training the full range of the movement.
cues: Hips back first, then knees bend — keep your weight over your heels throughout
Elbows stay up — if they drop, your torso will fall forward
Push your knees actively outward as you squat — do not let them cave inward
modification: Squat to a chair or bench behind you for a depth reference. Hold the band at chest level with crossed arms if the front-rack position is uncomfortable.

sensation.feelHere: Front of your thighs and glutes, plus your upper back holding the front-rack position.
sensation.notHere: Your low back, or the front of your shoulders from the band pulling on your arms.
sensation.firstCue: Keep your elbows up and chest tall. Lower for a slow 3 count.

wrongSpot.fix: Your elbows are dropping and your torso is folding forward. Keep elbows lifted and sit back rather than down.
Sit your hips back first before bending your knees; don't let your shins drive forward.
Shorten the band or stand slightly forward on it so tension isn't yanking your arms down.
Push your knees outward over your toes as you descend, actively resisting the band's pull.

sensation.nextDay: Thighs and glutes ache for 1–3 days. Low back or shoulder soreness the next day is not expected.
sensation.backNote: If your elbows drop, your torso folds forward and load shifts to your spine. Keep elbows up, chest tall, and stop the descent once you feel that fold starting.
sensation.stopIf: Sharp pain, or any shooting, numbness, or tingling down a leg.

mistakes.right: Keep elbows lifted to shoulder height throughout the entire set.
Actively push your knees out over your toes, especially as you stand up.
Control the top of the rep instead of jerking to lockout against the band's pull.

name: Resistance Band Romanian Deadlift
instructions: Stand on the middle of your resistance band with feet hip-width apart. Hold the band ends in each hand at your sides, palms facing inward. Stand tall with a neutral spine and core braced.

Take a breath in. Begin the hinge by pushing your hips straight back — think of reaching your glutes toward the wall behind you. Your spine stays completely long and neutral as your torso tips forward.

As your hips push back, your torso tips forward and the band travels down the front of your thighs. Keep the band close to your body throughout. The band stretches and increases resistance as you hinge.
Lower until you feel a strong hamstring stretch — typically when your torso is roughly parallel to the floor. Do not go past where you can maintain a neutral spine. Pause briefly.
Exhale and drive your hips forward, squeezing your glutes aggressively as you return to standing. Think 'hips forward' not 'lift up' — the power comes from the glutes completing the hip extension.
cues: Push your hips backward, not your body downward — this is a hinge, not a squat
Keep the band dragging along your legs — letting it drift away shifts load to your lower back
Squeeze your glutes hard at the top — full hip extension is what makes this an RDL
modification: Reduce the range of motion to where you can comfortably maintain a neutral spine. Place a hand lightly on a wall for balance support if needed.

sensation.feelHere: Both hamstrings stretching against band tension, then a strong glute squeeze as you stand tall.
sensation.notHere: Your low back, or gripping tension in your forearms from holding the band handles too tightly.
sensation.firstCue: Keep the band pressed against your legs as hips push back. Lower for a slow count.

wrongSpot.fix: The band pulled away from your legs as you hinged, shifting load to your spine. Keep it dragging against your thighs the entire way down.
You hinged below where your hamstrings run out of length. Stop the descent the moment the hamstring first feels tight.
You're squatting instead of hinging. Send your hips straight back and keep the knees only softly bent.
You're gripping the band too hard. Relax your hands — the band tension is the resistance, not your grip strength.

sensation.nextDay: A stretch-type ache through both hamstrings and a glute ache for 1–2 days is expected.
sensation.backNote: Same hinge risk as any RDL, band tension included. Hips travel back toward a wall, not down; stop the descent the instant the hamstrings feel tight, not at the floor.
sensation.stopIf: Anything shoots or tingles down either leg, or your low back sharply pinches at any point.

mistakes.wrong: Letting the band drift away from the legs
mistakes.right: Keep the band in contact with your thighs and shins throughout the entire hinge.

mistakes.wrong: Standing up with the arms instead of hips
mistakes.right: Drive your hips forward to finish the rep — the arms and band are passive, just along for the ride.

mistakes.wrong: Rounding the back at the bottom
mistakes.right: Stop wherever your spine stays neutral, even if that's a shorter range than the band allows.

name: Dumbbell Overhead Tricep Extension
instructions: Stand with feet shoulder-width apart, core braced. Hold one 10 lb dumbbell vertically with both hands — grip the handle just below the top plate, thumbs wrapped around for security. Raise it overhead with arms fully extended, palms facing up.

Set your upper arms: they should point straight up, close to your ears, and stay there for the entire set. Only your forearms will move from here. Your elbows are the fixed hinge — lock them in place.
Take a breath in. As you inhale, bend at the elbows and slowly lower the dumbbell behind your head, feeling the triceps stretch deeply. Lower until your forearms are roughly parallel to the floor.
Without letting your elbows flare outward or your upper arms drift forward, exhale and press the dumbbell back to the start by straightening your arms. Squeeze your triceps hard at the top.
Control the lowering phase over 2 seconds on every rep. This is one rep.
cues: Upper arms stay vertical and close to your ears — if they drift forward, you have lost the position
Think of your elbows as hinges fixed in place — only the forearms move
Do not arch your lower back to compensate — keep your core braced throughout
modification: Sit cross-legged on the floor to remove lower back demand. Or use a single 10 lb dumbbell held with one hand at a time for unilateral tricep work.

sensation.feelHere: The back of your upper arm, especially the stretch as it lowers behind your head.
sensation.notHere: Your elbow joint at the bottom, or your lower back arching to help lower the weight.
sensation.firstCue: Keep upper arms fixed by your ears. Lower for a slow 3 count.

wrongSpot.fix: You're lowering too deep into the stretch. Stop a bit higher, before you feel it in the joint, and use a neutral grip if you can.
Your upper arms are drifting forward. Keep them vertical, close to your ears, for the whole set.
You're arching to control the weight overhead. Brace your core and tuck your pelvis slightly.
Keep your elbows pointing forward, close together, instead of winging out to the sides.

sensation.nextDay: A deep stretch-related ache on the back of the arm for 1-3 days is normal. Elbow joint pain is not.
sensation.backNote: Overhead loading with the arms behind your head is where a low back arch sneaks in. Brace your core and tuck your pelvis; stop if you feel it in your low back.
sensation.stopIf: Sharp elbow pain, or any numbness or tingling in the hand.

mistakes.right: Keep them pointed forward and close together throughout the movement.
Keep your upper arms vertical, close to your ears, for the entire set.
Brace your core and keep your ribs down instead of arching to lower the weight.

name: Dumbbell Bench Press
instructions: Lie flat on a gym bench with feet flat on the floor. Hold a dumbbell in each hand at chest level, elbows at roughly 45-50 degrees from your torso. Squeeze your shoulder blades together and press them into the bench before you start.
Take a breath in and brace your core. Press your feet firmly into the floor to create full-body tension — this protects your shoulders and improves pressing power.
As you exhale, press both dumbbells upward and slightly inward in a gentle arc, extending your arms until nearly locked out above your chest. The dumbbells should nearly touch at the top.
Pause briefly at the top. Maintain your shoulder blade squeeze throughout — do not let your shoulders roll forward.
Inhale and lower the dumbbells with control back to chest level over 2-3 seconds, elbows at 45-50 degrees. Touch the sides of your chest lightly before pressing again.
cues: Shoulder blades squeezed together and pressed into the bench — this protects your shoulders and increases pressing power
Elbows at 45-50 degrees — not flared wide (AC joint stress) or tucked too tight
Press up and slightly inward — the inward arc at the top increases chest activation
modification: Use lighter dumbbells (10-15 lb) to start. Perform a floor chest press if you are not comfortable loading heavy dumbbells on a bench alone.

sensation.feelHere: The middle of your chest, with some work in the back of your upper arms.
sensation.notHere: The front point of your shoulder. If that's where it's loudest, chest isn't doing the work.
sensation.firstCue: Squeeze your shoulder blades into the bench. Lower for a slow 3 count.

wrongSpot.fix: Your shoulder blades have rolled forward off the bench. Pin them back and down before you press, and hold that the whole set.
Your elbows are too wide. Bring them to 45-50 degrees from your torso instead of flared to 90.
That's the joint, not the muscle. Stop the set, drop the weight, and shorten how deep you lower.
Keep your wrists straight and stacked over your elbows instead of letting the dumbbells tip backward.

sensation.nextDay: A broad ache across the chest for 1-3 days is expected. Sharp pinpoint pain at the shoulder is not.
sensation.backNote: Feet pressed into the floor create tension, not an arch. Keep your low back lightly in contact with the bench — don't overarch to press more weight.
sensation.stopIf: Anything shoots down your arm, or your hand goes numb or tingly.

mistakes.right: Keep them at 45-50 degrees from your torso to keep the load off the shoulder joint.

mistakes.wrong: Shoulders rolling forward at the top
mistakes.right: Keep your shoulder blades squeezed together and pinned to the bench throughout the set.
Touch your chest lightly with control, then press again without a rebound.

name: Chest Press Machine
instructions: Sit in the chest press machine. Adjust the seat height so the handles are at chest level — roughly nipple height. Adjust the starting position so your elbows are slightly behind your torso when gripping, creating a stretch across your chest.
Feet flat on the floor, back pressed firmly against the seat pad. Grip the handles at a comfortable width. Squeeze your shoulder blades back against the pad.

Take a breath in. As you exhale, press both handles forward by extending your elbows. Push until your arms are nearly fully extended — do not lock your elbows. Keep your back and head against the pad throughout.
Pause briefly at the extended position, feeling the chest contraction.
Inhale and slowly return the handles toward you over 2-3 seconds. Lower until you feel a good chest stretch — your elbows should travel slightly behind your torso. This is one rep.
cues: Keep your back pressed against the pad throughout — avoid arching away from the seat
Control the return — 2-3 seconds back maximizes chest engagement
Squeeze your shoulder blades together before pressing — this creates a stable base and protects the shoulder joint
modification: Reduce the machine weight and use a limited range of motion if shoulder discomfort occurs. Ask gym staff to help set the seat position on your first use.

sensation.feelHere: The middle of your chest as you press, with some burn in the back of your upper arms.
sensation.notHere: The front of your shoulder. If that's what's loud, your setup or seat height is off.
sensation.firstCue: Squeeze your shoulder blades against the pad first. Press for a slow 3 count.

wrongSpot.fix: Your seat is likely too high or too low. Adjust it so the handles sit at chest height, roughly nipple level.
You're letting your shoulder blades round forward off the pad. Squeeze them back before every rep.
You're stretching too deep. Stop the return a few inches short of your usual depth.
Keep your head resting against the pad instead of craning forward as you press.

sensation.nextDay: A broad ache across the chest for 1-2 days is normal. Sharp pinpoint pain at the shoulder is not.
sensation.backNote: The seat back supports your spine here — keep it pressed against the pad and don't arch away from it to move more weight.
sensation.stopIf: Anything shoots down your arm, or your hand goes numb or tingly.

mistakes.right: Extend until arms are nearly straight, stopping just short of a hard lockout.
Take 2-3 seconds to bring the handles back — this is where most of the chest work happens.
Keep your back pressed against the pad for the entire set.

name: Machine Shoulder Press
instructions: Sit in the shoulder press machine and adjust the seat so the handles are at about ear level with your elbows at 90 degrees. Feet flat on the floor. Sit tall and press your back against the pad.
Grip the handles with palms facing forward. Take a breath in and brace your core lightly.
As you exhale, press both handles straight up overhead until your arms are nearly fully extended. The handles should travel directly above your shoulders, not forward in front of your head.
Pause briefly at the top. Look straight ahead — do not crane your neck upward.
Inhale and slowly lower the handles back to ear level over 2-3 seconds. Do not let the weight stack touch between reps — maintain constant tension throughout.
cues: Sit tall throughout — do not let your lower back arch away from the pad
Press directly overhead, not forward of your ears
2-second lowering phase doubles the effectiveness — resist the urge to let it drop
modification: Reduce the weight. Raise the seat if shoulder discomfort occurs at the starting position — higher seat reduces the external rotation demand.

sensation.feelHere: The top and side of your shoulders, with the back of your upper arms assisting.
sensation.notHere: Your neck or upper traps taking over the lift, or your lower back arching off the pad.
sensation.firstCue: Press straight overhead, not forward. Lower for a slow 3 count.

wrongSpot.fix: You're shrugging to finish the press. Stop a few inches short of lockout and keep your shoulders down.
You're pressing forward of your ears instead of straight up. Keep the handles traveling directly above your shoulders.
Sit taller and press your back into the pad. If you have to arch to press, drop the weight.
You're pressing to a hard lockout. Stop just short of full extension at the top.

sensation.nextDay: A dull ache across the shoulders for 1-2 days is normal. Sharp joint or neck pain is not.
sensation.backNote: The seat back supports your spine here — keep it pressed against the pad throughout and don't arch away from it to finish a rep.
sensation.stopIf: Anything shoots down your arm, or your hand goes numb or tingly.

mistakes.right: Keep your gaze level and let the machine track do the overhead work.

mistakes.wrong: Letting the stack bang between reps
mistakes.right: Keep constant tension — don't let the weight fully rest between reps.
Sit tall and keep your back pressed against the seat for the entire set.

name: Lat Pulldown Machine
instructions: Sit at the lat pulldown machine and adjust the knee pad so it rests firmly on your thighs, preventing you from rising when pulling. Grip the bar with an overhand grip, hands slightly wider than shoulder-width. Sit down and secure your knees. Allow your arms to fully extend and your lats to stretch at the top.
Lean back very slightly — about 10-15 degrees — and brace your core. This slight lean puts your lats in a more efficient pulling angle. Fix your gaze at mid-chest level.
Take a breath in. As you exhale, drive both elbows down and toward your hips — think of putting your elbows in your back pockets. Pull the bar toward your upper chest.
Pull until the bar reaches your upper chest or collarbone. Squeeze your lats hard — the muscles just under your armpits — and hold for one second.
Inhale and slowly let the bar rise back to the start over 2-3 seconds. Allow your arms to fully extend and your lats to stretch at the top before the next rep.
cues: Drive elbows down toward your hips, not straight back — this maximizes lat engagement over bicep use
Do not lean back more than 15 degrees — excessive lean turns it into a row
Full extension at the top matters — the lat stretch at the top is where development happens
modification: Reduce the weight. A neutral-grip (palms facing each other) bar attachment is more comfortable for beginners and equally effective.

sensation.feelHere: Under your armpits and down the sides of your back, from the top to your ribs.
sensation.notHere: Your biceps or the top of your shoulders near your neck. That's the wrong muscle taking over.
sensation.firstCue: Drive elbows down toward your hips first. Control the return over 2–3 seconds.

wrongSpot.fix: You're pulling with the arm bending first. Start the pull by driving the elbows down before the hands move much.
You're leaning back too far or shrugging. Sit tall, lean only 10–15 degrees, and keep shoulders down.
You're gripping the bar too hard. Loosen your hands — they only need to hold the bar, not squeeze it.
You're leaning back excessively to move more weight. Reduce the load and keep the lean small.

sensation.nextDay: Soreness under the armpits and along the sides of the back for 1–2 days is expected.
sensation.stopIf: Any pain shooting down an arm, or numbness or tingling in your hands during the pull.

mistakes.right: Keep your lean to about 10–15 degrees — more turns this into a back extension, not a pulldown.
Always pull the bar to your upper chest, never behind your neck — that strains the shoulder joint.

mistakes.wrong: Not fully extending at the top
mistakes.right: Let your arms fully straighten and lats stretch between every rep for full range of motion.

name: Single-Arm Dumbbell Row
instructions: Place your left knee and left hand on a flat gym bench for support. Torso parallel to the floor, neutral spine. Hold a dumbbell in your right hand at arm's length directly below your right shoulder.
Squeeze your right shoulder blade inward and down to create initial tension. Take a breath in and brace your core.
As you exhale, row the dumbbell upward by driving your right elbow toward the ceiling and back. Keep the dumbbell close to your body throughout.
Pull until your right elbow is clearly above the level of your back and you feel a strong contraction in your lat and upper back. Squeeze your shoulder blade toward your spine at the top.
Inhale and lower the dumbbell back to the starting position with full control over 2 seconds. Complete all reps on the right side, then switch to the left.
cues: Drive your elbow up and back — the dumbbell follows the elbow, not the other way around
Squeeze your shoulder blade at the top — if you don't feel your back, the bicep is doing all the work
Keep your torso parallel to the floor — rotating your shoulders to help the weight up is cheating
modification: Use a lighter dumbbell. Brace one hand on a countertop or rack with both feet on the floor if no bench is available.

sensation.feelHere: The side of your back under the armpit on the working side, near the shoulder blade.
sensation.notHere: Your bicep or the front of your shoulder. Those mean the arm is doing what the back should.
sensation.firstCue: Squeeze the shoulder blade down and back before the elbow bends. Lower on a 2-count.

wrongSpot.fix: You're curling the weight up. Start the pull by drawing the shoulder blade toward your spine, then let the elbow follow.
You're squeezing the dumbbell too hard. Relax your hand — it only needs to hold on, not clamp.
You're rotating to lift the weight. Keep both shoulders square to the floor throughout the rep.
You're shrugging the shoulder up toward your ear. Keep it pulled down and back instead.

sensation.nextDay: Soreness under the armpit and along the shoulder blade for 1–2 days is normal and expected.
sensation.backNote: Your knee and hand on the bench support your spine, so this is fairly back-friendly — but don't let your low back sag or twist to finish a rep.
sensation.stopIf: Any pain shooting down your arm or leg, or numbness or tingling in the hand.

mistakes.right: Keep your torso square to the floor and let the back muscles pull, not momentum from twisting.
Keep the elbow tracking close to your ribs, driving up and back toward the ceiling.
Keep your spine flat from head to tailbone — a rounded back reduces the pull's effectiveness.

name: Cable Face Pull
instructions: Set a cable machine pulley with a rope attachment to approximately face height. Stand facing the machine and hold the rope with both hands, thumbs pointing up. Step back until there is tension in the cable with arms extended in front of you.
Take a light staggered stance for stability. Starting position: arms extended, rope at face height, core lightly braced.

Take a breath in. As you exhale, pull the rope toward your face by driving both elbows out to the sides and slightly upward. Split your hands apart as you pull — one end toward each side of your face.

Externally rotate your shoulders as you pull: elbows flare out and hands end up beside your temples with palms facing forward. Your upper arms should be roughly parallel to the floor at the end. Squeeze your rear delts and rhomboids.
Hold the contracted position for one second. Inhale and slowly return to the starting extended position. This is one rep.
cues: Pull toward your nose or ears, not your chin — lower trajectory loses the rear delt and rotator cuff benefit
Elbows flare out and UP at the end, not straight back
Keep your torso still throughout — no leaning backward to help the weight
modification: Reduce the cable weight. Stand closer to the machine to reduce effective resistance. A rope attachment is strongly preferred over a straight bar.

sensation.feelHere: The back of your shoulders and between your shoulder blades, especially as your hands split apart.
sensation.notHere: The top of your traps near your neck. That means the weight is too heavy or you're shrugging.
sensation.firstCue: Lead with your elbows, pulling them out and up. Keep it light — no shrug.

wrongSpot.fix: You're going too heavy or leading with your hands. Drop the weight and lead the pull with your elbows instead.
You're straining upward to help pull. Keep your neck relaxed and let your shoulder blades do the squeezing.
You're pulling with your arms bent from the start. Drive your elbows sideways before your hands move much.
You're not externally rotating enough at the end. Finish with your hands beside your temples, palms forward.

sensation.nextDay: A light ache across the shoulders and upper back for a day is normal — this should feel light.
sensation.stopIf: Sharp pinching in the shoulder joint, or any numbness or tingling down your arm.

mistakes.right: Keep your torso still and upright — let your shoulder muscles do the work, not body momentum.
Aim the rope toward your nose or ears — a lower pull skips the rear delts and rotator cuff.
Use a light weight — this should feel like a light squeeze and burn, not a grind.

name: Dumbbell Romanian Deadlift
instructions: Stand holding a dumbbell in each hand in front of your thighs, palms facing inward. Feet hip-width apart, knees soft. Shoulders retracted, chest tall, core braced.
Take a breath in. Begin the hinge by pushing your hips straight back — think of reaching your glutes toward the wall behind you. Your spine stays completely long and neutral throughout.

As your hips push back, your torso tips forward and the dumbbells travel down the front of your thighs and shins. Keep the dumbbells in contact with or very close to your legs to maintain proper center of gravity.
Lower until you feel a strong hamstring stretch — typically mid-shin depending on flexibility. Do not go past where you can maintain a neutral spine. Pause briefly.
Exhale and drive your hips forward, squeezing your glutes aggressively as you stand back up. Think 'hips forward' not 'lift the weight' — the glute squeeze completes the hip extension.
cues: Hips go backward first — this is a hip hinge, not a squat or a forward bend
Keep the dumbbells dragging along your legs — drifting forward shifts dangerous load to the lumbar spine
Squeeze your glutes hard at the top — this is what completes the movement and protects the lower back
modification: Use lighter dumbbells and reduce range of motion to where you can perfectly maintain spinal alignment. Perform in front of a mirror to check your form.

sensation.feelHere: Both hamstrings stretching, then a hard glute squeeze as your hips drive forward to standing.
sensation.notHere: Your low back. If it's doing the work, the hinge broke down somewhere in the descent.
sensation.firstCue: Keep the dumbbells against your legs as hips push back. Lower slowly for 3 counts.

wrongSpot.fix: The weight drifted away from your legs, pulling load into your spine. Keep the dumbbells dragging against your thighs and shins the whole way down.

wrongSpot.felt: Low back, and depth feels excessive
wrongSpot.fix: You hinged past where your hamstrings can hold a neutral spine. Stop the descent when the hamstring first feels tight, not at a fixed height.
You're bending your knees like a squat instead of hinging. Keep the knees only softly bent and send the hips backward.
You're shrugging to hold the dumbbells. Let your arms hang heavy and relaxed, gripping only enough to not drop them.

sensation.nextDay: A deep stretch-soreness through both hamstrings and a glute ache for 1–2 days is normal.
sensation.backNote: The hip hinge is where load reaches the low back fastest. Hips travel back, not down; stop the descent the moment the hamstrings feel tight, never when the weight nears the floor.
sensation.stopIf: Anything shoots, burns, or tingles down either leg, or your low back sharply pinches at any point.

mistakes.wrong: Weight drifting forward away from legs
mistakes.right: Keep the dumbbells brushing your thighs and shins throughout the entire hinge, both down and up.

mistakes.wrong: Standing up by leading with the chest
mistakes.right: Drive your hips forward first — think 'hips forward,' not 'lift the weight' — and let the torso follow.

mistakes.wrong: Locking the knees at the top
mistakes.right: Keep a soft bend in the knees throughout; a hard lockout shifts strain toward the low back.

name: Lying Leg Curl Machine
instructions: Lie face-down on the leg curl machine. Adjust the ankle pad so it rests just above your heels on the lower Achilles area. Your knees should be just off the edge of the bench when legs are straight. Grip the handles under the bench for stability.
Press your hips firmly into the pad throughout the movement. Starting position: legs fully extended.
As you exhale, curl both legs simultaneously by bending your knees, pulling your heels toward your glutes against the machine's resistance.
Curl until your knees are fully bent as far as the machine allows. Squeeze your hamstrings hard at this contracted position for one second.
Inhale and slowly extend your legs back to the starting position over 2-3 seconds. Do not let the weight stack bang down. Maintain controlled tension throughout the return.
cues: Keep your hips pressed into the pad — if they lift, the weight is too heavy
Full range: straight to fully bent — partial curls significantly reduce effectiveness
Slow on the way down — the controlled lowering phase builds hamstring resilience
modification: Reduce the machine weight significantly on your first session — leg curl machines vary widely between brands. A seated leg curl machine is an alternative if lying face-down causes discomfort.

sensation.feelHere: The back of your thighs, building to a strong contraction as your knees fully bend.
sensation.notHere: Behind your knee joint itself, or your low back — neither should be doing the work.
sensation.firstCue: Press your hips into the pad. Lower for a slow 2–3 count.

wrongSpot.fix: The ankle pad may sit too low. Reposition it just above your heel, not on the joint.
Your hips are lifting off the pad. Reduce the weight until you can keep your hips pinned down.
Point your toes slightly up rather than pointed, which shifts emphasis off the calf.
Check both legs are curling evenly; a stronger leg can take over if you let it.

sensation.nextDay: Deep hamstring soreness for 1–3 days is normal, especially after the eccentric lowering. Knee joint soreness is not.
sensation.backNote: Lying face-down keeps your spine largely out of this one. Just keep your hips pressed into the pad rather than lifting to cheat the weight up.
sensation.stopIf: Any sharp pain behind the knee, or shooting pain, numbness, or tingling down your leg.

mistakes.right: Reduce the weight so you can keep your hips pinned down the whole set.
Curl through the full range, straight to fully bent, rather than short reps.

mistakes.wrong: Letting the weight stack slam down
mistakes.right: Lower over 2–3 seconds under control instead of letting it drop.

name: Leg Press Machine
instructions: Sit in the leg press machine with your back and hips pressed firmly against the back pad. Feet hip-width apart on the footplate, toes turned out 15-20 degrees, positioned mid-plate. Unlock the safety handles before starting.
Starting position: knees at roughly 90 degrees. Your lower back should not peel away from the back pad at your working depth — if it does, reduce your range of motion.

Take a breath in and brace your core. As you exhale, press through your full foot to extend your legs and push the footplate away. Keep a soft bend in your knees at the top — do not fully lock them out.
Press until your legs are nearly extended (about 170 degrees). Pause briefly.
Inhale and slowly lower the footplate back to your starting depth over 2-3 seconds. Re-engage the safety handles before exiting the machine.
cues: Never lock your knees at the top — always maintain a soft, slight bend
Keep your back pressed against the pad throughout — if it peels away, you have gone too deep
Press through your full foot, heels included — this better targets the glutes
modification: Start with a very light weight to find your comfortable range. Wider foot placement targets glutes more; closer/lower placement targets quads.

sensation.feelHere: Front of your thighs and glutes, building to a burn by the last few reps of a set.
sensation.notHere: Your low back rounding off the pad, or sharp pain in the front of your knees.
sensation.firstCue: Stop the descent before your back lifts off the pad. Lower for a slow 3 count.

wrongSpot.fix: Your pelvis is tucking under at the bottom. Reduce your range of motion and stop before your back peels off the pad.
Move your feet slightly higher on the platform to shift load toward your hips and glutes.
Check your feet are evenly placed and pressing evenly; uneven pressure loads one leg more.
Stop just short of locking your knees out at the top of each rep.

sensation.nextDay: Front-of-thigh and glute soreness for 1–3 days is normal. Low back soreness the next day is not.
sensation.backNote: The real danger here is your low back rounding off the pad at the bottom under load — 'butt wink.' Stop the descent the instant your back starts to peel away, even if that means less range.
sensation.stopIf: Any shooting pain, numbness, or tingling down a leg, or sharp low back pain.

mistakes.right: Stop the descent at the point where your back is still flat against the pad.

mistakes.wrong: Locking knees out hard at the top
mistakes.right: Keep a soft bend in your knees at full extension instead of slamming them straight.
Lower over 2–3 seconds under control instead of letting the weight fall.

name: Kettlebell Swing
instructions: Stand with feet shoulder-width apart, toes slightly outward. Place a kettlebell on the floor about a foot in front of you. Hinge at the hips to grip the handle with both hands, arms inside your legs. Back flat, core braced, hips higher than knees.
Hike the kettlebell back between your legs with a sharp hip hinge — like a center snap in football. This backswing loads your hamstrings and creates the stretch reflex you will convert into power.

As the kettlebell swings back and your hips are fully loaded, snap your hips forward aggressively and squeeze your glutes. This explosive hip drive is the power source — your arms are just a pendulum.
The kettlebell floats to chest or shoulder height. At the top, your body is fully upright, glutes squeezed hard, core braced — a standing plank. Do not lean back.
As the kettlebell descends, hinge your hips back again to receive it and guide it between your legs. This is a continuous, fluid motion. Complete all reps without stopping.
cues: The power comes from snapping your hips forward, not from swinging your arms — your arms are a rope, your hips are the engine
Hinge, do not squat — on the backswing your hips go back, not down
Stand completely tall and squeeze your glutes hard at the top of each swing
modification: Use a lighter kettlebell (8-12 kg for beginners). Practice the hip hinge first: stand arm's length from a wall, push your glutes back to touch it, then drive forward.

sensation.feelHere: A sharp glute and hamstring snap at the top of each swing, like an explosive jump.
sensation.notHere: Your shoulders, arms, or low back. None of them should be doing the lifting here.
sensation.firstCue: Snap your hips forward hard; keep arms loose like a rope. Start slow and light.

wrongSpot.fix: You're squatting it up or lifting with the back instead of snapping the hips. Practice the wall hip-hinge drill before swinging again.
You're lifting the bell with your arms instead of the hips throwing it. Relax your arms — they only guide it, they never lift it.

wrongSpot.felt: Front of the thighs, like a squat
wrongSpot.fix: You're bending the knees and squatting the weight instead of hinging. Keep the knees soft and push the hips back on the backswing.
You're letting the bell pull your spine into a round on the way back. Hike it between your legs like a football snap, chest up.

sensation.nextDay: A deep glute and hamstring ache the next day is normal; low back soreness is not.
sensation.backNote: You've never used a kettlebell before. This is a hip snap, not a squat or an arm lift — if the hinge doesn't feel solid, master the RDL and good-morning first.
sensation.stopIf: Anything shoots down a leg, your low back sharply pinches, or the bell pulls you off balance.

mistakes.wrong: Squatting the weight up and down
mistakes.right: This is a hinge, not a squat — hips travel back and snap forward, knees barely bend.

mistakes.wrong: Lifting the bell with the arms
mistakes.right: Let the hips throw it; arms only guide the path and stay relaxed the entire swing.

mistakes.wrong: Leaning back at the top to add height
mistakes.right: Finish standing tall in a straight line — leaning back overextends the low back for no benefit.

name: Kettlebell Goblet Squat
instructions: Stand with feet slightly wider than shoulder-width, toes turned out 30-45 degrees. Hold a kettlebell by both sides of the handle (the horns) at your chest, close to your sternum. Elbows point down.
Take a breath in and brace your core. Begin by pushing your hips back and out, then bend your knees to descend between your legs. The kettlebell stays close to your chest throughout.
Descend as deep as comfortable — ideally thighs parallel or below. As you descend, use your elbows to push your knees outward, opening your hips for depth. Heels stay flat on the floor.
Pause briefly at the bottom. Drive through your full foot to press back up to standing, exhaling on the way up. Squeeze your glutes at the top.
The front-loaded kettlebell naturally keeps your torso upright — this is what makes goblet squats excellent for teaching squat mechanics.
cues: Keep the kettlebell close to your chest — letting it drift forward pulls you forward
Use your elbows to push your knees outward as you descend — this opens the hips
Heels stay flat on the floor throughout — if they rise, widen your stance or work on ankle mobility
modification: Squat to a bench or box behind you as a depth reference. Use a lighter kettlebell (8-12 kg for beginners).

sensation.feelHere: Front of your thighs and glutes, with your midsection and upper back working to stay upright.
sensation.notHere: Your low back, forearms, or the front of your shoulders under the kettlebell.
sensation.firstCue: Keep the kettlebell tight to your chest. Lower for a slow 3 count.

wrongSpot.fix: The kettlebell is drifting away from your chest. Pin it to your sternum through the whole descent.
Sit your hips back further before your knees bend, rather than dropping straight down.
Let the horns rest in your palms rather than gripping hard; relax your grip between reps.
Use your elbows to push your knees outward as you sink into the squat.

sensation.nextDay: Thighs and glutes ache for 1–3 days. Low back or forearm soreness the next day is not expected.
sensation.backNote: The front-loaded kettlebell should keep you upright naturally. If your back rounds, the weight has drifted forward — reset it against your chest and reduce depth.
sensation.stopIf: Any shooting pain, numbness, or tingling down a leg.

mistakes.right: Widen your stance or work on ankle mobility so your heels stay planted.
Keep the kettlebell pinned tight to your sternum for the entire rep.
Drive up evenly through hips and knees together rather than shooting your hips up first.

name: Dumbbell Walking Lunge
instructions: Stand tall holding a dumbbell in each hand at your sides. Find a clear path of about 10 metres. Chest up, shoulders back throughout.
Step your right foot forward, taking a large step. Land with your right foot flat and your right knee tracking directly over your right ankle — not pushing past your toes.
Lower your back (left) knee toward the floor by bending both knees simultaneously. Stop when your back knee is about 1-2 inches from the floor. Both knees should reach roughly 90 degrees.
Drive through your right heel and step your left foot forward past your right foot into the next lunge step. This continuous walking motion continues for the full set.
Continue alternating legs for 10 steps per side (20 total steps). Keep your torso completely upright throughout — do not lean over your front thigh. Dumbbells hang at your sides.
cues: Stay completely tall — the most common error is the torso leaning forward over the front thigh
Front knee over ankle — step far enough forward that your knee does not go past your toes
Control the descent — 2 seconds down prevents the back knee from crashing to the floor
modification: Perform static lunges (step forward and drive back to start) instead of walking lunges. Reduce dumbbell weight or use bodyweight only.

sensation.feelHere: Front thigh and glute of your leading leg on every step, plus your core staying braced.
sensation.notHere: Your low back, or the front knee — sharp knee pain there is not the target.
sensation.firstCue: Stay tall through your torso. Take 2 seconds to lower each step.

wrongSpot.fix: Step further forward so your knee doesn't push past your toes as you descend.
You're leaning over the front thigh, likely from the dumbbells' weight. Keep your chest stacked over your hips.
Let the dumbbells hang relaxed at your sides rather than gripping them tightly.
Control the descent and stop an inch or two above the floor each step.

sensation.nextDay: Front thigh and glute soreness for 1–3 days is normal. Low back or knee soreness the next day is not.
sensation.backNote: Added weight makes forward lean more tempting as you fatigue. Stay upright through your torso; if your back rounds, reduce the dumbbell weight.
sensation.stopIf: Any shooting pain, numbness, or tingling down a leg, or sharp knee pain.

mistakes.right: Keep your chest tall and stacked over your hips on every step.
Take a longer stride so your knee stays above your ankle, not past it.
Take 2 seconds to lower each step instead of rushing into the next one.

name: Seated Calf Raise Machine
instructions: Sit at the seated calf raise machine. Adjust the knee pad so it rests firmly just above your knees. Place the balls of your feet on the footplate edge with heels hanging off. Starting position: heels lowered as far as comfortable into a full stretch.
From the fully stretched position, press through the balls of both feet to rise as high as possible, lifting your heels. Rise as high as the machine allows.
Hold at the top for 1-2 seconds, feeling the full calf contraction. Do not cut the range short.
Slowly lower your heels back down over 2-3 seconds, allowing the calves to fully stretch at the bottom. The eccentric (lowering) phase is critical for calf and Achilles strengthening.
Pause briefly in the fully stretched position before the next rep. Do not bounce from the bottom.
cues: Full range of motion both ways: maximum stretch at the bottom, maximum height at the top
Slow on the way down — 2-3 seconds on the lowering phase is where the Achilles strengthening occurs
Keep your knee angle constant — do not let your knees rise or dip as you move
modification: Perform bodyweight standing calf raises on the edge of a step if no machine is available.

sensation.feelHere: A burn low in your calf, closer to the ankle, more than the upper bulge.
sensation.notHere: Your Achilles tendon or the arch of your foot — sharp pain there is a tendon signal, not muscle work.
sensation.firstCue: Rise as high as the machine allows. Lower over a slow 2–3 count.

wrongSpot.fix: You may be going too heavy or too fast. Reduce the weight and slow the lowering phase.
Reposition your feet so the balls, not your toes, are on the platform edge.
