Keep your knee angle constant throughout; don't let your knees rise or dip as you press.
Loosen the knee pad slightly — it may be pressing too hard on your shin.

sensation.nextDay: A deep, low calf ache for 1–2 days is normal. Achilles soreness is not.
sensation.stopIf: Sharp Achilles pain, or any pain that feels like a pull rather than a burn.

mistakes.right: Pause briefly in the full stretch before each rep instead of bouncing out.
Rise as high as the machine allows and stretch fully at the bottom each rep.
Keep your knee angle steady under the pad throughout the set.

name: Cable Tricep Pushdown
instructions: Set a cable machine with a straight bar or rope attachment at a high position. Face the machine and hold the attachment with both hands, shoulder-width apart, overhand grip. Step back slightly for cable tension.
Bring your elbows to your sides, bent at 90 degrees. This is your starting position. Your elbows stay pinned to your sides throughout — they are the pivot point.
Take a breath in. As you exhale, push the bar or rope downward by extending your elbows against the cable resistance.
Extend until your arms are fully straight alongside your thighs — elbows locked out. Squeeze your triceps hard at this fully extended position for one second.
Inhale and slowly allow the weight to bring your forearms back up to the 90-degree starting position over 2 seconds. Do not let your elbows drift forward during the return.
cues: Elbows stay pinned at your sides throughout — when elbows drift forward, load shifts off the triceps
Full extension: lock out at the bottom for maximum tricep contraction
Stand closer to the stack if the cable is pulling you onto your toes
modification: Reduce the cable weight. A rope attachment (where you can flare the ends out at the bottom) is preferred for achieving full extension.

sensation.feelHere: The back of your upper arm, from the elbow up toward your shoulder.
sensation.notHere: Your shoulder pulling forward, or your wrists straining to hold the bar.
sensation.firstCue: Pin your elbows to your sides. Lower for a slow 2 count on the return.

wrongSpot.fix: Your elbows are drifting forward off your sides. Pin them to your ribs and keep them there the whole set.
You're locking out hard at the bottom. Stop just short of a full lockout and squeeze instead.
You're bending your wrists to control the bar. Keep them straight and let your grip stay neutral.
You're using your torso to help push. Stand tall and let your arms do the work, with lighter weight if needed.

sensation.nextDay: A focused ache on the back of the upper arm for 1-2 days is normal. Elbow joint pain is not.
sensation.stopIf: Sharp elbow pain, or any numbness or tingling in the hand.

mistakes.right: Keep your elbows pinned to your sides as the fixed pivot point throughout.

mistakes.wrong: Using body weight to lean into it
mistakes.right: Stand tall and stationary; let your arms move the weight, not your torso.
Let the weight come back up over 2 seconds instead of letting it snap back.

name: Treadmill Walk / Run
instructions: Set the treadmill to a moderate pace that gets your heart rate up but still allows short sentences — typically 3.5-4.5 mph for a brisk walk or 5-6 mph for a light jog. For a greater challenge without more speed, add a 2-4% incline.
Step on, stand tall, and let the belt bring you into your stride. Chest lifted, arms swinging naturally. Avoid holding onto the handrails — it reduces calorie burn and disrupts natural gait.
Breathe steadily. At a good challenge pace, you should be able to say a short sentence but not hold a full conversation.
Maintain this pace for the full 10 minutes. This is the cardiovascular finish of your circuit — aim for a satisfying challenge rather than easy movement.
In the final 1-2 minutes, gradually reduce your speed as a natural cool-down. Step off carefully only when the belt has slowed.
cues: Look forward, not down at your feet — looking down promotes a hunched, inefficient posture
Do not hold the handrails — it significantly reduces the workout and disrupts natural movement
Add incline to increase intensity without increasing impact if joint discomfort is a concern
modification: Walk at a slower pace (2.5-3.5 mph) or reduce to 5 minutes if 10 feels too challenging. Flat setting is fine — incline is optional.

sensation.feelHere: Steadily rising warmth in your legs and a slightly quickened breath — nothing more.
sensation.notHere: Sharp joint pain in the knees, hips, or low back with each step.
sensation.stopIf: Sharp joint pain, dizziness, or chest pain. The goal is warm and slightly breathless, not tired.

name: Rowing Machine Warm-Up
instructions: Sit on the rowing machine and strap your feet in securely. Grip the handle with both hands, arms fully extended and relaxed. Sit with a neutral spine, knees bent, shins roughly vertical. This is the catch position.

Begin with an easy, light row. The stroke has four phases in sequence: push with legs, lean back slightly, pull arms to your lower ribs — then reverse: arms extend, lean forward, knees bend. Follow this sequence every stroke.

For the warm-up, row at approximately 18-22 strokes per minute — an unhurried, comfortable pace. Focus on smooth technique rather than power: legs push first (60% of power), then hips hinge back slightly, then arms pull.
Breathe in sync: exhale on the drive (power phase), inhale on the recovery (return phase). Keep your shoulders relaxed and down throughout.
After 5 minutes your joints should feel warm and loose. Ease off in the final 30 seconds.
cues: Legs first, then lean, then arms — this stroke sequence is fundamental
Legs generate most of the power (about 60%) — do not skip straight to pulling with your arms
Keep your grip relaxed — squeezing too tight fatigues the forearms quickly
modification: Row at a slower pace (16-18 SPM) if 5 minutes feels challenging. Focus entirely on learning the stroke sequence rather than the pace.

sensation.feelHere: Steadily rising warmth through your legs and back and a slightly quickened breath.
sensation.notHere: A rounding, straining pull in the low back at the catch position — that's a technique issue, not warm-up.
sensation.backNote: Keep your spine neutral at the catch — don't let your low back round forward to reach further. Sit tall instead.
sensation.stopIf: Sharp low-back pain, or tingling down either leg.

name: Elliptical Warm-Up
instructions: Step onto the elliptical and place your feet in the pedals. Grip the moving handles lightly. Start pedaling forward at a low resistance level (1-3 on most machines).
Find a comfortable rhythm — aim for about 60-70 RPM. The elliptical simulates a running motion with zero joint impact, making it ideal for active recovery days.

Push through your heels and engage your glutes as you pedal — avoid riding entirely on the balls of your feet. Use the moving handles lightly to involve your upper body, or hold the stationary handles if preferred.
Breathe easily and steadily. On an active recovery day, keep your heart rate low-to-moderate (about 50-65% of your maximum). You should be able to hold a conversation comfortably.
After 10 minutes, gradually reduce resistance and slow your pace over the final minute as a natural transition into the mobility work that follows.
cues: Push through your heels to engage your glutes — pedaling from your toes bypasses the glutes entirely
Keep your chest lifted and core lightly engaged throughout
This is active recovery — keep the intensity genuinely low; today is about movement, not training
modification: Reduce to 5 minutes at an even lower resistance. A stationary bike is a fine alternative if the elliptical is unavailable.

sensation.feelHere: Steadily rising warmth in your legs and a slightly quickened breath — nothing more.
sensation.notHere: Sharp pain in the knees or hips with each stride.
sensation.stopIf: Sharp joint pain, dizziness, or chest pain. Aim for warm and slightly breathless, not tired.

name: Sphinx Pose
instructions: Lie face down on your mat with your legs extended behind you, tops of the feet on the floor. Place your forearms on the mat with elbows directly under your shoulders, palms flat.

Press gently through your forearms and lift your chest, letting your lower back settle into a comfortable, supported arch. Your forearms carry the weight — this is a passive, gentle extension, not a push.
Keep your glutes and legs relaxed. Let gravity and your breath do the work. Your hips and thighs stay in contact with the mat throughout.
Hold for 40 seconds, breathing slowly and deeply. With each exhale, allow your lower back to relax a little more into the position.

This gentle spinal extension counterbalances the sitting and forward-bending of daily life. The sensation should be a comfortable stretch or pressure in the lower back — never pain, and never anything radiating into the leg. If you feel leg symptoms, stop and skip this exercise today.
cues: Elbows under shoulders, forearms carrying the load — this is a supported, passive arch
Relax your glutes and legs completely — tensing them works against the stretch
Comfortable pressure in the lower back is fine; any pain or leg tingling means come down immediately
modification: Lower to a smaller arch by sliding your elbows further forward, or rest on a pillow placed under your chest.

sensation.feelHere: A comfortable, supported pressure or gentle stretch across the low back as your chest lifts.
sensation.notHere: Any sensation radiating down into the buttock or leg — that's a warning sign, not part of the stretch.
sensation.backNote: This is a McKenzie-style movement chosen deliberately for your back. If symptoms move toward your spine (centralise), that's good — keep going. If they move further down the leg, stop.
sensation.stopIf: Any pain or tingling radiating into the leg. Come down immediately and skip the exercise for today.

name: Cobra Press-Up (McKenzie)
instructions: Lie face down on your mat with your hands flat on the floor under your shoulders, as if at the bottom of a push-up. Legs extended, tops of the feet on the floor, glutes and legs fully relaxed.

Take a breath in. As you exhale, press through your hands to slowly straighten your arms, lifting your chest and upper torso off the mat. Your hips and pelvis remain on the floor — only your spine extends.
Press up only as far as comfortable. Your lower back relaxes into the extension; your arms do all the work. Full elbow extension is the eventual goal, not a day-one requirement.
Pause for one breath at your comfortable top position, then slowly lower back down to the mat. That is one repetition.

This is the classic McKenzie press-up used in disc rehabilitation. The movement should feel like a progressively easier stretch across the front of your torso and gentle pressure in the lower back. Centralizing sensation (moving toward your spine) is good; anything radiating down a leg means stop immediately.
cues: Hips stay glued to the mat — if they lift, you have turned it into an upward dog, which is a different exercise
Glutes and legs stay relaxed — let your arms lift and your spine simply extend
Range of motion grows over weeks; never push through pain or leg symptoms
modification: Press up onto your forearms only (Sphinx Pose) until full press-ups feel comfortable. Reduce the range to whatever depth is pain-free.

sensation.feelHere: A progressively easier stretch across the front of the torso and gentle pressure in the low back as you press up.
sensation.notHere: Any sensation radiating into the buttock or down the leg — that's a warning sign, not deeper progress.
sensation.backNote: Hips stay glued to the mat and legs stay relaxed. Watch for centralisation: symptoms moving toward your spine as you press up is good and means keep going; symptoms moving further down the leg is bad and means stop.
sensation.stopIf: Any pain or tingling radiating into the leg. Stop immediately and try Sphinx Pose instead today.

name: Pelvic Tilts
instructions: Lie on your back with your knees bent and feet flat on the floor, hip-width apart. Arms rest at your sides. Notice the small natural gap between your lower back and the mat.

As you exhale, gently flatten your lower back into the mat by tilting your pelvis backward — think of drawing your belly button down toward your spine and your tailbone slightly up. Hold for 2 seconds.
As you inhale, reverse the motion: tilt your pelvis forward to slightly increase the arch in your lower back, creating a small gap under it again. Hold for 2 seconds.
Rock slowly and smoothly between these two positions — flatten on the exhale, arch on the inhale. The movement is small and entirely within a comfortable range.
Complete 10 slow cycles. This re-teaches pelvic control and gently mobilizes the lumbar segments — ideal as the very first or very last movement of a session.
cues: Small, slow, and smooth — this is a control drill, not a strength exercise
Sync with your breath: exhale to flatten, inhale to arch
Stay inside the completely pain-free range — even a tiny rocking motion is effective
modification: Reduce the range of motion to a barely visible rock, or perform only the flattening half of the movement.

sensation.feelHere: A small, controlled shift of pressure in your low back as it flattens and arches gently.
sensation.notHere: Any pain or a hard pinch at the end of either direction — the whole range should stay comfortable.
sensation.backNote: This is a deliberately gentle control drill for your back. Keep the whole motion inside a completely pain-free range — small is correct, not a limitation.
sensation.stopIf: Any pain, or tingling or numbness anywhere in the legs.

name: McGill Curl-Up
instructions: Lie on your back. Extend your left leg flat and bend your right knee so your right foot is flat on the floor. Slide both hands, palms down, into the natural arch under your lower back — they preserve the spine's neutral curve throughout.
Keep your elbows resting on the floor. Take a breath in and brace your core lightly, as if preparing for a gentle poke in the stomach.

Lift your head, shoulders, and upper chest off the floor as ONE rigid unit — just an inch or two. Your spine does not bend or curl; the movement happens by hinging slightly through the upper back. Imagine your head resting on a bathroom scale and just unweighting it.
Hold the lift for 8 seconds, breathing steadily — do not hold your breath. Then lower back down with control.

Complete 6 reps, then switch legs (left knee bent, right leg straight) for the next set. Designed by spine researcher Dr. Stuart McGill, this builds core strength with virtually zero load on the discs — the spine never flexes.
cues: Do NOT curl or crunch — head, shoulders, and chest lift together as one stiff plank
Hands stay under your lower back to keep its natural arch the whole time
Small lift, long hold — an inch off the floor held for 8 seconds beats a big sit-up
modification: Shorten the hold to 4 seconds, or simply lift the weight of your head off the floor without raising the shoulders.

sensation.feelHere: A light bracing tension across your upper stomach, just under the ribs.
sensation.notHere: Your neck straining, or any bending or rounding sensation in your low back.
sensation.firstCue: Just unweight your head off the floor, like off a scale. Hold rigid, don't curl.

wrongSpot.fix: You're pulling with your neck like a sit-up. Lead with your chest lifting as one rigid block, not your chin.
Your spine is bending. Keep your hands under your low back and only lift an inch — the spine stays still.
You're not bracing before lifting. Tighten your stomach lightly, like bracing for a poke, before you lift.

sensation.nextDay: A light, shallow ab ache for a day is normal. Neck or low-back soreness is not.
sensation.backNote: This is deliberately a tiny movement — head and shoulders lift a few centimetres as one rigid unit, spine never bends. That's exactly why it's safe for your discs; treating it like a sit-up defeats the purpose.
sensation.stopIf: Any shooting or electric pain, or numbness or tingling in a leg.

mistakes.right: Lift only an inch or two, keeping head, shoulders, and chest rigid as one block — the spine never bends.
Let your chest lead the small lift; keep your chin at a neutral angle, not tucked to your chest.

mistakes.wrong: Hands not under the low back
mistakes.right: Keep both hands under your low back's natural arch the whole time to preserve that curve.

name: Kettlebell Deadlift
instructions: Stand with feet shoulder-width apart and set the kettlebell on the floor between your feet, in line with your shoelaces. The handle is the metal loop on top; the two curved sides of that loop are called the horns.

Push your hips straight back — not down — until your hands reach the handle. Your shins stay close to vertical and your knees only bend a little. This backward hip travel is the hip hinge, and it is the one pattern every kettlebell movement is built on.
Grip the handle with both hands. Flatten your back, pull your shoulders down away from your ears, take a breath in and brace your stomach like you are about to be poked.
Stand up by driving your feet into the floor and pushing your hips forward. Finish tall with your glutes squeezed. The bell hangs at arm's length — your arms never pull, they are just hooks.
Lower by pushing your hips back again, keeping the bell tracking close to your legs. Touch the floor lightly and reset your brace before the next rep.
cues: Hips go back, not down — imagine closing a car door with your backside
Keep the bell close to your shins the whole way; letting it drift forward loads your low back
Squeeze your glutes to finish, do not lean back at the top
modification: If you cannot reach the floor with a flat back, stand the kettlebell on a box or a couple of weight plates so it starts higher. Start light — 12-16 kg is plenty for learning the pattern.

sensation.feelHere: A strong stretch up the back of your thighs on the way down, glutes squeezing at the top.
sensation.notHere: A tight band of ache across your low back. That means your back is lifting instead of your hips.
sensation.firstCue: Push your hips straight back and lower for a slow 3 count.

wrongSpot.fix: The bell drifted forward. Keep it brushing your shins and start the stand-up by driving your feet down, not by pulling with your back.
You are squatting it up. Let your knees stay mostly straight and send your hips further back until you feel your hamstrings load.
Your range is too short or the bell is too light. Go one size heavier and lower until the hamstrings first pull tight.
Pull your shoulder blades down into your back pockets before you stand, and keep them there for the whole rep.

sensation.nextDay: Hamstrings and glutes ache for 1-3 days. Low-back stiffness on waking is not expected.
sensation.backNote: The failure mode is your low back rounding at the bottom. Stop lowering the moment your hamstrings feel tight — not when the bell reaches the floor. Raise the bell on a box if needed.
sensation.stopIf: Anything shoots, burns or tingles down a leg, or a foot goes numb or feels weak.

mistakes.wrong: Rounding the back to reach lower
mistakes.right: Keep your chest proud and your back flat. If you cannot reach the handle flat-backed, raise the bell on a box.
Knees bend only slightly. The movement is hips travelling backward, then forward — not up and down.
Finish standing straight with glutes squeezed and ribs down. Leaning back jams your lower spine.

name: Kettlebell Good Morning
instructions: Hold the kettlebell at your chest in the front rack — that means one bell held close to your sternum with the ball of the bell resting against your chest and forearms, elbows tucked down at your ribs. Here you can simply hold it by both horns with two hands, like the top of a goblet squat.
Stand with feet hip-width apart, knees softly unlocked. Take a breath in and brace your stomach.
Push your hips straight back and let your chest travel forward as one solid piece. Your spine does not change shape — your whole torso tips like a drawbridge from the hip joints.

Stop the moment you feel your hamstrings pull tight. For most people that is somewhere between 30 and 45 degrees of forward lean, well above horizontal. Going lower than your hamstrings allow is what makes the back round.

Drive your hips forward to stand tall and squeeze your glutes. This is step two of the ladder to the kettlebell swing: the deadlift taught you the hinge, this teaches you to hold it under a load that is trying to tip you over.
cues: Hinge from the hips only — your spine stays one rigid piece from tailbone to head
Stop when the hamstrings first feel tight, not when you run out of nerve
Keep the bell glued to your chest; if it pulls away, your upper back is rounding
modification: Learn it with no weight first, hands crossed over your chest. Stand a fist's distance from a wall and tap it with your backside each rep — that teaches the hips to go back instead of down.

sensation.feelHere: A deep stretch up the back of both thighs, and your upper back working to hold the bell in.
sensation.notHere: A pinching or gripping ache low in the spine. That is flexion, not hamstring load.
sensation.firstCue: Unlock your knees and push your hips back — lower for a slow 3 count.

wrongSpot.fix: You went past your hamstrings' range and the spine picked up the slack. Cut the depth by a third and stop at first hamstring tension.
The bell has drifted away from your body. Pull it back into your sternum and keep your elbows pointing down at your ribs.
Your knees are bending too much, turning this into a squat. Keep the shins vertical and send the hips further behind your heels.
You are craning to look forward. Let your eyes travel down the floor with your chest so your neck stays in line with your spine.

sensation.nextDay: Hamstring soreness for 1-2 days is expected. Low-back soreness means the depth was too deep.
sensation.backNote: This loads the spine in front, so any rounding is magnified. Hips go back, not down, and the descent ends at first hamstring tightness — depth is never the goal here.
sensation.stopIf: Pain travels from your back down into the buttock or leg, or a leg tingles or goes numb.

mistakes.right: Range is set by your hamstrings, not by ambition. A 30-45 degree lean done rigid beats a deep lean done rounded.
Keep it pinned to your sternum with elbows down. A bell out in front multiplies the load on your spine.

mistakes.wrong: Bending the knees like a squat
mistakes.right: Knees stay softly unlocked and roughly still. Only the hips move backward.

name: Kettlebell Hike Pass
instructions: Set the kettlebell on the floor about a foot in front of your toes. Feet shoulder-width, toes slightly out. Push your hips back and reach forward for the handle so your arms are long and your back is flat — hips higher than knees.

Tilt the bell back toward you so it is tipped up on its edge and the handle points at you. Pull your shoulders down and squeeze your armpits as if crushing a newspaper under each arm — this stops the bell yanking your shoulders forward.

Hike the bell: sharply throw it back and up between your legs, like a football centre snapping the ball. It passes high, close to your groin — not down near the floor. This is the hike, and it is where a kettlebell behaves nothing like a dumbbell: the weight hangs below the handle so it wants to keep travelling.

The instant the bell reaches the back of its arc, drive your hips forward and stand tall — glutes squeezed, ribs down, a standing plank. Let the bell swing forward only to about hip height. Do not try to float it up. There is no swing yet.

Let it come back down, hinge to receive it between your legs again, then park it on the floor. This is step three of the ladder to the kettlebell swing — hike plus stand. Once these feel automatic, adding hip snap turns it into the swing.
cues: The bell passes high between your thighs, close to your groin — not scraping the floor
Your arms are ropes; your hips do all the work
Stand tall and stop — resist the urge to swing the bell up. That comes later
modification: Practise single hikes: hike back, stand, park the bell, reset. One rep at a time until the hinge is automatic, then link them into continuous reps.

sensation.feelHere: A sharp stretch in the hamstrings at the back of the hike, then a hard glute squeeze standing up.
sensation.notHere: A jolt or ache in the low back at the back of the hike. That is your spine catching the bell.
sensation.firstCue: Hike the bell high and close to your groin, then stand tall and pause one full second.

wrongSpot.felt: Low back jolts on the backswing
wrongSpot.fix: The bell is passing too low and dragging you into a round back. Aim it higher, right up against your groin, with the arms tight to your ribs.
You are lifting with the arms. Squeeze your armpits down hard so the arms stay connected to your torso and just follow the hips.
You are squatting the bell back. Keep the shins vertical and send only the hips backwards.
Normal at first — the offset weight tugs the handle. Hold with a relaxed hook grip rather than a white-knuckle squeeze, and rest longer.

sensation.nextDay: Hamstrings, glutes and forearms sore for 1-2 days. Low-back soreness is a form signal, not progress.
sensation.backNote: The one real risk is the spine rounding as the bell travels back. Keep it passing high and close to your groin, and stop the set the moment your back rounds — not when you run out of reps.
sensation.stopIf: Anything shoots into the buttock or down a leg, or a leg tingles, goes numb, or feels weak.

mistakes.wrong: Letting the bell dip near the floor
mistakes.right: It should pass high and tight to your groin. A low pass forces the back to round to catch it.

mistakes.wrong: Swinging the bell up with the arms
mistakes.right: Stand tall and let the bell rise no higher than your hips. This drill is deliberately not a swing.

mistakes.wrong: Standing with a soft, unbraced middle
mistakes.right: Brace your stomach before every hike. A loose middle passes the force straight into your spine.

name: Kettlebell Halo
instructions: Hold a light kettlebell upside down at chest height, gripping the horns — the two curved sides of the handle — so the ball of the bell sits above your hands. Elbows tucked in, bell close to your chest.
Stand tall with feet hip-width, ribs pulled down, glutes lightly squeezed. Your body from hips to head stays perfectly still — only your arms move.
Circle the bell around your head: take it past one ear, behind your head at the base of your skull, past the other ear, and back to the front. Keep it grazing close to you the whole way.

The bell can clip your head if you let it swing wide or lose the horns, so start with the lightest bell available and go slowly. Keep your elbows tucked in tight, keep the bell touching or nearly touching you throughout, and never let it orbit out at arm's length.
Complete the reps circling one direction, then reverse. Ten reps means ten circles — count each full lap.
cues: Move slowly — the bell's weight sits above your hands, so it wants to tip and pull
Only your arms move; your ribcage and hips stay locked in place
Keep the bell hugging close to your head, never out at arm's length
modification: Start with the lightest bell in the rack (6-8 kg) — this is a mobility drill, not a strength lift. If reaching behind your head is tight, circle in front and only as far back as feels easy, widening the circle over weeks. Kneeling on both knees removes any temptation to lean.

sensation.feelHere: A stretch and light burn across the tops of the shoulders and the muscles between your shoulder blades.
sensation.notHere: A sharp pinch at the front point of the shoulder as the bell passes behind. That is the joint, not the muscle.
sensation.firstCue: Keep your ribs pulled down and take a slow 4 count per full circle.

wrongSpot.felt: Sharp pinch at the front of the shoulder
wrongSpot.fix: That is joint, not muscle. Stop the set, drop to a lighter bell and shrink the circle so the bell stays nearer your ears.
Your ribs are flaring as the bell goes behind. Pull your ribs down, squeeze your glutes, and reduce how far back you take it.
You are ducking to get out of the bell's way. Keep your head still and instead widen your path slightly around the skull.
Grip the horns lower and keep your knuckles stacked over your forearms. The bell's mass sits above your hands and will fold the wrist if you let it.

sensation.nextDay: Mild tightness across the shoulders and upper back for a day. Sharp shoulder pain is not expected.
sensation.backNote: Only if you let your ribs flare and arch backwards as the bell passes behind your head. Keep ribs down and glutes lightly squeezed and the spine stays out of it.
sensation.stopIf: Pain or tingling runs down your arm, or your hand goes numb.

mistakes.wrong: Circling the bell at arm's length
mistakes.right: Keep it close — elbows tucked, bell almost grazing your head. A wide orbit is what makes it hit you.

mistakes.wrong: Leaning the torso to make room
mistakes.right: Body stays still; only the arms move. If you have to lean, the bell is too heavy or the circle too wide.
This is a mobility drill. The lightest bell available is the right bell — heavier just risks your head and shoulders.

name: Kettlebell Single-Arm Row
instructions: Place your left hand and left knee on a flat bench, right foot on the floor a little behind you. The kettlebell sits on the floor under your right shoulder. Your back should be flat and roughly parallel to the floor — supported like this, the bench carries the load instead of your spine.
Reach down and grip the handle. Pull your right shoulder blade down and back before your elbow bends at all. Brace your stomach.

Row the bell up to the side of your ribcage, driving your elbow back past your torso rather than flaring it out. Because the weight hangs below the handle, the bell wants to swing — keep it tracking in a straight line beside your body.
Pause for a beat at the top with the shoulder blade squeezed toward your spine, then lower for a slow 3 count until your arm is fully straight and you feel the stretch down the side of your back.
Complete all reps on one side, then swap. Keep your shoulders level with each other throughout — do not let your torso twist to help the bell up.
cues: Lead with the elbow, not the hand — think of your arm as a hook
Pull the shoulder blade down and back first, then bend the elbow
Keep your shoulders square to the floor; twisting turns this into a back-strain exercise
modification: No bench available: stagger your stance and rest your free hand on a rack upright or the top of a heavy dumbbell for support. Start with 12-16 kg and add weight only once your torso stays completely still.

sensation.feelHere: The side of your back under the armpit doing the pulling, plus the muscles between your shoulder blades.
sensation.notHere: Mostly the front of your upper arm. That means your biceps took over from your back.
sensation.firstCue: Pull your shoulder blade down and back before bending the elbow. Lower for a slow 3 count.

wrongSpot.felt: Front of the upper arm only
wrongSpot.fix: Your biceps are leading. Start each rep by drawing the shoulder blade toward your spine, then let the elbow follow.

wrongSpot.felt: Top of the shoulder or neck
wrongSpot.fix: You are shrugging the bell up. Pull your shoulder down away from your ear at the start and keep it there the whole rep.

wrongSpot.felt: Low back on the working side
wrongSpot.fix: Your torso is twisting to help. Go lighter and keep both shoulders level with the floor for every rep.
You are gripping too tight and pulling with the hand. Loosen the grip and think of dragging the elbow toward your back pocket.

sensation.nextDay: The side of your back and between the shoulder blades ache for 1-2 days. Elbow soreness is not expected.
sensation.backNote: Supported on a bench this barely loads the spine. Keep your back flat and level — the risk is twisting or letting your low back sag, not the rowing itself.
sensation.stopIf: Pain or tingling runs down your arm, or your hand goes numb or feels weak.

mistakes.right: Keep both shoulders level with the floor. If you have to rotate to finish the rep, the bell is too heavy.
Drive the elbow backwards close to your ribs. A flared elbow shifts the work off your back and onto the shoulder joint.
Let the arm straighten fully each rep. That stretch at the bottom is where most of the back work happens.

name: Kettlebell Suitcase Carry
instructions: Stand the kettlebell beside one foot. Pick it up by hinging — hips back, back flat, one hand on the handle — exactly as you would in a deadlift. Never stoop down with a rounded back to grab it.
Stand tall with the bell hanging at your side like a heavy suitcase. Pull your shoulders down and back, ribs down, stomach braced. Both shoulders should be level and both hips should be level.
Walk at a normal, unhurried pace for the full time. The whole point is that your torso does NOT bend sideways toward the weight — you should look, from behind, exactly as you would carrying nothing.
Do not lean away from the bell to counterbalance it either. Stay stacked and let the muscles down the opposite side of your torso do the work of keeping you upright.
At the end, set the bell down by hinging again, then repeat carrying it in the other hand. One set means one carry per side.
cues: Stand as tall as if you were carrying nothing — no side lean either way
Shoulders level, hips level, ribs down, stomach lightly braced the whole walk
If your torso starts tipping toward the bell, the set is over — put it down
modification: Too heavy to stay upright? Go lighter — this is a stability drill, and a bell you can only carry crooked teaches the wrong thing. To progress, add time before you add weight: 30 seconds, then 45, then 60 per side.

sensation.feelHere: The side of your waist opposite the bell working hard to hold you upright, plus a burning grip.
sensation.notHere: The low back on the same side as the bell. That means you are side-bending toward the weight.
sensation.firstCue: Stand tall with both shoulders level, then walk slowly without letting the bell tip you over.

wrongSpot.felt: Low back on the loaded side
wrongSpot.fix: You are side-bending toward the bell. Go lighter, pull the shoulder on that side down and back, and keep both hips level as you walk.
Also a fail — you are counterbalancing instead of bracing. Go lighter and stay stacked over your feet.

wrongSpot.felt: Neck and top of the shoulder
wrongSpot.fix: The bell is dragging your shoulder down and you are fighting it with your trap. Pull the shoulder blade down and back and keep it packed.

wrongSpot.felt: Grip gives out before time is up
wrongSpot.fix: That is fine and expected early on. Set it down, rest, and count grip as the limiter rather than reducing the carry time.

sensation.nextDay: Sides of the waist and forearms mildly sore for a day. Low-back soreness means you were side-bending.
sensation.backNote: This is one of the most back-friendly loaded exercises there is — it trains your spine to resist bending. The only failure mode is letting your torso tip sideways. Any low-back ache on the loaded side means stop and go lighter.
sensation.stopIf: Anything shoots into the buttock or down a leg, or a leg tingles or goes numb.

mistakes.right: Stay perfectly upright. Bending toward the bell removes the exercise and puts the load into your low back.
Keep the loaded shoulder pulled down and back. A dragged-down shoulder collapses that whole side of your torso.

mistakes.wrong: Stooping to pick it up or set it down
mistakes.right: Hinge at the hips with a flat back both ways. More backs are hurt picking bells up than carrying them.

name: Hollow Hold
instructions: Lie on your back on the mat. Press your low back flat into the floor and hold it there — this is the position you must keep for the whole hold, so find it before you move anything else.

Lift your shoulders and head slightly off the floor, and raise your legs to whatever height lets your low back stay pressed down. For most people starting out that means knees bent, feet just off the floor, or even just heels down and legs flat.
Reach your arms long overhead, just off the floor, so your body makes a shallow curve from fingertips to toes. Breathe normally through the hold — do not hold your breath.

The moment your low back lifts away from the floor, the hold has already ended even if you keep your shape — bring your legs higher or bend your knees more and reset. A smaller shape with a flat back beats a bigger shape with an arch.
Hold for the set time, then lower everything down gently and rest. Build the time before you ever lower the legs further.
cues: Low back stays glued to the floor the entire time — that is the whole exercise
Legs higher and knees bent is the regression, not the failure — use it
Breathe steadily, do not brace by holding your breath
modification: Bend your knees to 90 degrees and keep feet flat or just hovering, and keep your shoulders barely off the floor. Shrink the shape until your low back stays flat.

sensation.feelHere: A deep, steady clench low across your stomach, below the belly button.
sensation.notHere: Your low back pressing up off the floor, or a pulling ache in the front of your hips.
sensation.firstCue: Press your low back flat first. Only then lift shoulders and legs a little.

wrongSpot.felt: Low back lifting off the floor
wrongSpot.fix: That means the range is too big. Bend your knees more and bring your legs higher until your back re-flattens.
Bend your knees and shorten the reach of your legs — this is a hip flexor overload, not a core one.
Lower your head back down and only lift your shoulder blades, not your chin.

sensation.nextDay: A deep central-ab ache for a day or two is normal. Low back soreness is not.
sensation.backNote: The whole point of this exercise is teaching your spine to hold still under tension. If your back arches even slightly, the exercise has stopped working for you — shorten it immediately rather than fighting to hold the bigger shape.
sensation.stopIf: Any shooting or electric pain, or numbness or tingling anywhere down a leg.

mistakes.right: Keep legs higher and knees bent until your low back stays flat the whole time — smaller and correct beats bigger and arched.
Breathe steadily through the nose or mouth the entire hold; bracing does not require breath-holding.

name: Reverse Crunch
instructions: Lie on your back with knees bent to 90 degrees, shins roughly parallel to the floor, and arms flat on the mat at your sides for support. Press your low back gently into the floor before you start.
Exhale and curl your hips slightly off the floor, drawing your knees a small amount toward your chest. The movement is small — think an inch or two of hip lift, not a big swing.
Pause briefly at the top with your low back still touching the floor, then inhale and lower your hips back down under control until your tailbone rests down again.
Keep the motion slow and deliberate throughout. This is a short, controlled range exercise, not a momentum swing — resist the urge to rock or use your arms to push off the floor.
Repeat for the set number of reps, resetting your low back against the floor before each one.
cues: Small controlled range — an inch or two of hip lift is enough
Low back stays down; if it arches at the bottom, you went too far
Curl, don't swing — no momentum from your arms or legs
modification: Do the movement with knees bent even tighter and only lift the hips a very small amount, focusing entirely on the low-back-stays-down cue before adding range.

sensation.feelHere: A tight squeeze low in your abdomen, just below the belly button, as your hips curl.
sensation.notHere: Your low back arching at the bottom, or your hip flexors doing all the work with no ab squeeze.
sensation.firstCue: Press low back down first, then curl hips up a small, controlled amount.

wrongSpot.felt: Low back arching at the bottom
wrongSpot.fix: You're lowering too far and too fast. Stop the lower a little sooner and control it down slowly.
Slow down. Use your arms flat on the floor for stability, not to push you up.
Keep your head and shoulders resting on the floor — this is a hip movement, not a shoulder crunch.

sensation.nextDay: A central lower-ab ache for a day or two is expected. Low back soreness is not.
sensation.backNote: A small controlled range is the entire point — a bigger swing lets the low back arch at the bottom, which is the failure mode to avoid. Keep it short.
sensation.stopIf: Any shooting or electric pain, or numbness or tingling down a leg.

mistakes.right: Keep the hip lift small — an inch or two — and control every inch of it.

mistakes.wrong: Letting the low back arch at the bottom
mistakes.right: Stop the descent before your back lifts and reset your low back against the floor each rep.

name: Plank Shoulder Tap
instructions: Set up in a high plank with hands under your shoulders, feet set a little wider than hip-width for a stable base, and your body in a straight line from head to heels. Brace your core before you move.
Keeping your hips as still and level as possible, lift one hand and tap the opposite shoulder, then set it back down exactly where it started.
Repeat with the other hand tapping its opposite shoulder. Your hips should stay square to the floor the whole time — no rocking side to side.
If your hips start to twist or rock with each tap, that is the exercise breaking down, not a minor detail. Slow down until they stop moving, and if they still move, widen your feet further.
Alternate sides for the set count, keeping the pace slow and controlled rather than fast.
cues: Hips stay square and still — that is the entire exercise
Widen your feet if you feel yourself rocking
Slow, controlled taps beat fast sloppy ones
modification: Do the taps from a plank on your knees instead of your toes, keeping the same wide hand and knee base for stability.

sensation.feelHere: A steady brace through your sides and stomach, resisting the urge to rotate.
sensation.notHere: Your hips swaying or twisting with each tap, or your low back sagging toward the floor.
sensation.firstCue: Brace your core hard, widen your feet, then tap slowly.

wrongSpot.fix: Widen your feet and slow the tap down — the tap should not move your hips at all.
Squeeze your glutes and brace your stomach before each tap; you may be losing your plank shape from fatigue.
Spread your fingers wide and stack your wrist directly under your shoulder.

sensation.nextDay: A broad ache across your sides and stomach for a day or two is normal. Low back soreness is not.
sensation.backNote: The hips rocking is the anti-rotation challenge working against you — that IS the exercise failing, not just imperfect form. Slow down or widen your stance rather than pushing through a twisting hip.
sensation.stopIf: Any shooting or electric pain, or numbness or tingling anywhere down a leg.

mistakes.wrong: Letting hips rock with each tap
mistakes.right: Widen your base and slow down until your hips stay completely still through every tap.
Treat each tap as a slow, controlled movement — speed is not the goal here.

name: Side Plank Rotation
instructions: Set up in a side plank on your forearm, elbow under your shoulder, knees bent for a stable version or legs straight if that's comfortable for you. Lift your top arm straight toward the ceiling and brace your side.
Slowly rotate your torso and thread your top arm underneath your body, through the gap between your torso and the floor, following your hand with your eyes.
Pause briefly once your arm has threaded through as far as feels controlled, then rotate back and reach your arm back up toward the ceiling.
Keep the movement small and slow rather than reaching for maximum rotation — the goal is a controlled twist through your side, not a big swing that drops your hips.
Repeat for the set number of reps, then switch sides and repeat with the other arm.
cues: Small, slow rotation — control beats reach
Keep your hips lifted and stacked throughout, don't let them sag or drop
Follow your hand with your eyes to keep the movement smooth
modification: Keep your knees bent and stacked on the floor for a shorter lever, and rotate through a smaller range until your side gets stronger.

sensation.feelHere: A deep working burn along the side of your waist and stomach as you thread the arm.
sensation.notHere: Your hips dropping toward the floor, or a pinch in your shoulder as you thread through.
sensation.firstCue: Lift hips first, brace your side, then thread the arm slowly.

wrongSpot.fix: Shrink the range of the thread — only rotate as far as your hips stay lifted.
Slow down the thread and keep your supporting elbow stacked directly under your shoulder.
Bend your knees and stack them on the floor for a wider, more stable base.

sensation.nextDay: A working ache through your side and waist for a day or two is normal.
sensation.stopIf: Any shooting or electric pain, or numbness or tingling down a leg or arm.

mistakes.right: Keep the rotation small and controlled — only go as far as your hips stay lifted and stacked.

mistakes.wrong: Letting hips sag toward the floor
mistakes.right: Keep your hips lifted throughout; if they drop, shorten the rotation.

name: Bear Crawl Hold
instructions: Start on all fours with hands under shoulders and knees under hips, spine in a neutral, flat line — not arched, not rounded. This is your quadruped tabletop position.
Curl your toes under and lift your knees just an inch off the floor. That's the whole lift — this is not a push-up-height hover, it's barely off the ground.
Hold this position, keeping your back flat and your hips level with your shoulders. Breathe steadily; do not hold your breath while bracing.
If your low back rounds up toward the ceiling or sags down, the hold has broken even if your knees are still hovering — lower your knees back to the floor, reset your flat spine, and lift again.
Hold for the set time. As you build strength, hold longer before you ever try lifting your knees higher.
cues: Knees hover just an inch off the floor — no higher
Flat back the whole time, not rounded or sagging
Breathe steadily, don't hold your breath to brace
modification: Keep your knees resting lightly on the floor while you practice bracing a flat back — build the brace before you add the lift.

sensation.feelHere: A steady, whole-body brace through your stomach, shoulders, and hips.
sensation.notHere: Your low back rounding upward, or your shoulders shaking and collapsing.
sensation.firstCue: Flatten your spine first, then lift knees just an inch.

wrongSpot.fix: Lower your knees back to the floor, reset a flat spine, and lift only an inch this time.
Brace your stomach harder before lifting — you're letting your midsection relax under the hold.
Spread your fingers wide and shift a little weight back toward your knees.

sensation.nextDay: A broad ache through your stomach, shoulders, and hips for a day or two is normal. Low back soreness is not.
sensation.backNote: The failure mode here is the spine rounding or sagging out of its flat line — if that happens, the hold has already ended even if your knees are still up. Reset rather than fight to hold the shape.
sensation.stopIf: Any shooting or electric pain, or numbness or tingling anywhere down a leg or arm.

mistakes.right: Keep the lift to about an inch — this is a hover, not a push-up height plank.
Reset to a flat back the moment you feel your low back rounding, rather than holding through it.

name: Dumbbell Farmer's Carry
instructions: Pick up a 15 lb dumbbell in each hand and stand tall — shoulders back and down, chest up, core braced, like you're carrying two suitcases that are trying to pull you forward.
Walk forward at a normal, controlled pace, keeping your torso upright and still. Don't let the weights swing or your shoulders hike up toward your ears.
Keep your steps even and your breathing steady throughout. Your grip will want to fatigue before your core does — that's normal.
Walk for the set time, in a straight line or back and forth across the room if space is limited, then set the dumbbells down under control rather than dropping them.
This is one of the most underrated things you can do for your core and back — it trains real-world bracing under load, not just isolated ab work.
cues: Stand tall — shoulders back, chest up, don't let the weight round you forward
Steady, even steps — no swinging the dumbbells
Keep your core braced the entire walk, like carrying full suitcases
modification: Use 10 lb dumbbells or shorten the carry time to 20 seconds while you build grip and core endurance.

sensation.feelHere: A steady, whole-body brace through your core, plus grip fatigue in your forearms.
sensation.notHere: A pulling ache in your low back, or your shoulders shrugging up toward your ears.
sensation.firstCue: Stand tall and brace your core before your first step.

wrongSpot.fix: You're leaning back to counterbalance the weight. Stand taller and brace your core rather than arching your back.
Actively pull your shoulders down and back every few steps — don't let the weight shrug you up.
Keep your torso centered between both hands — resist the urge to lean away from either weight.

sensation.nextDay: Forearm and core fatigue for a day or two is normal. Low back soreness is not.
sensation.backNote: Stand tall throughout — the risk here is leaning back to counterbalance the load, which loads the low back. Keep your ribs stacked over your hips.
sensation.stopIf: Any shooting or electric pain, or numbness or tingling down a leg or arm.

mistakes.right: Stand tall with ribs stacked over hips — let your core carry the load, not a backward lean.
Keep a steady, controlled pace — this is a bracing exercise, not a race.

name: Dumbbell Suitcase Carry
instructions: Pick up a single 15 lb dumbbell in one hand only and stand tall, letting it hang naturally by your side like a suitcase. Your other hand stays free at your side.
Brace your core and stand as level as possible — your torso should not lean toward the weight to compensate, nor lean away from it.
Walk forward at a steady, controlled pace for the set time, keeping your shoulders level and your torso upright the entire way.

Anti-side-bend is the entire point here — your obliques on the loaded side are working to keep you upright against the pull of the weight. If your torso tips either direction, that's the exercise breaking down.
Set the weight down under control at the end, then switch hands and repeat on the other side.
cues: Torso stays level — no leaning toward or away from the weight
Shoulders even, not one hiked higher than the other
Steady steps, core braced the whole way
modification: Use a 10 lb dumbbell or shorten the carry to 15 seconds per side while you build the anti-side-bend strength.

sensation.feelHere: A steady working burn along the side of your waist on the carrying side, holding you upright.
sensation.notHere: A low-back ache on the loaded side — that's a sign you're side-bending instead of staying level.
sensation.firstCue: Stand level before your first step — no lean either direction.

wrongSpot.felt: Low back ache on the loaded side
wrongSpot.fix: You're side-bending toward the weight. Stand taller and keep your torso vertical — brace your obliques instead of leaning.
Overcorrecting is just side-bending the other direction. Aim for dead level, not a lean either way.
Let the weight hang naturally — don't shrug it up to shorten the arm.

sensation.nextDay: A working ache along the side of your waist for a day or two is normal. Low back soreness on the loaded side is not.
sensation.backNote: The tell for doing this wrong is a low-back ache on the loaded side — that means you're side-bending rather than holding level. Stay upright; the weight should not tip your torso in either direction.
sensation.stopIf: Any shooting or electric pain, or numbness or tingling down a leg or arm.

mistakes.right: Keep your torso vertical and level — resist the pull with your side, not by leaning.
Aim for dead level, not a lean in either direction.

name: Bird Dog Row
instructions: Start on all fours with one hand holding a 10 lb dumbbell and the other flat on the mat, knees under your hips, spine neutral. This is your tabletop position — set your hips level before you move.
Extend the leg on the opposite side of the dumbbell straight back behind you, foot flexed, keeping your hips square to the floor.
With your leg still extended, row the dumbbell up toward your ribs, keeping your elbow close to your body, then lower it back down under control without letting your torso rotate.
Your hips must stay square through the entire row — if they rock or twist as the dumbbell comes up, that is the exercise failing, not a small detail. Slow down or use a lighter weight if needed.
Complete all reps on one side with the leg extended, then switch — opposite hand holds the dumbbell, opposite leg extends back.
cues: Hips stay square through the entire row — that is the whole exercise
Elbow stays close to your body as you row
Slow down if you feel any twist through your hips
modification: Do the row with your knee down on the floor instead of the leg extended, to remove the balance challenge while you learn the anti-rotation cue.

sensation.feelHere: A steady brace through your stomach and low back, plus a squeeze between your shoulder blade and spine as you row.
sensation.notHere: Your hips twisting open, or your low back sagging as you pull the weight up.
sensation.firstCue: Square your hips first, then row slowly without letting them move.

wrongSpot.fix: That IS the exercise failing. Slow down, use a lighter weight, or keep your knee down until your hips stay square.
Re-brace your core before the row — you may have lost the tabletop position.
Pull your shoulder blade down and back before rowing, keep the elbow close to your ribs.

sensation.nextDay: A working ache through your back and stomach for a day or two is normal. Low back soreness is not.
sensation.backNote: Square hips are the whole point of this exercise. If your hips rock or twist during the row, that is the failure mode — slow down or drop the weight rather than push through a twisting hip.
sensation.stopIf: Any shooting or electric pain, or numbness or tingling down a leg or arm.

mistakes.wrong: Letting hips twist during the row
mistakes.right: Keep hips square the whole time — go lighter or slower rather than let them rotate.
Bend your elbow and pull it close to your ribs so your back does the work, not your arm swinging.

name: Heel Taps
instructions: Lie on your back with knees bent to 90 degrees, shins parallel to the floor, arms flat at your sides. Press your low back firmly into the floor before you start moving.
Slowly lower one heel down to tap the floor, keeping the knee bent at the same angle the whole way down, then bring it back up to the starting height.
Alternate heels, tapping one down and back, then the other, in a slow and controlled rhythm.

The legs going lower toward the floor makes this harder, so keeping the knees higher — a smaller range — is the regression, not a shortcut. The moment your low back lifts off the floor, you've gone too low; raise your starting knee height.
Continue alternating for the set number of reps, keeping your breathing steady throughout.
cues: Low back stays flat on the floor — that's the rule, every rep
Legs higher is the easier version — use it if the back lifts
Slow, controlled taps, not fast kicking
modification: Keep your knees higher, closer to your chest, and tap down only a short distance — the smaller the range, the easier it is to keep the low back flat.

sensation.feelHere: A steady clench low across your stomach as each heel lowers.
sensation.notHere: Your low back lifting off the floor, or a pulling cramp at the front of your hip.
sensation.firstCue: Press low back flat first, then tap one heel down slowly.

wrongSpot.felt: Low back lifting off the floor
wrongSpot.fix: Raise your starting knee height — a smaller range with a flat back is correct, a bigger range with an arch is not.
Keep the knees higher and shorten how far the heel travels toward the floor.
Slow each tap down — this is a control exercise, not a speed one.

sensation.nextDay: A deep central-ab ache for a day or two is normal. Low back soreness is not.
sensation.backNote: The rule is simple: if the low back lifts away from the floor, the range is too big — shorten it. Legs going lower makes it harder; keeping them higher is always the correct regression, not a compromise.
sensation.stopIf: Any shooting or electric pain, or numbness or tingling down a leg.

mistakes.right: Raise your knee height and tap less far down until your back stays flat the whole time.
Slow every tap down — control matters more than range here.

name: Weighted Dead Bug
instructions: Lie flat on your back with knees bent to 90 degrees in tabletop position. Hold a single 10 lb dumbbell in both hands, arms straight up over your chest, directly above your shoulders.
Press your low back into the floor and brace before you move. Exhale and slowly lower one leg toward the floor while keeping the dumbbell steady overhead — the weight does not move, only the leg.
Lower the leg only as far as your low back stays pressed flat into the floor. If it starts to arch, that's your limit for today — stop there.
Inhale and bring the leg back to tabletop under control, keeping the dumbbell steady overhead throughout the entire rep.
Alternate legs for the set number of reps, resetting your low back against the floor before each one.
cues: Low back stays flat — the moment it arches, shorten the range
Dumbbell stays steady overhead, arms don't wobble or drift
Slow leg lower, slow leg return — no rushing
modification: Do the movement without the dumbbell first, or hold it at chest height instead of fully overhead until your core control catches up.

sensation.feelHere: A deep, steady brace low across your stomach, plus your shoulders working to keep the weight steady.
sensation.notHere: Your low back arching off the floor, or the dumbbell wobbling side to side.
sensation.firstCue: Press low back flat, steady the weight overhead, then lower one leg slowly.

wrongSpot.fix: That's the failure mode — shorten how far you lower the leg, going only as low as your back stays flat.
Lighten the pace and keep your arms locked straight, shoulders pulled down away from your ears.
Lower the leg less far and keep a slight bend in the knee.

sensation.nextDay: A deep central-ab ache and some shoulder fatigue for a day or two is normal. Low back soreness is not.
sensation.backNote: The rule is simple and worth repeating here too — if the low back lifts away from the floor, the range is too big. Shorten the leg lower, don't push through an arching back to hold the weight steady.
sensation.stopIf: Any shooting or electric pain, or numbness or tingling down a leg or arm.

mistakes.wrong: Letting the back arch to lower the leg further
mistakes.right: Stop the leg lower the instant your low back lifts — a shorter range with a flat back is the correct version.

mistakes.wrong: Letting the dumbbell drift or wobble
mistakes.right: Keep your arms locked and steady overhead the entire time — the weight should not move at all.

name: Copenhagen Plank (Short Lever)
instructions: Lie on your side facing a bench or step, and rest your top leg's knee (not your ankle) on the raised surface, with that knee bent. Your bottom leg stays free underneath you.
Prop yourself up on your bottom forearm, elbow under your shoulder, and lift your hips off the floor into a side plank shape, supported by your forearm and your top knee on the bench.
Hold this position, squeezing your top inner thigh against the bench to keep your hips lifted and level. Keep your body in a straight line from shoulder to knee.
This short-lever version — knee supported rather than ankle — is the sane starting point. Going to the longer ankle-supported version too early is how groin strains happen, so don't rush toward it.
Hold for the set time, then lower down and switch sides.
cues: Knee on the bench, not the ankle — this is the short-lever starting point
Squeeze the inner thigh to hold your hips level and lifted
Genuinely hard — a shorter hold with good shape beats a longer one that sags
modification: Rest your bottom knee on the floor as well for extra support, or reduce the hold to 8-10 seconds while your adductors build capacity.

sensation.feelHere: A deep, hard working burn in your inner thigh, right where your top knee presses the bench.
sensation.notHere: A pinching or sharp pain in your groin, or your low back doing the work instead of your inner thigh.
sensation.firstCue: Squeeze the inner thigh into the bench before you lift your hips.

wrongSpot.fix: Shorten the hold time rather than fight to keep bad form — a shorter, well-held rep beats a longer sagging one.
Stop the set. This muscle group strains easily — back off to a shorter hold and don't progress to the ankle version yet.
Reset your body in a straight line and rely on your inner thigh squeeze to hold you up, not a back arch.

sensation.nextDay: A deep inner-thigh ache for 1-3 days is normal and expected — this muscle group is rarely trained. Sharp groin pain is not.
sensation.stopIf: Any sharp, sudden, or pulling pain in the groin — stop immediately and do not push through it.

mistakes.wrong: Progressing to the ankle-supported version too soon
mistakes.right: Stay with the knee-supported short lever until it feels genuinely manageable — groin strains come from rushing this progression.

mistakes.wrong: Letting hips sag to extend the hold time
mistakes.right: Shorten the hold rather than let your shape collapse — good shape at a shorter time is the actual progress.

name: Standing Band Anti-Rotation Press
instructions: Stand with feet hip-width apart and step one end of the resistance band under the same-side foot. Hold the other end with both hands at chest height — your own foot is the anchor, there is no need for a wall or post.
Stand tall with the band pulling across your chest toward the anchored foot. Brace your core so your hips and torso stay square and facing forward.
Press both hands straight out in front of your chest against the band's pull, keeping your hips completely still and square — resist the urge to let your torso twist toward the anchor side.
Pause briefly at full extension, then bring your hands back to your chest under control, still resisting the band's pull the entire way.
Complete all reps on one side, keeping your hips square throughout, then switch which foot anchors the band and repeat facing the same direction.
cues: Hips stay square and still — if they rock or twist, that is the exercise failing
Your own foot is the anchor — no wall or door needed
Slow press out, slow return, resisting the band both ways
modification: Use a lighter step-on grip closer to the band's slack end to reduce resistance, or reduce reps to 8 while you build the anti-rotation brace.

sensation.feelHere: A steady bracing burn through your side and stomach, resisting the band's pull to twist you.
sensation.notHere: Your hips or shoulders rotating toward the anchor side, or your low back arching to compensate.
sensation.firstCue: Brace your core and square your hips before you press out.

wrongSpot.fix: That is the exercise failing — slow down, shorten the press, or step further from the band's anchor point on your foot to lighten it.
Brace your stomach harder and keep your ribs stacked over your hips rather than leaning back against the pull.
Keep the press at chest height, elbows slightly bent, rather than locking them out hard.

sensation.nextDay: A working ache through your side and stomach for a day or two is normal. Low back soreness is not.
sensation.backNote: The hips staying square is the entire test here. If they rock or twist as you press, slow down or lighten the band tension rather than push through a twisting hip.
sensation.stopIf: Any shooting or electric pain, or numbness or tingling down a leg or arm.

mistakes.wrong: Letting hips twist toward the anchor
mistakes.right: Keep hips square and facing forward the entire rep — go lighter or slower if they twist.
Press and return slowly, resisting the band's pull the whole way rather than snapping through it.

name: TRX Plank
instructions: Adjust the TRX straps to about ankle height and slide your feet into the foot cradles, laces down. Walk your hands out onto the mat until you're in a forearm plank position, elbows under your shoulders.
Brace your core hard before you settle into the hold — the straps make your feet unstable, so your core has to work much harder than a normal floor plank just to keep you still.
Hold a straight line from your head to your heels, resisting the sway and wobble the straps introduce. Keep breathing steadily; do not hold your breath.
Because it is genuinely much harder than a floor plank, halve whatever time you'd normally hold on the floor — a short, stable TRX hold beats a longer one that shakes and sags.
Lower your knees to the mat to come out of the hold, then unclip your feet from the cradles.
cues: Straps make this much harder than floor planks — halve your usual floor time
Brace hard against the wobble; still shape beats fighting the sway
Breathe steadily, don't hold your breath to fight the instability
modification: Set the straps higher, closer to knee height, to reduce the instability while you build up to full ankle-height TRX planks.

sensation.feelHere: A much stronger, whole-body brace through your core and shoulders than a regular plank, fighting constant small wobbles.
sensation.notHere: Your low back sagging or your hips piking up to fight the instability.
sensation.firstCue: Brace hard before you settle — expect more wobble than a floor plank.

wrongSpot.fix: Reset with a harder core brace, or set the straps to knee height for less instability while you build up.
You're bracing by folding at the hips instead of the core — focus on a flat line from head to heels.
Shorten the hold time — a stable 10 seconds beats a shaking 20.

sensation.nextDay: A stronger core and shoulder ache than a floor plank for a day or two is normal.
sensation.backNote: The instability is the whole point, but if your low back sags to fight it, the hold has broken. Shorten the time rather than hold through a sagging back.
sensation.stopIf: Any shooting or electric pain, or numbness or tingling down a leg or arm.

mistakes.wrong: Holding for as long as a floor plank
mistakes.right: Halve your usual floor-plank time — the instability makes this significantly harder per second.

mistakes.wrong: Fighting a sagging or piking hold
mistakes.right: Shorten the hold and reset rather than hold through a shape that's already broken down.

name: Single-Leg Stand, Eyes Closed
instructions: Stand near a wall or countertop you can catch yourself on if needed, but don't hold it. Shift your weight onto one foot and lift the other knee slightly, hovering that foot just off the floor.
Once you feel steady, close your eyes. This removes your visual balance reference and puts the work entirely onto your foot, ankle, and hip.
Hold the position, letting your standing foot make small constant adjustments — that's the sensation you're after here, not a burn.

There is no muscle burn to chase in this exercise. If you feel nothing happening, you're not actually being challenged — that's a sign to move to a harder surface or close your eyes sooner in the hold, not that you're doing it wrong.
Hold for the set time, open your eyes, and switch to the other leg. Rest between sides as needed.
cues: The goal is constant small foot and ankle corrections, not a muscle burn
Stand near something to catch yourself, but don't hold it
Feeling nothing means it's too easy — that's useful information
modification: Keep your eyes open until your balance improves, or stand with a fingertip lightly touching a wall for extra security.

sensation.feelHere: Constant small adjustments in your standing foot and ankle as they work to keep you upright.
sensation.notHere: A muscle burn anywhere — that's not what this exercise produces, and its absence doesn't mean you're failing.
sensation.firstCue: Get steady with eyes open first, then close them.

wrongSpot.fix: That means it's too easy for you right now — try a slightly harder surface like a folded towel, or hold longer.

wrongSpot.felt: Immediate loss of balance on eye closure
wrongSpot.fix: That's normal at first. Keep a hand near the wall and build the time gradually — this skill improves quickly with practice.
Relax your shoulders and let the correcting happen at your foot and ankle, not by stiffening everywhere.

sensation.nextDay: No soreness is expected from this exercise — it's a skill practice, not a strength one.
sensation.stopIf: Any dizziness beyond normal balance wobble, or sudden sharp pain anywhere.

mistakes.right: Look for constant small foot and ankle corrections instead — that's the actual sign this is working.
Let your foot and ankle move and adjust naturally rather than locking everything still.

name: Split Squat
instructions: Stand in a staggered stance with one foot about two to three feet in front of the other. Both feet point straight ahead, hip-width apart side to side. Keep your torso tall and place your hands on your hips or let them hang at your sides.

Bend both knees to lower straight down, not forward. Your front knee should stay stacked over your front ankle rather than driving past your toes, and your back knee drops toward the floor without touching it.
Lower until your front thigh is close to parallel with the floor, or as deep as you can go while keeping your torso upright and your front heel flat on the ground.
Push through your front heel to drive back up to the starting height. Keep your torso tall throughout the movement rather than leaning forward to help yourself up.
Complete all reps on one side, then switch your stance so the opposite foot is forward and repeat.
cues: Sit straight down between your feet, not forward over your front knee
Front knee tracks over your front ankle, not past your toes
Keep your torso tall and stacked over your hips the entire rep
modification: Shorten your stance and reduce depth. Hold a wall or the back of a chair for balance support.

sensation.feelHere: Front thigh and glute of your forward leg, with a stretch through the front of the back hip.
sensation.notHere: Your front knee joint, or your low back rounding forward.
sensation.firstCue: Keep your torso tall. Sit straight down between your feet for a slow 2 count.

wrongSpot.fix: Your knee is drifting past your toes. Lengthen your stance so your shin stays closer to vertical as you lower.
Your torso is pitching forward. Stand taller and reduce your depth until you can stay upright.
You're touching down hard. Stop an inch above the floor and control the last few inches.

sensation.nextDay: Front thigh and glute soreness for 1–3 days is normal. Knee soreness is not.
sensation.backNote: Leaning your torso forward shifts load onto your low back. Sit straight down and reduce depth if you can't stay tall.
sensation.stopIf: Any shooting pain, numbness, or tingling down a leg, or sharp knee pain.

mistakes.right: Lengthen your stance so your front knee doesn't travel past your toes as you lower.
Keep your chest tall and lower straight down between your feet.
Control the descent and stop just short of the floor each rep.

name: Bulgarian Split Squat
instructions: Stand a couple of feet in front of a sturdy chair or step, facing away from it. Reach one foot back and rest the top of your foot, laces down, on the chair seat or step. Hop your front foot forward slightly until your stance feels balanced.
Stand tall on your front leg with your hands on your hips, or holding a wall for balance if you need it — this is genuinely hard and holding on is not a failure.
Bend your front knee to lower straight down, keeping most of your weight on your front leg. Your back knee drops toward the floor behind you as your front thigh approaches parallel with the ground.
Keep your front knee tracking over your front ankle rather than caving inward or shooting past your toes. Your torso stays tall rather than pitching forward over the front thigh.
Push through your front heel to rise back to standing. Complete all reps on one side before resting and switching legs.
cues: Most of your weight stays on the front leg — the back foot is just for balance
Front knee tracks over your ankle, not caving in or shooting forward
Hold a wall for balance if you need it — that's a legitimate way to do this, not a shortcut
modification: Reduce the height of the rear foot elevation, or perform a regular split squat with the back foot on the floor instead.

sensation.feelHere: A deep burn in the front thigh and glute of your front leg, plus real balance demand.
sensation.notHere: Your front knee joint, or your low back from leaning forward.
sensation.firstCue: Hold a wall if needed. Lower straight down for a slow 2 count.

wrongSpot.fix: Your knee is caving in or drifting past your toes. Slow down and keep it tracking straight over your ankle.
Your torso is tipping forward over your front thigh. Stay tall, and hold a wall for balance instead of leaning.
That's normal on this one at first — hold a wall or chair back until it settles.

sensation.nextDay: A deep quad and glute ache for 1–3 days is normal. This one is humbling for most people.
sensation.backNote: Leaning forward to compensate for balance shifts load onto your low back. Stay tall and hold a wall rather than pitching forward.
sensation.stopIf: Any shooting pain, numbness, or tingling down a leg, or sharp knee pain.

mistakes.wrong: Refusing to hold a wall for balance
mistakes.right: Holding a wall or chair is a legitimate way to do this exercise, not a failure — use it.
Keep it tracking straight over your ankle throughout the descent.

mistakes.wrong: Rear foot too high off the ground
mistakes.right: Use a lower step until your balance and strength catch up.

name: Dumbbell Step-Up
instructions: Stand facing a sturdy step or bench, holding a 10 lb dumbbell in each hand at your sides. Place your right foot fully on top of the step, your whole foot flat, toes pointing forward.
Brace your core and press through your right heel to stand up onto the step, bringing your left foot up to meet it. Avoid pushing off your back foot — let your front leg do the lifting.
Stand tall on top of the step for a moment, then step back down with your left foot first, followed by your right, returning to the starting position under control.
Keep your torso upright throughout rather than leaning forward toward the step, and make sure your whole front foot stays planted so your heel doesn't lift off the step.
Complete all reps leading with your right leg, then switch so your left leg leads for the next set.
cues: Push through the heel of the foot on the step — don't spring off the back foot
Keep your torso tall, not leaning toward the step
Step down with control instead of dropping
modification: Use a lower step, drop to bodyweight only, or hold a wall lightly with one hand for balance.

sensation.feelHere: Front thigh and glute of the leg doing the stepping, plus some calf work at the top.
sensation.notHere: Your front knee joint, or your low back from leaning toward the step.
sensation.firstCue: Push through the heel on the step. Keep your torso tall the whole way up.

wrongSpot.fix: You're pushing off your back foot instead of your front heel. Slow down and drive up through the stepping leg.
You're leaning your torso toward the step to help momentum. Stay upright and let the leg do the work.
Use a lower step, or hold a wall lightly with your free hand.

sensation.nextDay: Front thigh and glute soreness for 1–3 days is normal. Knee soreness is not.
sensation.stopIf: Any shooting pain, numbness, or tingling down a leg, or sharp knee pain.

mistakes.right: Drive up through the heel of the leg on the step; let the back foot come along passively.

mistakes.wrong: Step too high for your strength
mistakes.right: Choose a step height where your knee doesn't pass 90 degrees at the bottom.

mistakes.wrong: Dropping down instead of controlling it
mistakes.right: Lower yourself with control on the way down instead of stepping off quickly.

name: Lateral Lunge
instructions: Stand tall with feet together, hands clasped at your chest or hanging at your sides. Take a big step directly out to your right side, landing with your right foot flat and toes pointing slightly outward.

Bend your right knee and push your hips back and down, keeping your left leg straight. Your right shin stays roughly vertical and your right knee tracks over your right foot rather than caving inward.
Lower until you feel a stretch through your left inner thigh, keeping your torso upright and your chest lifted rather than folding forward over your right thigh.
Push through your right heel to drive back up to standing, bringing your right foot back in next to your left.
Complete all reps on the right, then repeat stepping out to the left.
cues: Push hips back and down, like sitting into the bent leg
Keep the straight leg's foot flat and knee soft, not locked
Bent knee tracks over the foot, not caving inward
modification: Take a shorter step out to the side and reduce depth. Hold onto a wall or chair for balance.

sensation.feelHere: Inner thigh of your straight leg, and the outer hip and glute of your bent leg.
sensation.notHere: Your bent knee joint, or your low back from folding forward.
sensation.firstCue: Step out and sit back into the bent leg. Keep your chest lifted.

wrongSpot.fix: It's caving inward. Slow down and push the knee out over your toes as you lower.
You're folding your torso forward. Keep your chest lifted and push your hips back rather than down and forward.
You're locking that knee hard. Keep a soft bend in it throughout.

sensation.nextDay: Inner thigh and outer hip soreness for 1–2 days is normal.
sensation.stopIf: Any shooting pain, numbness, or tingling down a leg, or sharp groin pain.

mistakes.right: Push it out over your toes as you sink into the lunge.
Keep your chest lifted and push your hips back rather than bending at the waist.
Take a bigger step out to the side to get a real stretch through the inner thigh.

name: Curtsy Lunge
instructions: Stand tall with feet hip-width apart, hands on your hips or hanging at your sides. Step your right foot diagonally behind and across your left leg, as if curtsying, so your right foot lands outside your left foot.
Bend both knees to lower your hips straight down, keeping your torso upright. Your left knee tracks over your left foot and your right knee drops toward the floor behind and to the side.
Lower until you feel your left outer hip and glute working, stopping well short of your right knee touching the floor. Keep your weight primarily on your front, left, leg throughout.
Push through your left heel to return to standing, bringing your right foot back to the starting position next to your left.
Complete all reps on one side, then switch so your left foot crosses behind for the next set.
cues: Weight stays mostly on the front leg — the back foot is a light kickstand
Keep your torso upright, not leaning forward as you cross behind
Front knee tracks over your front foot, not caving in
modification: Use a smaller cross-behind step and reduce depth. Hold onto a wall for balance.
