sensation.feelHere: Outer hip and glute of your front leg, plus the front thigh working to control the descent.
sensation.notHere: Your front knee joint, or your low back from leaning forward.
sensation.firstCue: Cross behind and sit down through the front leg. Keep your torso upright.

wrongSpot.fix: It's caving inward as you cross. Slow the rep down and keep it tracking over your front foot.
You're leaning forward to balance. Keep your torso tall and take a smaller cross-behind step.
That's common here — hold a wall lightly with one hand until it feels stable.

sensation.nextDay: Outer hip and glute soreness for 1–2 days is normal, especially if this muscle is new to you.
sensation.stopIf: Any shooting pain, numbness, or tingling down a leg, or sharp knee pain.

mistakes.right: Keep your torso upright and let your outer hip control the movement instead.
Take a moderate step — enough to feel the outer hip, not so far you lose balance.

mistakes.wrong: Weight shifting to the back foot
mistakes.right: Keep most of your weight on the front leg throughout the rep.

name: Sumo Squat
instructions: Stand with your feet wider than shoulder-width apart, toes turned out roughly 30 to 45 degrees. Hold your hands together at your chest or let them hang between your legs.
Take a breath and brace your core. Bend your knees and push your hips straight back and down, keeping your knees tracking in the same direction as your toes throughout the descent.
Lower until your thighs are close to parallel with the floor, or as deep as you can go while keeping your heels flat and your torso reasonably upright rather than pitching forward.
Pause briefly at the bottom, then exhale and push through your whole foot — heels and mid-foot, not just your toes — to stand back up to the starting position.
Keep your chest lifted throughout the entire movement so the work stays in your hips and thighs rather than shifting into your low back.
cues: Knees track over your toes — same direction, wide stance
Sit back and down, keeping your heels planted
Chest lifted throughout, not folding forward as you descend
modification: Reduce your depth to a comfortable range and narrow the stance slightly. Elevate your heels slightly on a folded towel if ankle mobility limits you.

sensation.feelHere: Inner thighs and glutes working together, plus the front of the thighs on the way up.
sensation.notHere: Your low back, or sharp pain in either knee.
sensation.firstCue: Sit back and down with knees tracking over your toes. Keep your chest lifted.

wrongSpot.fix: Your torso is pitching forward. Reduce your depth, elevate your heels slightly, and keep your chest lifted before you descend.
They're drifting inward rather than tracking over your toes. Widen the stance slightly and push them out.
You may be going too deep for your current mobility. Reduce depth until the effort feels like work, not a stretch.

sensation.nextDay: Inner thigh and glute soreness for 1–3 days is normal.
sensation.backNote: A forward-pitching torso shifts this squat's load onto your spine. Sit back rather than down, reduce depth, and elevate your heels slightly if that helps you stay upright.
sensation.stopIf: Any shooting pain, numbness, or tingling down a leg, or sharp knee pain.

mistakes.right: Reduce your depth and keep your chest lifted so the load stays out of your low back.
Keep them tracking in the same direction as your toes, wide and out.
Push through your whole foot, heels included, to stand back up.

name: Dumbbell Sumo Deadlift
instructions: Stand with feet wider than shoulder-width apart, toes turned out, holding one 15 lb dumbbell with both hands in front of you, hanging between your legs. Stand tall with your chest up and core braced.

Take a breath in. Push your hips straight back — not down — as you hinge forward, letting the dumbbell travel down the middle of your legs. Your knees bend slightly to allow the hinge, but this is driven by the hips, not the knees.
Lower only until you feel your hamstrings and inner thighs first go tight, keeping your spine long and neutral the entire way down. That point, not the floor, is where the rep turns around.
Exhale and drive your hips forward to return to standing, squeezing your glutes hard at the top to finish the movement rather than yanking the weight up with your arms or back.
Keep the dumbbell close to your body throughout both the descent and the rise — it should stay nearly touching your legs the whole rep.
cues: Hips travel back, not down — stop the descent the moment your hamstrings feel tight
Keep the dumbbell dragging close to your legs the entire rep
Finish by squeezing your glutes, not by yanking with your back
modification: Use a 10 lb dumbbell, or reduce range of motion to well above where the hamstrings tighten while you build hip-hinge control.

sensation.feelHere: Both inner thighs and hamstrings stretching, then a hard glute squeeze as you return to standing.
sensation.notHere: Your low back doing the lifting. If it's working hard, the hinge broke down.
sensation.firstCue: Push hips straight back. Stop when your hamstrings first feel tight, not at the floor.

wrongSpot.fix: You likely hinged past where your hamstrings can hold a neutral spine, or let the weight drift away from your body. Stop higher and keep the dumbbell close.
You're bending the knees like a squat instead of hinging at the hip. Send the hips back first.
You're shrugging to hold the dumbbell. Let your arms hang heavy and relaxed.

sensation.nextDay: A deep stretch-soreness through the hamstrings and inner thighs, plus a glute ache, for 1–2 days is normal.
sensation.backNote: This is a hinge — where load reaches the low back fastest with any history like yours. Hips travel back not down, and the descent stops the instant your hamstrings feel tight, never when the weight nears the floor.
sensation.stopIf: Anything shoots, burns, or tingles down either leg, or your low back sharply pinches at any point.

mistakes.wrong: Weight drifting away from the body
mistakes.right: Keep the dumbbell close to your legs throughout the entire hinge, down and up.

mistakes.wrong: Going all the way to the floor
mistakes.right: Stop the descent the moment your hamstrings first feel tight, regardless of how close the weight is to the floor.

mistakes.wrong: Standing up by yanking with the back
mistakes.right: Drive your hips forward and squeeze your glutes to finish the rep instead.

name: Dumbbell Hip Thrust
instructions: Sit on the floor with your upper back resting against the edge of a sturdy step or low, stable sofa cushion behind you. Bend your knees, feet flat on the floor, hip-width apart. Rest a 15 lb dumbbell across your hips, holding it in place with both hands.
Brace your core and drive through your heels to lift your hips up off the floor, pressing the dumbbell straight up toward the ceiling as your hips extend.

Stop the moment your body forms a straight line from your shoulders through your hips to your knees. This straight line is the target — do not push higher or arch your lower back to gain extra height.
Squeeze your glutes hard at the top for a one-second pause, ribs pulled down rather than flared up, then lower your hips back down under control until they lightly touch the floor.
Reset your breath and repeat, keeping the movement driven by your hips extending rather than your lower back arching to make up the difference.
cues: Stop at a straight line from shoulders to knees — height beyond that is not the goal
Ribs down, not flared, at the top of every rep
Squeeze the glutes to finish the lift, not the lower back
modification: Use a 10 lb dumbbell, or perform the same movement with just body weight and hands resting lightly on your hip bones.

sensation.feelHere: A strong squeeze across both glutes at the top of each rep.
sensation.notHere: Your low back arching to gain height. That means the lift kept going after the hip was already extended.
sensation.firstCue: Drive through your heels. Stop at a straight line, ribs down.

wrongSpot.fix: You're arching to finish the lift instead of stopping at hip extension. Stop the moment shoulders-hips-knees form a straight line and hold there.
Move your feet slightly closer to your hips so your shins are closer to vertical at the top.
Keep your chin tucked slightly and your weight on your upper back, not your neck, against the step.

sensation.nextDay: A deep glute ache for 1–2 days is normal and a good sign this one landed correctly.
sensation.backNote: The failure mode here is finishing the lift by arching the lower back instead of extending the hip. Stop at a straight line from shoulders to knees, ribs down — going higher does not mean more glute work, it means more spine.
sensation.stopIf: Any shooting pain, numbness, or tingling down a leg, or sharp low-back pinching.

mistakes.wrong: Arching the back to lift higher
mistakes.right: Stop at a straight line from shoulders to knees — that is full hip extension, not a height contest.

mistakes.wrong: Ribs flaring up at the top
mistakes.right: Keep your ribs pulled down and your core braced through the whole rep.
Move your feet closer so your shins are near vertical when your hips are up, reducing hamstring cramping.

name: Glute Kickback
instructions: Get onto your hands and knees on a mat, hands stacked under your shoulders and knees under your hips. Keep your back flat and your core lightly braced — imagine a cup of water balanced on your low back that shouldn't spill.

Keeping your right knee bent at roughly 90 degrees, drive your right foot up and back toward the ceiling by extending through your hip. The movement comes from your glute pressing your heel upward, not from your back arching.
Rise only until your thigh is in line with your torso — your hips and spine should stay level and square to the floor throughout, not rotating or arching to gain extra height.
Pause briefly at the top, feeling the squeeze in your glute, then lower your knee back down under control to the starting position without letting it rest fully on the mat between reps.
Complete all reps on one side, keeping your back flat throughout, then switch to the left leg.
cues: Small range — stop when your thigh lines up with your torso
Keep your hips square to the floor, not rotating open
Move from the hip, not by arching your back
modification: Reduce the range of motion further, or perform the movement lying on your stomach with a small pillow under your hips instead.

sensation.feelHere: A focused squeeze in the glute of your working leg.
sensation.notHere: Your low back. If you feel it there, you're arching to gain height instead of moving from the hip.
sensation.firstCue: Keep hips square. Small lift, driven by the glute.

wrongSpot.fix: You're arching to get more range. Shrink the movement and stop the moment your thigh lines up with your torso.
Keep both hip bones pointing straight at the floor throughout — don't let the working side twist upward.
Place a folded towel under your knees or hands for cushioning.

sensation.nextDay: A focused glute ache on the working side for 1–2 days is normal.
sensation.backNote: Arching the back to gain extra range is the main failure mode here. Keep the movement small and square, and let the glute — not the spine — produce the lift.
sensation.stopIf: Any shooting pain, numbness, or tingling down a leg, or sharp low-back pain.

mistakes.wrong: Arching the back for more height
mistakes.right: Keep the range small and square; stop when your thigh lines up with your torso.
Keep both hip bones facing the floor throughout the movement.
Move slowly and pause at the top to keep the glute, not momentum, doing the work.

name: Fire Hydrant
instructions: Get onto your hands and knees on a mat, hands stacked under your shoulders and knees under your hips. Keep your back flat and your core lightly braced throughout the set.

Keeping your right knee bent at roughly 90 degrees, lift your right knee out and up to the side, away from your body, like a dog at a fire hydrant. The movement comes from your outer hip, not from twisting your torso.

Rise only until your hips start to want to rotate — that's your natural limit. Your low back and hips should stay level and square to the floor throughout, not tipping or twisting to gain extra height.
Pause briefly at the top, feeling the squeeze along your outer hip, then lower your knee back down under control to the starting position.
Complete all reps on one side, keeping your hips square throughout, then switch to the left leg.
cues: Small range — stop the moment your hips want to rotate
Keep your hips level and square, not tipping to the side
Move from the outer hip, not by arching your low back
modification: Reduce the range of motion further and focus on keeping the hips completely still.

sensation.feelHere: A burn along the side of your hip, below your hip bone.
sensation.notHere: Your low back. If you feel it there, you're arching or twisting to gain height instead of moving from the hip.
sensation.firstCue: Keep hips square. Small lift out to the side.

wrongSpot.fix: You're arching to get more range. Shrink the movement and stop the moment your hips start to rotate.
Keep both hip bones pointing straight at the floor — brace your core to hold them still.
Place a folded towel under your knees or hands for cushioning.

sensation.nextDay: A burn along the outer hip for 1–2 days is normal, especially if this muscle is new to you.
sensation.backNote: Arching or twisting the back to gain extra range is the main failure mode here. Keep the movement small and square, and let the outer hip — not the spine — produce the lift.
sensation.stopIf: Any shooting pain, numbness, or tingling down a leg, or sharp low-back pain.

mistakes.wrong: Arching or twisting for more height
mistakes.right: Keep the range small and square; stop the moment your hips want to rotate.
Brace your core and keep your shoulders level throughout.
Move slowly and pause at the top to keep the outer hip, not momentum, doing the work.

name: Single-Leg Calf Raise
instructions: Stand on your right foot near a wall or stable surface, fingertips resting lightly on it for balance only — not pressing or holding weight. Let your left foot hover just off the floor, or rest it lightly against your right ankle.
Press through the ball of your right foot to rise up onto your toes as high as you can. Pause at the top for one full second, feeling the contraction through your calf.
Slowly lower your heel back to the floor over 2 to 3 seconds. This slow lowering is the most important part — it's where the real strengthening happens.
Let your heel fully return to the floor between reps rather than bouncing or springing from the bottom. A brief pause at the bottom before each rep ensures the full range of motion.
Complete all reps on the right foot, then switch and repeat on the left.
cues: Rise as high as you can on one foot — full range matters more than speed
Lower slowly, 2–3 seconds, for the real strengthening effect
Fingertips on the wall for balance only, not for pushing off
modification: Keep light two-finger contact with a wall throughout, or reduce to a half range of motion until single-leg balance improves.

sensation.feelHere: A deep burn in the calf of your standing leg, both the upper bulge and lower toward the ankle.
sensation.notHere: Your Achilles tendon or the arch of your foot — sharp pain there is a tendon signal, not muscle work.
sensation.firstCue: Rise as high as you can. Lower over a slow 3 count.

wrongSpot.fix: Reduce your range slightly and rise less explosively; sharp tendon pain means back off, not push through.
That's normal balance demand on one foot — keep light fingertip contact with the wall until it settles.
Press through the ball of your foot evenly rather than rolling onto your big toe.

sensation.nextDay: A deep calf ache for 1–2 days is normal, especially after the slow lowering. Achilles soreness is not.
sensation.stopIf: Sharp Achilles pain, or any pain that feels like a pull rather than a burn.

mistakes.right: Pause briefly with your heel down before each rep instead of springing up.

mistakes.wrong: Pushing off the wall for help
mistakes.right: Use fingertips only for balance — the working leg should do all the lifting.
Rise as high onto your toes as you can to get the full range.

name: Band Good Morning
instructions: Stand on the middle of your resistance band with both feet hip-width apart. Take the other end of the band up and over your head, resting it across the back of your shoulders like a bar — hold it in place with both hands.
Stand tall with a neutral spine and your core braced. Take a breath in, then begin the hinge by pushing your hips straight back, keeping your knees only softly bent throughout.
Let your torso tip forward as your hips travel back, keeping your spine long and neutral the whole way. The band tension increases as you hinge, adding resistance across your upper back.
Lower only until you feel your hamstrings first go tight, or your torso reaches roughly parallel to the floor, whichever comes first. That point, not any fixed depth, is where the rep turns around.
Exhale and drive your hips forward to return to standing, squeezing your glutes at the top to complete the movement rather than using your lower back to pull yourself upright.
cues: Hips travel back, not down — this is a hinge, not a bow
Stop the descent the instant your hamstrings feel tight
Squeeze your glutes to stand back up, don't yank with your back
modification: Use a lighter band or stand on more of its length to reduce tension. Reduce your range of motion while building hip-hinge control.

sensation.feelHere: Both hamstrings stretching against the band, then a strong glute squeeze as you return to standing.
sensation.notHere: Your low back doing the lifting. If it's straining, the hinge broke down.
sensation.firstCue: Push hips straight back. Stop the moment your hamstrings feel tight.

wrongSpot.fix: You likely hinged past where your hamstrings can hold a neutral spine. Stop higher, closer to where the stretch first appears.
You're bending the knees like a squat instead of hinging at the hip. Send the hips back first, knees only softly bent.
The band is pressing uncomfortably. Reposition it slightly lower across your shoulders, away from your neck.

sensation.nextDay: A stretch-type ache through both hamstrings and a glute ache for 1–2 days is expected.
sensation.backNote: This is a hinge under load with the band adding resistance right where your spine is most vulnerable. Hips travel back not down, and the descent stops the instant your hamstrings feel tight — never at a fixed depth.
sensation.stopIf: Anything shoots, burns, or tingles down either leg, or your low back sharply pinches at any point.

mistakes.wrong: Rounding the back to go deeper
mistakes.right: Stop the descent wherever your spine stays neutral, even if that's a shorter range.

mistakes.wrong: Standing up by pulling with the back
mistakes.right: Drive your hips forward and squeeze your glutes to finish the rep.
Keep them only softly bent — this is a hip hinge, not a squat.

name: TRX Squat
instructions: Set the TRX straps to full length. Face the anchor point and hold a handle in each hand, arms extended in front of you at chest height. Stand with feet shoulder-width apart, a comfortable distance back so the straps are taut with your arms straight.

Brace your core and, using the straps for light counterbalance, push your hips back and bend your knees to lower into a squat. Lean back slightly against the strap tension as you descend, letting your arms straighten.
Lower as deep as you comfortably can while keeping your heels flat on the floor and your torso reasonably upright — the straps let you go deeper and with more control than a bodyweight squat alone.
Push through your whole foot to stand back up, using the straps for balance rather than pulling yourself up with your arms. Your legs, not your arms, should do the work of standing.
Keep the tension in the straps light and steady throughout — they're there to support your balance and depth, not to haul you up.
cues: Lean back against the straps as you lower — they're your counterbalance
Legs do the standing up, not your arms pulling on the straps
Heels flat, knees tracking over your toes throughout
modification: Hold the straps higher up, shorter length, for more support, or reduce your squat depth.

sensation.feelHere: Front thighs and glutes working through a fuller range than a regular bodyweight squat.
sensation.notHere: Your arms or shoulders straining to pull you up — that means you're relying on the straps too much.
sensation.firstCue: Lean back against the straps. Sit down between your heels.

wrongSpot.fix: You're pulling yourself up with the straps instead of standing with your legs. Use them for balance only.
Your torso is pitching too far forward. Lean back more into the strap tension and keep your chest lifted.
They're caving in or shooting past your toes. Slow down and keep them tracking over your feet.

sensation.nextDay: Front thigh and glute soreness for 1–3 days is normal.
sensation.stopIf: Any shooting pain, numbness, or tingling down a leg, or sharp knee pain.

mistakes.right: Use the straps for balance only — push through your legs to stand.
Adjust the length so there's light, steady tension throughout the movement.
Lower slowly and with control, leaning back against the strap tension.

name: TRX Hamstring Curl
instructions: Set the TRX straps to a low, mid-calf length. Lie on your back on a mat with your heels resting inside the foot cradles, legs straight, arms flat on the floor at your sides for stability.
Brace your core and squeeze your glutes to lift your hips up off the floor until your body forms a straight line from shoulders to heels. This is your starting position for every rep.

Keeping your hips lifted and level, bend your knees to draw your heels in toward your glutes, letting the straps roll with your feet. Your hips should stay up throughout — they are the anchor, not the knees.
Pause briefly once your knees are bent, then straighten your legs back out slowly, still keeping your hips lifted the entire time, back to the starting straight-line position.
If your hamstrings cramp, that's common on this exercise — pause, straighten your legs fully, and shake it out before continuing. The real risk to watch for is your hips sagging toward the floor.
cues: Hips stay lifted and level for the entire set — that's the anchor point
Cramping hamstrings are common here — pause and straighten out if it happens
Curl heels in slowly, don't yank them toward your glutes
modification: Keep your hips on the floor throughout and only curl your heels in, removing the hip-lift component until you build strength.

sensation.feelHere: A strong contraction through the back of your thighs, and glutes working to hold your hips level.
sensation.notHere: Your low back sagging under load — that means your hips have dropped and taken over.
sensation.firstCue: Lift hips first, then curl heels in slowly.

wrongSpot.fix: Your hips sagged and the low back took over. Reset with a strong glute squeeze and keep the hips higher throughout.
This is common and normal here. Pause, straighten your legs fully, and shake it out before continuing.
Keep your arms relaxed and flat on the floor for support rather than pressing hard.

sensation.nextDay: A deep hamstring ache for 1–2 days is normal and expected after this one.
sensation.backNote: The risk here is the hips sagging so the low back takes over holding you up. Keep the hips lifted and level for the whole set, and reset with a glute squeeze if they start to drop.
sensation.stopIf: Any shooting pain, numbness, or tingling down a leg, or sharp low-back pain — not the same as normal hamstring cramping.

mistakes.right: Squeeze your glutes to keep hips lifted and level throughout every rep.
Curl in slowly and with control, then straighten back out just as slowly.

mistakes.wrong: Stopping entirely at the first cramp
mistakes.right: Pause, straighten your legs, and shake it out — cramping is common and not a reason to end the set.

name: Wall Sit March
instructions: Stand with your back flat against a wall, feet about two feet in front of you and shoulder-width apart. Slide down until your thighs are close to parallel with the floor, knees stacked over your ankles, just like a regular wall sit.
Keep your entire back pressed flat against the wall — head, shoulders, and low back all in contact — and brace your core lightly before you begin marching.
Slowly lift your right foot a few inches off the floor, keeping your hips level and square. Hold for a moment, feeling your left leg and core work harder to keep you steady.
Place your right foot back down and repeat by lifting your left foot. Continue alternating feet for the full duration, keeping your back flat against the wall throughout.
Breathe steadily the entire time — do not hold your breath. If your hips start to tip side to side, slow the marching down rather than stopping the hold.
cues: Back stays flat against the wall the entire time — that's what keeps this back-safe
Keep hips level as you lift each foot, don't let them tip side to side
Slow, controlled lifts, not fast stomping
modification: Reduce the hold time, sit at a shallower knee angle, or hold the march at the top instead of alternating feet.

sensation.feelHere: A deep burn in the front of your thighs, plus extra work in the standing leg and core with each lift.
sensation.notHere: Your knees themselves, or your low back — both should stay quiet and flat against the wall.
sensation.firstCue: Keep your back flat. Lift one foot slowly, then the other.

wrongSpot.fix: Your back is arching off the wall as you lift each foot. Press it flat and slow the marching down until you can maintain that.
Slow down and lift each foot only a few inches, keeping your hips square to the wall.
You're too low or too far from the wall. Slide up slightly and bring your feet closer.

sensation.nextDay: Quad and core soreness for 1–2 days is normal. Knee soreness the next day is not.
sensation.stopIf: Any sharp knee pain, or numbness or tingling in your legs.

mistakes.wrong: Back arching off the wall while marching
mistakes.right: Keep your entire back, including your low back, pressed flat against the wall throughout.

mistakes.wrong: Lifting feet too high or too fast
mistakes.right: Lift only a few inches, slowly and with control, keeping hips level.
Slow the tempo down and keep hips square to the wall with each lift.

name: World's Greatest Stretch
instructions: Start standing, then step your right foot forward into a long lunge, back knee resting lightly on the mat. Both hands rest on the floor inside your right foot, elbows soft. This is your base position for the whole movement.
Sink your hips forward and down until you feel a stretch through the front of your left hip. Hold that sink for a breath before you move on to the rotation.

Plant your left hand flat on the floor for support. Reach your right hand up toward the ceiling, rotating through your upper back and letting your eyes follow your hand. Open your chest as far as feels easy — this is the thoracic rotation that gives the stretch its name.
Bring the right hand back down to the floor, then straighten your right leg for a couple of seconds to add a light hamstring stretch behind that leg, keeping your back flat rather than rounded.
Bend the right knee again and return to the base lunge, then step back to standing. That's one rep — switch sides and repeat, alternating for the full set.
cues: Sink the hips forward first — the rotation comes after, not instead of it
Rotate from your upper back, not by twisting your lower back
Move slowly through each position rather than flowing fast — this is a warm-up, not a stretch to hold
modification: Skip the straight-leg hamstring reach and just do the lunge-and-rotation if balance is an issue. Use a folded towel under the back knee for comfort.

sensation.feelHere: Front of the hip in the lunge, and a broad opening feeling across your upper back and chest during the rotation.
sensation.notHere: Any pulling or pinching in your lower back — that means you're twisting from the belt line instead of the ribs.
sensation.firstCue: Sink the hips down and forward before you rotate anything.

wrongSpot.fix: You're twisting from the waist. Keep your hips square to the front and let the turn come from your ribs and shoulders only.
Your front foot is too far back. Step it out further so the knee stacks over the ankle, not ahead of the toes.

sensation.nextDay: Mild looseness or a light stretch feeling in the hips and upper back is normal. Nothing here should leave you sore.
sensation.backNote: Keep the rotation coming from your upper back and shoulders — if you feel it in your low back, you're rotating too far or from the wrong spot. Shorten the range.
sensation.stopIf: Any shooting, electric, or tingling sensation down a leg or arm. Stop and reset your base position.

mistakes.right: Keep your hips facing forward and let the rotation come from your upper back and chest.
Pause briefly in the hip sink and again at the top of the rotation before moving on.

name: Inchworm Walkout
instructions: Stand tall with your feet hip-width apart. Bend your knees slightly and hinge forward at the hips to place both hands flat on the floor in front of your feet — bend your knees as much as you need to get there comfortably.

Keeping your legs mostly straight, walk your hands forward one at a time, letting your hips lower gradually until you reach a plank position with your shoulders stacked over your wrists. Keep your core lightly braced so your hips don't sag.
Pause for a breath in the plank, then walk your hands back toward your feet the same way you came, small step by small step. Let your knees bend again as needed on the way back.
Stand all the way back up to finish the rep. Roll up through your spine slowly rather than snapping upright.
Repeat for the full set, keeping the pace unhurried — this is about warming up the whole back chain, not moving fast.
cues: Take small steps with your hands rather than big lunging ones
Keep light tension in your stomach in the plank so your hips don't drop
Bend the knees as much as you need to — a straight-leg version isn't the goal here
modification: Bend your knees more throughout, or stop at a half-walkout without reaching full plank if that's more comfortable.

sensation.feelHere: The back of your legs as your hands walk out, and your shoulders and core once you reach the plank position.
sensation.notHere: Any pulling sensation in your lower back as you hinge forward — that means you're rounding through the spine instead of the hips.
sensation.firstCue: Hinge at the hips first, then walk the hands out in small steps.

wrongSpot.felt: Lower back pulling on the walkout
wrongSpot.fix: Bend your knees more. A straighter leg isn't worth a rounded lower back.
Lightly brace your stomach, like you're bracing for a light tap, before you pause there.

sensation.nextDay: A light stretch feeling in the hamstrings and calves is normal. No soreness expected from this one.
sensation.backNote: Keep your core lightly braced through the plank portion so your hips don't sag and pull on your low back. Bend your knees on the walkout rather than forcing straight legs.
sensation.stopIf: Any shooting, electric, or tingling sensation down either leg. Bend the knees more and shorten the range.

mistakes.wrong: Forcing straight legs to reach the floor
mistakes.right: Bend your knees generously — the stretch still works and your back stays safe.

mistakes.wrong: Letting the hips sag in plank
mistakes.right: Keep a light brace through your stomach so your body stays in one line.

name: Wall Angel
instructions: Stand with your back against a wall, feet a few inches out from it. Try to get your head, upper back, and low back all lightly touching the wall — don't force it if your low back won't reach; more on that below.
Raise your arms so your elbows and wrists are also against the wall, forearms up like a goalpost shape. This is your starting position.
Slowly slide your arms up the wall, straightening toward overhead, keeping wrists, elbows, and forearms in contact with the wall as long as you possibly can without your low back arching off it.

Slide back down to the starting goalpost position under control. The range where you can keep everything in contact — wrists, elbows, and low back — is your real range for today, even if it feels small.
Repeat for the set, moving slowly. It's normal for the usable range to be just a few inches when you start.
cues: Only go as high as you can while keeping your low back on the wall
Move slowly — this is about control, not reaching maximum height
If your low back wants to arch to let your arms go higher, that's your stopping point for the rep
modification: Do the movement seated in a chair with a backrest if standing against a wall is uncomfortable, or reduce the range further.

sensation.feelHere: Between your shoulder blades and along the back of your shoulders as your arms slide up.
sensation.notHere: Your lower back working to hold an arch — if you feel that, you've gone past your real range.
sensation.firstCue: Press your low back gently toward the wall before you start sliding your arms.

wrongSpot.felt: Low back arching off the wall
wrongSpot.fix: Most people can't keep everything in contact through a full range, and that's fine — stop sliding the moment your low back lifts off.
Keep your chin gently tucked and your head resting on the wall rather than pushing forward to see your hands.

sensation.nextDay: A bit of looseness between the shoulder blades is normal. Nothing here should cause soreness.
sensation.backNote: Your low back staying flat against the wall defines your true range for this exercise. Arching it to chase a bigger arm slide defeats the point — the small range with good contact is the win, not the compromise.
sensation.stopIf: Any shooting or tingling sensation into an arm or hand. Reduce the range and check your wall contact.

mistakes.wrong: Arching the low back to raise the arms higher
mistakes.right: Stop the slide the instant your low back lifts — that reduced range is your actual range, not a failure.
Slide slowly enough that you'd notice the moment contact breaks anywhere.

name: Open Book Rotation
instructions: Lie on your side on a mat with your knees stacked and bent to about 90 degrees, hips stacked directly on top of each other. Stretch both arms straight out in front of you, palms together, resting on the floor.
Keep your knees glued together and your hips stacked the whole time — they act as an anchor so the rotation happens through your upper back, not your low back.
Slowly open your top arm like turning the page of a book, sweeping it up and across your body toward the floor on the other side, letting your gaze follow your hand and your upper back rotate open.
Go only as far as feels easy, keeping your knees pinned together. Pause briefly at the end of the range, then reverse the arm back to the starting palms-together position.
Complete the reps on one side, then roll over and repeat on the other side.
cues: Keep your knees stacked and still — they're the anchor that keeps this in your upper back
Let your head turn with your hand so your neck isn't twisted separately
Open only as far as feels easy — the far side of the floor is not the goal
modification: Place a small pillow between your knees to make it easier to keep them stacked, or shorten the arm sweep.

sensation.feelHere: A broad opening feeling across your upper back and chest as your arm sweeps across.
sensation.notHere: Any pulling low in your back or hips — that means your knees have come apart and the low back is rotating instead.
sensation.firstCue: Pin your knees together first, then start the arm sweep slowly.

wrongSpot.fix: Your knees have separated. Squeeze them back together — that's what keeps the rotation upstairs.
Let your head turn naturally with your hand instead of holding it still or forcing it further.

sensation.nextDay: A light openness across the chest and upper back is normal. Nothing here should be sore the next day.
sensation.backNote: Keeping your knees and hips stacked and still is what isolates this to your upper back. If you feel it in your low back, your knees have drifted apart — reset them and use a smaller range.
sensation.stopIf: Any shooting, electric, or tingling sensation anywhere. Reset your knee position and reduce the sweep.

mistakes.right: Keep them stacked and lightly pressed together for the whole set — a pillow between them helps.

mistakes.wrong: Forcing the arm all the way to the floor
mistakes.right: Go only as far as feels easy today; the range will open up over time.

name: Ankle Rock
instructions: Set up in a half-kneeling position: right foot flat on the floor in front, left knee down on a mat behind you. Rest your hands lightly on your right thigh for balance and support.

Keeping your right heel glued to the floor, slowly rock your right knee forward over your toes as far as feels comfortable, letting your ankle bend more deeply. Your knee will travel past your toes a little — that's the point of the drill, not something to avoid here.
Pause briefly at the end of the range, feeling the front of your ankle and shin working, then rock back to the starting position without lifting your heel.

This limited ankle range is one of the main reasons a squat pitches you forward onto your toes and loads your lower back more than it should — better ankle range lets your torso stay upright under load.
Complete the reps on one side, then switch legs and repeat.
cues: Keep the heel glued to the floor the entire time — that's what makes it an ankle drill
Move slowly and stop where you feel a stretch, not pain, at the front of the ankle
Think of this as squat prep — better ankle range means a more upright torso when you squat
modification: Reduce how far the knee travels forward, or hold onto a chair or counter for extra balance support.

sensation.feelHere: A stretch at the front of your ankle and down your shin as the knee travels forward.
sensation.notHere: Pain in the kneecap itself — that means you're pushing the knee forward faster than the ankle is opening up.
sensation.firstCue: Keep the heel down and rock the knee forward slowly over the toes.

wrongSpot.fix: You've gone past your current ankle range. Rock back slightly and work within the range where the heel stays down.
Ease off how far forward the knee travels and let the stretch come from the ankle, not the knee joint.

sensation.nextDay: A bit of looseness around the ankle is normal. No soreness expected from this drill.
sensation.stopIf: Any shooting or tingling sensation down the leg or foot. Reduce the range and check your heel stays down.

mistakes.right: Keep it glued to the floor — lifting it means you're borrowing range from the wrong joint.
Better ankle range means your torso can stay more upright in a squat, which takes load off your lower back.

name: Calf Stretch at the Wall
instructions: Stand facing a wall, hands flat against it at about shoulder height. Step your right foot back a long stride, keeping it flat on the floor and pointed straight ahead, not turned out.
Keep your right leg straight and lean your hips toward the wall until you feel a stretch up the back of your calf. Hold this for 20 seconds — this targets the upper calf muscle, the gastrocnemius.

Now bend your right knee slightly, keeping the heel down, and lean in a little further. This shifts the stretch lower and deeper, into the soleus muscle near the Achilles tendon. Hold this bent-knee position for the remaining time.
Breathe slowly throughout and let the stretch ease as you exhale, rather than forcing it deeper with muscle effort.
Switch legs and repeat the full straight-then-bent sequence on the other side.
cues: Keep the back heel pressed into the floor the entire time
Point the back foot straight ahead, not turned outward
Straight knee first for the upper calf, then a soft bend for the lower calf and Achilles
modification: Stand closer to the wall and take a shorter stride back to reduce stretch intensity.

sensation.feelHere: A steady pulling stretch up the back of your lower leg, shifting lower when you bend the knee.
sensation.notHere: Tingling or burning traveling into your foot — that's a nerve signal, not a muscle stretch.
sensation.firstCue: Press the back heel down first, then lean your hips toward the wall.

wrongSpot.felt: Back heel lifting off the floor
wrongSpot.fix: You've stepped too far back or leaned too hard. Shorten your stride and keep the heel glued down.
Step your back foot further from the wall, or check that your back foot is pointed straight ahead, not turned out.

sensation.nextDay: A light looseness in the calf is normal. Nothing here should be sore the next day.
sensation.stopIf: Any tingling, numbness, or shooting sensation into your foot. Ease off the lean and keep the heel down.

mistakes.right: Keep it pointed straight ahead so the stretch loads the calf evenly.
Lean in steadily and hold — let your breath ease you deeper, not bouncing.

name: Kneeling Lat Stretch
instructions: Kneel on a mat facing a step, low bench, or sturdy chair seat. Sit back toward your heels slightly and place both hands on the edge of the step, arms straight.
Walk your hands slightly forward and let your chest sink down and back toward your heels, keeping your arms extended overhead and your ears between your upper arms.
You should feel a long stretch down the side of your back, under your armpit, running toward your hip. Let your chest relax down with each exhale rather than forcing it lower.
Keep your hips sitting back toward your heels throughout — this is what isolates the stretch to your upper body rather than your lower back.
Hold for the full time, breathing slowly, then walk your hands back in and sit up to finish.
cues: Sit your hips back toward your heels and keep them there the whole time
Let your chest sink with each exhale rather than pressing down with effort
Keep your arms straight and close to your ears, not flared out to the sides
modification: Use a lower or higher surface so your hips can stay comfortably back toward your heels, or shorten the hold time.

sensation.feelHere: A long stretch down the side of your back, under the armpit, running toward your hip.
sensation.notHere: Any pinching in your shoulder joint itself, or pulling low in your back.
sensation.firstCue: Sit your hips back toward your heels before you sink your chest down.

wrongSpot.fix: Your hips have drifted forward off your heels. Sit them back and let the stretch come from the sunk chest position instead.
Bring your arms slightly narrower and closer to your ears rather than wide and flared.

sensation.nextDay: A long, broad stretch feeling down the side of the back is normal. No soreness expected.
sensation.backNote: Keeping your hips sitting back toward your heels takes the stretch out of your lower back. If your low back feels the pull instead of your side, sit further back onto your heels.
sensation.stopIf: Any shooting or tingling sensation down an arm. Ease the reach and check your hip position.

mistakes.wrong: Letting the hips drift forward off the heels
mistakes.right: Keep sitting back toward your heels — that's what protects your low back during the stretch.

mistakes.wrong: Forcing the chest lower with effort
mistakes.right: Let gravity and your exhale do the work instead of pressing down.

name: Neck Side Stretch
instructions: Sit or stand tall with your shoulders relaxed down and away from your ears. Let your right arm hang loosely at your side or rest your right hand lightly on the seat beside you.
Gently tilt your left ear toward your left shoulder, keeping your right shoulder down and relaxed rather than shrugging it up to meet your ear.
You can add a very light touch with your left hand resting on the side of your head for a small amount of extra weight — no pulling or forcing, just resting.
Hold this gentle position, breathing slowly, and allow the muscles on the right side of your neck to soften with each exhale.
Return your head to center slowly, then repeat on the other side, tilting your right ear toward your right shoulder.
cues: Keep the opposite shoulder relaxed and down, not shrugged up
This should feel gentle throughout — no pulling with the hand
Breathe slowly and let the muscle soften rather than forcing the stretch deeper
modification: Skip the hand entirely and use only the weight of your head tilting for a gentler version.

sensation.feelHere: A gentle stretch along the side of your neck and across the top of your shoulder.
sensation.notHere: Any tingling or shooting sensation down your arm — that's a nerve, not a muscle stretch, and means back off.
sensation.firstCue: Relax the opposite shoulder down before tilting your ear toward the other shoulder.

wrongSpot.felt: Shoulder shrugging up on the stretched side
wrongSpot.fix: Consciously drop that shoulder down and away from your ear before continuing.

wrongSpot.felt: Sharp pulling rather than a gentle stretch
wrongSpot.fix: You're using too much hand pressure. Rest the hand lightly or remove it and use head weight alone.

sensation.nextDay: A very light looseness in the neck is normal. This should never leave you sore.
sensation.stopIf: Any tingling, numbness, or shooting sensation down an arm or into the hand. Stop immediately and return your head to center.

mistakes.right: Use only light resting pressure, or none at all — this is a gentle stretch, not a deep one.
Keep it relaxed and down so the stretch isolates to the neck.

name: Jumping Jacks
instructions: Stand tall with your feet together and arms down at your sides. This is your starting position for every rep.
In one motion, jump your feet out wide while raising both arms out and up overhead. Land softly on the balls of your feet with your knees slightly bent.
Immediately jump back to the starting position, feet together and arms back down at your sides, landing softly again.
Keep a steady, controlled rhythm rather than maximum speed — this is a warm-up for your heart rate, not a race.
Continue for the full time. If your back feels stiff or unhappy with the impact on a given day, march-in-place is the better choice — impact is the variable that matters here, not effort.
cues: Land softly on the balls of your feet, not flat-footed
Keep a steady rhythm you can hold for the full time, not an all-out sprint
Swap to march-in-place on days your back feels stiff — same warm-up goal, no impact
modification: Step one foot out at a time instead of jumping, or switch to march-in-place entirely for a no-impact version.

sensation.feelHere: Your breathing and heart rate picking up, with light work in your calves and shoulders.
sensation.notHere: Any jarring feeling in your lower back on landing — that's a sign to switch to a low-impact option today.
sensation.firstCue: Land soft and quiet, knees slightly bent, every single rep.

wrongSpot.felt: Jarring in the lower back on landing
wrongSpot.fix: Switch to march-in-place for today — the impact, not the movement itself, is what's bothering your back.
Bend your knees a little more and land through the balls of your feet.

sensation.nextDay: Mild leg fatigue is normal. Back stiffness the next day means choose march-in-place next time.
sensation.backNote: Impact is the variable here. If your back is stiff on a given day, march-in-place gets you the same cardio warm-up without any landing force.
sensation.stopIf: Any shooting or jarring pain in your back or joints. Stop and switch to march-in-place.

mistakes.right: Land softly through the balls of the feet with a slight knee bend to absorb the impact.

mistakes.wrong: Doing jumping jacks on a stiff-back day
mistakes.right: Swap to march-in-place — it delivers the same warm-up without impact.

name: March in Place
instructions: Stand tall with your feet hip-width apart, arms relaxed at your sides. This is the low-impact alternative to jumping jacks — same goal of raising your heart rate, but one foot always stays on the floor.
Lift your right knee up toward waist height, swinging your left arm forward naturally as you do, like a relaxed walking motion.
Lower the right foot back down and immediately lift the left knee, swinging the right arm forward. Keep alternating sides in a steady rhythm.
Pick up the pace to whatever feels like a brisk march for you — this should raise your breathing rate without ever feeling jarring or effortful on the joints.
Continue marching for the full time, keeping your posture tall throughout rather than hunching forward as you tire.
cues: Keep one foot on the floor at all times — no impact, no jumping
Swing your arms naturally to add extra heart-rate work
Stand tall throughout — don't let your posture collapse as you tire
modification: Reduce how high you lift the knees, or hold onto a counter or chair for balance support.

sensation.feelHere: Your breathing and heart rate picking up, with light work in your hip flexors and stomach as you lift each knee.
sensation.notHere: Any strain or pulling in your lower back — this should feel easy on the spine throughout.
sensation.firstCue: Stand tall and lift the knees in a steady, brisk rhythm.

wrongSpot.fix: You're leaning back to lift the knee higher. Stand tall and lift only as high as feels easy without leaning.
Reset your posture tall — chest up, shoulders back — every few reps as you start to tire.

sensation.nextDay: Mild leg or breathing fatigue is normal. No back or joint soreness expected from this one.
sensation.backNote: This is the back-friendly cardio option — no landing impact at all, so it's a good default whenever your spine feels anything less than 100 percent.
sensation.stopIf: Any shooting or sharp sensation in your back or hips. Slow the pace or stop.

mistakes.wrong: Leaning back to lift the knees higher
mistakes.right: Stand tall and keep the lift height modest — speed and rhythm matter more than knee height.

mistakes.wrong: Letting posture collapse as you tire
mistakes.right: Keep your chest up and shoulders back for the full duration, even as you slow down.

name: Cable Seated Row
instructions: Sit at the cable row station and place your feet on the footplates with knees slightly bent. Adjust the seat or footplate position, if available, so that when you hold the handle with arms extended, your torso is upright and not straining forward — ask gym staff to help the first time if the adjustment isn't obvious.
Grip the handle with both hands, sit up tall, and pull your shoulder blades back slightly to set your starting posture. Your knees stay softly bent throughout, not locked straight.

Exhale and pull the handle toward your lower ribs by driving your elbows straight back, squeezing your shoulder blades together at the end of the pull. Keep your torso upright — do not lean back to help the pull.
Pause briefly at full contraction, feeling the squeeze between your shoulder blades.
Inhale and let the handle return slowly and under control, allowing your arms to extend and a light stretch through your upper back, without letting your torso collapse forward to add range.
cues: Sit tall and keep your torso still — the pull comes from your arms and back, not from rocking
Drive your elbows straight back and squeeze your shoulder blades together at the finish
Control the return — don't let the weight stack yank your arms forward
modification: Reduce the weight stack and shorten the range of motion if you feel your torso wanting to rock or lean.

sensation.feelHere: Between your shoulder blades and down the sides of your back, with some work in your biceps.
sensation.notHere: Your lower back working to heave the weight — that means you're using momentum instead of your back muscles.
sensation.firstCue: Sit tall, then pull your elbows straight back to your ribs.

wrongSpot.fix: Stop leaning your torso back and forward to add momentum. Keep your torso still and let your arms and back do the pulling.
Relax your shoulders down before you pull, and keep them down through the whole rep.

sensation.nextDay: A broad ache across the upper back for 1-2 days is normal. Sharp lower back pain is not.
sensation.backNote: Keep your torso upright and still throughout — rocking backward to help the pull is a common way this exercise sneaks load onto the spine. If you need momentum to move the weight, it's too heavy.
sensation.stopIf: Anything shoots down an arm, or your hand goes numb or tingly.

mistakes.wrong: Rocking the torso to add momentum
mistakes.right: Keep your torso still and upright; let your arms and shoulder blades do all the work.

mistakes.wrong: Letting the weight yank your arms forward on the return
mistakes.right: Control the return over 2-3 seconds instead of letting it snap you forward.

name: Leg Extension Machine
instructions: Sit in the leg extension machine and adjust the seat back so your knees line up with the machine's pivot point when your legs hang at 90 degrees. Adjust the padded lever so it rests just above your ankles, not on top of your feet — ask gym staff to help with this setup the first time.
Sit back against the pad and hold the side handles lightly for stability. Your knees should bend to about 90 degrees at the starting position, shins vertical.
Exhale and extend both legs, straightening your knees to lift the pad until your legs are nearly straight, without locking your knees hard at the top.
Pause briefly at the top, feeling the front of your thighs working, then inhale and lower the pad back down slowly over 2-3 seconds.
This is an accessory exercise for the quadriceps, not a main lift — keep the weight moderate and prioritize a controlled, pain-free range over how much weight is on the stack.
cues: Set the ankle pad and seat position carefully before your first rep — ask staff if unsure
Control the lowering phase over 2-3 seconds rather than letting the weight drop
This is an accessory move — moderate weight and clean reps beat heavy weight and knee pain
modification: Shorten the range of motion or reduce the weight if you feel any pain at the front of the kneecap. Treat this as optional accessory work, not essential.

sensation.feelHere: The front of your thighs, working hardest near the top of the movement.
sensation.notHere: Pain at the front of the kneecap — that's the joint, not the muscle, complaining.
sensation.firstCue: Extend smoothly to just short of a hard knee lockout.

wrongSpot.felt: Pain at the front of the kneecap
wrongSpot.fix: Shorten the range of motion and drop the weight. This machine can be hard on the kneecap for some people — there's no need to push through it.

wrongSpot.felt: Jerking the weight up at the start
wrongSpot.fix: Slow down the lift — a smooth extension protects the knee joint better than a fast one.

sensation.nextDay: A mild ache across the front of the thighs is normal. Kneecap pain of any kind is not — reduce range or weight next time.
sensation.stopIf: Sharp or pinching pain at the kneecap, or anything that feels like a joint rather than a muscle. Shorten the range or drop the weight.

mistakes.wrong: Chasing heavy weight on this machine
mistakes.right: Treat it as accessory work — moderate weight with clean, pain-free reps is the goal, not maxing out the stack.

mistakes.wrong: Ignoring kneecap pain and pushing through
mistakes.right: Shorten the range or lower the weight the moment you feel pain at the front of the knee.

name: Hip Abduction Machine
instructions: Sit in the hip abduction machine and adjust the seat and the range-limiter, if available, so your knees start together and the outer thigh pads rest comfortably against the outside of your knees or thighs. Ask gym staff for help setting the machine on your first visit.
Sit tall against the backrest with your back flat against the pad, and hold the side handles lightly. Sitting tall is the setup that matters most here.
Exhale and push your knees outward against the pads, opening your legs as far as comfortably possible while keeping your torso upright and still.
Pause briefly at the widest point, feeling the work in the outer hip and upper glute area, then inhale and let the pads return slowly to the starting position under control.
If you notice the work shifting into your lower back, you're likely leaning back into the pad to push harder — sit tall and reduce the weight instead.
cues: Sit tall against the backrest for the entire set — this is the single most important setup detail
Push against the pads smoothly rather than jerking the legs open
Control the return instead of letting the pads snap back in
modification: Reduce the weight and the range of motion if you feel any low back involvement. This exercise should feel like it's working only the outer hip.

sensation.feelHere: The outer hip and upper glute area on both sides as your knees press outward.
sensation.notHere: Your lower back working or tightening — that muscle should be completely uninvolved here.
sensation.firstCue: Sit tall against the pad before you push your knees outward.

wrongSpot.fix: You're leaning back into the pad to generate more force. Sit tall, and if you need to lean to push, the weight is too heavy — drop it.

wrongSpot.felt: Front of the hip instead of the outer hip
wrongSpot.fix: Check your seat position — your hips may be sitting too far forward or back relative to the pivot point.

sensation.nextDay: A mild ache in the outer hip and glute is normal. Lower back soreness means the weight was too heavy or your posture slipped.
sensation.backNote: Feeling this in your lower back is a clear sign you're leaning back to push harder. Sit tall throughout, and lower the weight if sitting tall makes the exercise feel harder — that's the honest difficulty level.
sensation.stopIf: Any shooting pain into the low back or down a leg. Sit tall, reduce the weight, and reassess.

mistakes.wrong: Leaning back into the pad to push harder
mistakes.right: Sit tall throughout; if that makes the weight feel too heavy, that's the right amount to reduce it by.
Push smoothly and control the return — speed doesn't add glute work, it just adds momentum.

name: Chest Fly Machine
instructions: Sit in the chest fly (pec deck) machine and adjust the seat height so the handles line up with your chest, roughly nipple height, when your arms are out to the sides. Ask gym staff to help set this on your first use if it isn't obvious.
Sit back firmly against the pad with your feet flat on the floor. Grip the handles or place your forearms on the padded arms, elbows bent slightly and roughly at chest height.

Exhale and bring your arms together in front of your chest in a smooth, wide arc, squeezing your chest as the handles meet. Keep the slight bend in your elbows constant throughout rather than straightening your arms.
Pause briefly at the point where the handles meet or nearly meet, feeling the squeeze across your chest.
Inhale and let your arms open back out slowly under control, stopping when you feel a comfortable stretch across your chest — do not let the pads yank your arms further back than feels easy.
cues: Set the seat so the handles line up with chest height before you start
Keep a constant, slight bend in your elbows throughout — this isn't a pressing motion
Squeeze your chest at the finish rather than just letting the machine do the work
modification: Reduce the weight and stop the backward stretch earlier if you feel any pinching at the front of the shoulder.

sensation.feelHere: Across the middle of your chest, especially as your arms come together and squeeze.
sensation.notHere: A pinching feeling at the front of the shoulder joint — that means the stretch position is going too far back.
sensation.firstCue: Keep your elbows at a constant slight bend and squeeze your chest at the finish.

wrongSpot.felt: Pinching at the front of the shoulder
wrongSpot.fix: Let the pads open less far back — stop the stretch a little earlier, before you feel the joint rather than the muscle.
Sit back firmly against the seat and keep your feet flat on the floor for a stable base.

sensation.nextDay: A broad ache across the chest for 1-2 days is normal. Sharp shoulder joint pain is not.
sensation.stopIf: Anything shoots down an arm, or you feel numbness or tingling in the hand.

mistakes.wrong: Straightening the elbows during the movement
mistakes.right: Keep a constant slight bend — this is a fly motion, not a press.

mistakes.wrong: Letting the arms swing too far back
mistakes.right: Stop the backward stretch at a comfortable point, well before you feel the shoulder joint.

name: Assisted Pull-Up Machine
instructions: Set the assistance weight on the machine before you climb on — this is the important part to get right, and it's counter-intuitive: MORE assistance weight makes the exercise EASIER, not harder, because the machine is pushing you up to help you. Start with a higher assistance weight than you think you need.

Kneel or step onto the platform as instructed by the machine, and grip the handles or bar slightly wider than shoulder width. Let yourself hang with arms extended, feeling the platform support most of your weight.
Exhale and pull yourself upward by driving your elbows down toward your hips, leading with your chest, until your chin nears the handles or bar. Avoid kicking or swinging your legs to help.
Pause briefly at the top, feeling your upper back and lats working, then inhale and lower yourself back down slowly under control until your arms are extended again.
If a set feels too hard to complete with good form, increase the assistance weight next time — that makes it easier. Reduce it later as you get stronger.
cues: More assistance weight equals an easier set — set it higher than feels intuitive when starting out
Lead with your chest and drive your elbows down, rather than just pulling with your arms
Control the lowering phase instead of dropping back down quickly
modification: Increase the assistance weight to make each rep easier, or reduce reps while keeping form clean.

sensation.feelHere: Your upper back and the sides of your back under the armpits, with your biceps assisting.
sensation.notHere: Your lower back straining, or a feeling of swinging momentum carrying you up instead of your back muscles.
sensation.firstCue: Check the assistance weight is set high enough to make this manageable, then pull with your elbows.

wrongSpot.felt: The set feels far too hard to complete
wrongSpot.fix: Remember: more assistance weight is easier, not harder. Increase the assistance setting before your next set.
Slow down and control the pull — swinging means the assistance weight may be set too low for now.

sensation.nextDay: A broad ache across the upper back for 1-2 days is normal. Sharp shoulder or lower back pain is not.
sensation.backNote: Keep your torso fairly still and avoid excessive swinging, which can transfer load to your lower back. Increase the assistance weight if you notice yourself needing to swing to complete reps.
sensation.stopIf: Anything shoots down an arm, or your hand goes numb or tingly.

mistakes.wrong: Setting the assistance weight too low to start
mistakes.right: Remember more assistance weight means an easier set — start higher than feels intuitive and work down over time.
Keep the movement controlled and let your back do the work; increase assistance if you can't avoid swinging.

name: Dumbbell Pullover
instructions: Lie on your back on a mat with knees bent and feet flat on the floor. Hold one 15 lb dumbbell with both hands, arms straight up over your chest, palms cupping the top of the dumbbell.
Press your ribs down and flatten your low back gently into the floor. Brace your core before you move — this brace is what keeps the next step safe.

Inhale as you lower the dumbbell slowly back and overhead in an arc, keeping your elbows only slightly bent. Stop the instant your ribs start to lift off the floor, even if your arms haven't gone far.
Exhale and pull the dumbbell back up and over your chest to the starting position, leading with your upper arms. Keep the motion slow and controlled in both directions.
Reset your brace between reps if you feel your ribs flaring. The range of motion is meant to be short here — this is about the stretch and pull, not how far back the weight travels.
cues: Ribs stay down and low back stays touching the floor the whole time
Stop the lower the moment your ribs start to lift, not before, not after
Lead the pull-up with your upper arms, not your hands
modification: Use a lighter household weight or no weight at all while you learn where your ribs lift, then add the 15 lb dumbbell.

sensation.feelHere: A stretch and pull along the sides of your back under your armpits, and across your chest.
sensation.notHere: Any arching or pressure in your low back as the weight goes overhead.
sensation.firstCue: Ribs pinned down. Lower only until they want to lift, then pull back up.

wrongSpot.fix: You've gone past your rib range. Shorten the lowering distance so your ribs stay flat on the floor the whole rep.
Your elbows are locking straight. Keep a slight, steady bend in the elbows throughout the arc.
You're craning your head to watch the weight. Keep your head resting on the floor and eyes on the ceiling.

sensation.nextDay: A stretch-related ache along the sides of your back and chest for a day or two is normal.
sensation.backNote: Arching the low back as the arms go overhead is the main risk here. Keep ribs down and low back on the floor; stop the range the instant ribs start to lift.
sensation.stopIf: Any pain shooting into a leg, or your low back lifting off the floor and staying lifted.

mistakes.right: Stop the backward lower the instant your ribcage wants to lift off the floor.
Start light or even empty-handed until you can feel exactly where your rib limit is.
Keep a slight, steady bend in your elbows through the whole arc to protect your shoulders.

name: Dumbbell Hammer Curl
instructions: Stand tall with feet shoulder-width apart, holding a 10 lb dumbbell in each hand at your sides. Turn your palms to face your body — this neutral, thumbs-forward grip stays the same for the entire set.
Keep your elbows pinned close to your sides and your upper arms still throughout the set. Set your shoulders back and down before you start the very first rep.
Exhale and curl both dumbbells straight up toward your shoulders, keeping your palms facing each other the whole way. Do not let your wrists rotate as you lift.
Pause for one second at the top once you feel a strong squeeze in the upper arm. Your elbows should still be at your sides, not drifting forward.
Inhale and lower the dumbbells back down over 2–3 seconds, keeping the same neutral grip throughout. Control the descent rather than letting the weight drop.
cues: Palms face each other the whole rep — the grip never rotates
Elbows stay pinned to your sides from start to finish
Lower slowly over 2–3 seconds instead of letting the weight drop
modification: Curl one arm at a time to reduce the total load and focus on each side individually.

sensation.feelHere: The front and outer part of your upper arm, and a bit into the top of your forearm.
sensation.notHere: Your wrist or the underside of your forearm straining to hold the grip.
sensation.firstCue: Keep palms facing in and elbows pinned. Lower slow, 2–3 seconds down.

wrongSpot.fix: You're letting the wrist bend or the grip rotate. Keep the dumbbell in a straight line with your forearm.
You're gripping too hard. Hold the dumbbell firmly but not with a death grip.
Your elbows are drifting forward as you curl. Keep them pinned to your sides the whole rep.

sensation.nextDay: A burn through the outer upper arm and top of the forearm for a day or two is expected.
sensation.stopIf: Numbness or tingling in your hand, or sharp pain at the wrist or elbow.

mistakes.right: Keep your palms facing each other from the first rep to the last.
Keep your upper arms still and let only the forearms move through the curl.
Lower over 2–3 seconds with control — that's where most of the strength gain happens.

name: Dumbbell Concentration Curl
instructions: Sit on the edge of a chair or bench with feet wide apart. Hold a 10 lb dumbbell in one hand and lean forward slightly, bracing the back of your upper arm against the inside of your thigh on the same side.
Let your arm hang straight down so the dumbbell rests just above the floor. This dead-hang bottom position is your starting point for every rep — reset here between reps.
Exhale and curl the dumbbell up toward your shoulder, keeping your upper arm pinned against your thigh the whole time. Only your forearm should move.
Pause and squeeze for one second at the top, then inhale and lower the dumbbell back to the full hang over 2–3 seconds. Complete all reps on one side before switching arms.
Keep your braced elbow anchored on your thigh throughout the set — if it lifts off, the weight is too heavy or you're rushing the rep.
cues: Brace the upper arm firmly against your inner thigh and keep it there
Full hang at the bottom every rep — do not shortcut the stretch
Squeeze at the top for one full second before lowering
modification: Rest your non-working hand on your other knee for extra stability, or reduce to 8 reps per side.

sensation.feelHere: A deep, isolated squeeze in the front of your upper arm, especially at the top of the curl.
sensation.notHere: Your shoulder or upper back straining to help lift the weight.
sensation.firstCue: Elbow braced on your thigh. Full hang at bottom, hard squeeze at top.

wrongSpot.fix: Your elbow has lifted off your thigh. Re-brace it and keep the upper arm still all rep.
Your wrist is bending back at the top. Keep it straight in line with your forearm.
You're leaning your torso to help swing the weight up. Sit tall and let the arm do the work alone.

sensation.nextDay: A focused burn in the front of the upper arm for a day or two, more than a normal curl.
sensation.stopIf: Numbness or tingling in the hand, or sharp pain at the elbow or wrist.

mistakes.right: Keep the upper arm braced against your inner thigh for the entire set on that side.
Let the arm fully straighten at the bottom of every rep before curling back up.
Slow down — a one-second squeeze at the top and a 2–3 second lower is the point of this exercise.

name: Dumbbell Incline Curl
instructions: Set a bench to a 45–60 degree incline. Sit back into it so your whole spine is supported, and let both arms hang straight down from your shoulders, holding a dumbbell in each hand with palms facing forward.

Let your shoulders relax back into the bench and allow your arms to hang slightly behind your torso line. This deep hang is the full stretch position and is the whole point of doing this on an incline.
Exhale and curl both dumbbells up toward your shoulders without swinging your upper arms forward. Let the bench keep your torso still so only your elbows bend.
Pause at the top for a strong squeeze, then inhale and lower back to the full hang over 2–3 seconds. Do not rush the descent — the stretch at the bottom is where this exercise earns its keep.
Choose your incline angle based on comfort — a steeper incline gives a deeper stretch in the shoulder, while a shallower incline is a gentler starting point for beginners.
cues: Let your shoulders sink back into the bench for a full arm hang
Curl without letting the upper arms swing forward off the bench
Lower slowly to the full stretch — that's the working phase, not just the curl
modification: Use a shallower incline angle or lighter dumbbells until the deep stretch feels comfortable in the shoulder.

sensation.feelHere: A strong stretch and burn low in the front of your upper arm, near the elbow.
sensation.notHere: Any pinch in the front of the shoulder at the bottom of the hang.
sensation.firstCue: Sink shoulders into the bench. Curl without swinging, lower slow to full stretch.

wrongSpot.fix: The stretch is too deep for you right now. Use a shallower incline until your shoulder tolerates it.
Your wrist is bending back as you curl. Keep it straight and let the elbow do the bending.
You're using momentum off the bench. Slow down and let the bench, not your shoulder, stay still.

sensation.nextDay: A deep stretch-soreness low in the upper arm for 1–2 days is normal for this exercise.
sensation.stopIf: Sharp pinching pain in the shoulder joint, or numbness or tingling in the hand.

mistakes.right: Let the bench support your torso and keep your upper arms still through the curl.
Lower all the way to a full arm hang every rep before curling back up.
Start shallower and increase the angle only once the stretch feels comfortable, not pinching.

name: Dumbbell Shrug
instructions: Stand tall with feet hip-width apart, holding a 15 lb dumbbell in each hand at your sides, palms facing your body. Let your arms hang straight and relaxed — they stay passive for the whole exercise.
Take a breath in, then exhale and lift your shoulders straight up toward your ears as high as they'll go. Your arms and elbows stay completely still — only the shoulders move.
Pause for one full second at the very top and feel the squeeze across the top of your shoulders and the base of your neck before lowering.
Inhale and lower your shoulders back down slowly over 2 seconds, letting them settle fully before the next rep. Do not roll the shoulders in a circle — straight up, straight down only.
cues: Straight up and straight down — no rolling the shoulders in a circle
Arms and elbows stay passive; only the shoulders lift
Pause and squeeze for a full second at the very top
modification: Use the 10 lb dumbbells or reduce reps to 10 while building tolerance in the neck and shoulders.

sensation.feelHere: The top of your shoulders and the base of your neck, working hardest at the very top.
sensation.notHere: Your biceps or forearms gripping to hold the weight up.
sensation.firstCue: Lift shoulders straight up toward your ears. Pause a full second at the top.

wrongSpot.fix: You're craning your neck forward or back. Keep your head level and let only the shoulders travel.
You're bending the elbows to help. Keep your arms fully straight and passive throughout.
You're leaning back to lift heavier. Stand tall and use a lighter weight instead.

sensation.nextDay: A tight ache across the top of the shoulders and neck for a day or two is normal.
sensation.stopIf: Numbness or tingling down an arm, or sharp pain in the neck.

mistakes.right: Move straight up and straight down only — rolling can irritate the shoulder joint.
Keep your arms straight and passive; the lift comes from the shoulders alone.
Hold the top position for a full second before lowering to get the full contraction.

name: Dumbbell Bent-Over Reverse Fly
instructions: Stand with feet hip-width apart holding a 10 lb dumbbell in each hand. Hinge forward from the hips until your torso is close to parallel with the floor — noticeably lower than a standing reverse fly — with a flat back and soft knees.
Let the dumbbells hang directly below your chest, palms facing each other, arms nearly straight with only a slight bend at the elbows. Brace your core here before the first rep.

Exhale and raise both arms out to the sides in a wide arc, leading with your elbows. Stop once your arms reach shoulder height or your shoulder blades are fully squeezed together, whichever comes first.
Hold the squeeze at the top for one second, then inhale and lower slowly back to the hang over 2 seconds. Keep your torso locked in the deep hinge throughout every rep.
If your low back starts to fatigue before your set is done, stand up between reps to rest the hinge rather than pushing through with a rounding back.
cues: Torso stays close to parallel with the floor — deeper than a standard reverse fly
Lead with your elbows in a wide arc, not your hands
Reset the hinge between reps if your low back fatigues
modification: Perform seated, folded forward over your thighs, to remove the hip-hinge hold entirely.

sensation.feelHere: The back of your shoulders and between your shoulder blades, more intensely than a standing version.
sensation.notHere: Your low back straining to hold the deep hinge position.
sensation.firstCue: Hinge low, torso near parallel. Lead the arc with your elbows, squeeze at the top.

wrongSpot.fix: The deep hinge is fatiguing before your reps are done. Stand up between reps or switch to the seated version.
You're shrugging to lift the weight. Keep shoulders down and go lighter if needed.
You're gripping too hard. Hold the dumbbells loosely — the hand is just along for the ride.

sensation.nextDay: A noticeable ache across the rear shoulders and upper back for 1–2 days is expected.
sensation.backNote: The deeper hinge here loads the low back more than a standing reverse fly. If it fatigues or aches, stand upright between reps or switch to the seated modification.
sensation.stopIf: Any pain shooting down a leg, or sharp low-back pain during the hinge.

mistakes.right: Hinge deeper than a standard reverse fly — torso should be close to parallel with the floor.
Stand up to rest the hinge between reps instead of grinding through a rounding back.
Lead every rep with your elbows moving out wide in an arc.

name: Band Seated Row
instructions: Sit on a mat with legs extended in front of you, knees slightly bent. Loop the middle of your resistance band around the soles of both feet and hold one end in each hand with palms facing each other.
Sit up tall with a long spine, not leaning back. Take up the slack in the band so there's tension even with arms extended toward your feet — this is your starting position.
Exhale and pull your shoulder blades back and down first, then drive your elbows back past your ribs, keeping them close to your sides. Sit tall throughout — do not lean back to help the pull.
Squeeze your shoulder blades together at the end of the pull and pause for one full second, chest lifted and tall, feeling the contraction across your upper back.
Inhale and let your arms extend back out slowly over 2 seconds, returning to the stretch position without letting your spine round forward or your shoulders slump.
cues: Shoulder blade pulls back first, elbow follows — not the other way around
Sit tall throughout; do not lean back to help the pull
Elbows stay close to your sides as they drive backward
modification: Bend your knees more to shorten the band's stretch and reduce resistance, or loosen your grip on the band ends.

sensation.feelHere: The middle of your back between your shoulder blades, and the sides of your back under your arms.
sensation.notHere: Your biceps doing most of the work, or your low back rounding to help the pull.
sensation.firstCue: Pull the shoulder blade back before the elbow bends. Sit tall the whole time.

wrongSpot.fix: You're bending the elbow before the shoulder blade moves. Start every rep with a blade squeeze first.
You're leaning back to help pull. Sit tall and keep your spine long throughout the row.
You're gripping the band too hard. Loosen your hold — a firm grip is enough.

sensation.nextDay: A broad ache across the middle back for 1–2 days is a good sign.
sensation.stopIf: Pain shooting down a leg, or numbness or tingling in your hands.

mistakes.right: Draw your shoulder blade back and down first, then let the elbow bend to finish the pull.
Keep your torso tall and still — let your arms and back do the work, not your body weight.

mistakes.wrong: Rounding the spine on the return
