mistakes.right: Extend your arms back out slowly while keeping your spine long, not curled forward.

name: Band Single-Arm Bicep Curl
instructions: Stand on the middle of your resistance band with the foot on your working side. Hold that end of the band, palm facing forward, upper arm pinned close to your side, other hand free at your side for balance.
Take up any slack in the band so there's tension even with your arm fully straight. Set your shoulders back and down, standing tall, before starting the first rep.
Exhale and curl your hand upward toward your shoulder, keeping your upper arm completely still and your torso facing forward the whole time, resisting the urge to twist.
Curl until you feel a strong squeeze in the upper arm, pause for one second, then inhale and lower back down over 2–3 seconds with full control.
Complete all reps on one side, then switch your stance so the band is under your other foot, and repeat the same curl on the opposite arm.
cues: Upper arm pinned to your side for the entire set on that arm
Face forward — don't twist your torso to help the pull
Lower slowly over 2–3 seconds instead of letting the band snap back
modification: Stand on less of the band for lighter resistance, or hold the band with a shorter length between hand and foot.

sensation.feelHere: The front of your upper arm on the working side, building to a burn.
sensation.notHere: Your torso twisting or your wrist straining to hold the band handle.
sensation.firstCue: Elbow pinned at your side. Curl straight up, lower slow against the band.

wrongSpot.fix: You're rotating to help the pull. Keep your hips and shoulders square to the front.
Your wrist is bending back as you curl. Keep it straight and let the elbow do the work.
You're leaning to one side to counterbalance. Stand tall with weight even on both feet.

sensation.nextDay: A one-sided burn in the working arm for 1–2 days, more noticeable than the two-arm version.
sensation.stopIf: Numbness or tingling in the hand, or sharp pain at the elbow or wrist.

mistakes.right: Keep your hips and shoulders facing forward and let the arm work alone.

mistakes.wrong: Letting the band snap back down
mistakes.right: Control the lower over 2–3 seconds — the band fights hardest near the top.
Keep your stance even and stable, weight balanced across both feet.

name: Band Standing Reverse Fly
instructions: Stand tall with feet hip-width apart. Hold one end of the resistance band in each hand and bring your arms straight out in front of you at chest height, with enough tension in the band that it's already slightly stretched.
Soften your knees and keep a small forward lean from the hips — just enough to keep the movement in front of your body, not a deep hinge.
Exhale and sweep both arms apart out to the sides, leading with your elbows, keeping a slight bend in them throughout. Squeeze your shoulder blades together as your arms reach out to the sides.
Pause for one second at full stretch across your upper back, then inhale and bring your hands back together slowly over 2 seconds, resisting the band's pull throughout.
Keep your torso still throughout the set — the arms sweep apart and together, but your chest and hips should stay facing forward the entire time.
cues: Lead the sweep with your elbows, not your hands
Squeeze shoulder blades together as your arms open out to the sides
Control the return — resist the band pulling your hands back together
modification: Choke up on the band for less resistance, or shorten the sweep range while you build strength.

sensation.feelHere: The back of your shoulders and between your shoulder blades as your arms sweep apart.
sensation.notHere: Your upper traps shrugging up near your neck.
sensation.firstCue: Lead with your elbows apart. Squeeze blades together, control the return.

wrongSpot.fix: You're shrugging to open your arms. Keep shoulders pulled down and choke up on the band for less resistance.
You're gripping the band ends too hard. Hold firmly, not tightly.
You're leaning too far forward from the hips. Stay closer to upright with just a small lean.

sensation.nextDay: A light ache across the back of the shoulders for a day is normal and expected.
sensation.stopIf: Any pain shooting down an arm, or sharp pain between the shoulder blades.

mistakes.wrong: Leading the sweep with the hands
mistakes.right: Lead with your elbows moving outward — the hands should trail slightly behind.
Resist the return over 2 seconds instead of letting the band do the work.

mistakes.wrong: Hinging too deep at the hips
mistakes.right: Stay close to upright with just a small forward lean, not a full bend.

name: Superman Hold
instructions: Lie face down on a mat with arms extended straight overhead and legs extended straight behind you. Rest your forehead lightly on the mat to keep your neck long and neutral.
Exhale and lift your arms, chest, and legs a small amount off the floor at the same time — just a few centimetres is the whole movement. This is not a big arch; think 'hover,' not 'launch.'
Hold the small lift, breathing normally, keeping the effort in the muscles either side of your spine and in your glutes. Your neck stays long — don't crane your head back to look up.
Lower everything back down slowly and rest for a breath before the next hold. Each hold should feel like steady work, never a pinch or a strain.
cues: A few centimetres of lift is the whole exercise — do not overreach
Keep your neck long; don't crane your head up to look forward
The effort belongs either side of the spine, never in the spine itself
modification: Lift only the arms or only the legs at first, or hold for 8–10 seconds while building tolerance.

sensation.feelHere: A steady, working burn in the muscles either side of your spine, and in your glutes.
sensation.notHere: A pinch or sharp point right on your spine itself. That's the joint, not the muscle.
sensation.firstCue: Lift just a few centimetres. Keep your neck long, breathe normally through the hold.

wrongSpot.fix: You've lifted too high. Bring the height down to a small hover and keep it there.
You're craning your head up. Keep your forehead in line with your spine, eyes toward the floor.
You may be lifting too little to engage the muscle. Add a small amount of height and hold steady.

sensation.nextDay: A mild ache either side of the spine and in the glutes for a day is expected.
sensation.backNote: This should feel like work in the muscles beside the spine, never a pinch in the spine itself, never into a leg. Keep the lift to a few centimetres.
sensation.stopIf: Anything shooting, electric, or burning down a leg, or any numbness or pins and needles.

mistakes.right: A few centimetres off the mat is the target — a big arch is not the goal here.

mistakes.wrong: Craning the neck to look up
mistakes.right: Keep your head in line with your spine and let your forehead point down at the mat.
Breathe normally through the hold — bracing your breath adds unnecessary tension.

name: Prone Swimmer
instructions: Lie face down on a mat with arms extended straight overhead, palms down, and legs long behind you. Lift your arms and chest just a few centimetres off the mat — the same small hover as a superman hold.
Keeping that small lift, exhale and sweep both arms out to the sides and back down toward your hips in a wide arc, like a slow swimming stroke, palms trailing down through the movement.
Squeeze your shoulder blades together as your hands pass by your hips, holding the small chest lift the whole time. Your neck stays long, forehead toward the mat.
Inhale and sweep your arms back overhead to the starting position, keeping the same small hover throughout. That is one rep — keep the motion slow and continuous.
Keep the lift height constant and small throughout every rep. If your low back starts to take over, lower your chest closer to the mat and keep the arm sweep smaller.
cues: Keep the chest lift small and constant — a few centimetres, not a big arch
Sweep slowly, like a stroke through water, squeezing the blades together at the hips
Keep your neck long; forehead points toward the mat throughout
modification: Keep your chest resting on the mat and sweep only the arms until you build tolerance for the added hold.

sensation.feelHere: A steady working burn in the upper back and rear shoulders, either side of your spine.
sensation.notHere: A pinch or sharp point right on your spine itself.
sensation.firstCue: Small chest hover throughout. Sweep arms slowly like a stroke, squeeze blades at the hips.

wrongSpot.fix: Your chest lift is too high. Bring it down to a small hover and keep it steady.
You're craning your head to look forward. Keep your forehead pointing down at the mat.
You're sweeping too fast or too wide. Slow the stroke and keep it smooth and controlled.

sensation.nextDay: A working ache across the upper back and shoulders for a day or two is expected.
sensation.backNote: Spinal extension should feel like effort in the muscles beside the spine, never a pinch in the spine itself, never travelling into a leg. Keep the chest lift small.
sensation.stopIf: Anything shooting, electric, or burning down a leg, or numbness or pins and needles.

mistakes.right: Keep the hover small and constant — a few centimetres is the whole exercise.
Slow the stroke down — this is about control, not speed.
Keep your head in line with your spine, forehead toward the mat throughout.

name: TRX Face Pull
instructions: Set the TRX straps to roughly chest length. Hold a handle in each hand with palms facing each other, and walk your feet back until your body leans away from the anchor at a comfortable angle, arms extended in front of you.
Brace your core so your body stays in a straight line from head to heels — this is a plank-like lean, not a bent-over row.
Exhale and pull both handles toward your face, leading with your elbows high and wide, so your hands finish level with your ears and your elbows point out to the sides.
Squeeze your shoulder blades together at the end of the pull and pause for one second, feeling the squeeze deep in your upper back and rear shoulders.
Inhale and extend your arms back out slowly over 2 seconds, returning to the lean with control, keeping your body straight and rigid throughout the whole movement.
cues: Elbows lead high and wide — hands finish level with your ears
Keep your body in a straight line from head to heels the whole set
Squeeze shoulder blades together at the end of every pull
modification: Walk your feet closer to the anchor to reduce the lean angle and make the pull easier.

sensation.feelHere: The back of your shoulders and between your shoulder blades, high up near your upper back.
sensation.notHere: Your low back sagging, or your neck straining to reach the handles.
sensation.firstCue: Elbows lead high and wide toward your ears. Squeeze blades, control the return.

wrongSpot.fix: Your hips are sagging out of the plank line. Brace your core and keep a straight line head to heels.
You're craning your neck to reach the straps. Pull the handles to your face, not your face to the handles.
You're shrugging to help the pull. Keep shoulders down and elbows high and wide instead.

sensation.nextDay: A broad ache across the upper back and rear shoulders for 1–2 days is a good sign.
sensation.stopIf: Pain shooting down a leg, or sharp low-back pain from the plank lean.

mistakes.right: Brace your core and keep a rigid, straight line from head to heels throughout the lean.
Lead with high, wide elbows so your hands finish level with your ears.

mistakes.wrong: Standing too close to the anchor
mistakes.right: Walk your feet back for enough lean angle to create real resistance.

name: TRX Bicep Curl
instructions: Set the TRX straps to mid-length. Hold a handle in each hand with palms facing up, and walk your feet forward until you're leaning back at a comfortable angle, arms extended toward the anchor, body straight.
Brace your core so your body forms a straight line from head to heels — the lean-back angle is what creates the resistance, so pick an angle you can hold with good form.
Exhale and curl your hands up toward your forehead by bending at the elbows, keeping your upper arms still and your body leaning at the same fixed angle throughout.
Pause at the top for a squeeze, then inhale and straighten your arms back out slowly over 2 seconds, letting your body return to the starting lean with control.
Keep your hips in line with your shoulders throughout — if they sag or pike, straighten up your stance to make the curl more manageable.
cues: Palms face up throughout — the lean-back angle creates the resistance
Keep a straight line from head to heels; hips don't sag or pike
Curl only with the elbows — the leaning body stays fixed
modification: Walk your feet back toward more upright to reduce the lean angle and lighten the resistance.

sensation.feelHere: The front of your upper arm, working harder the deeper you lean back.
sensation.notHere: Your low back sagging out of the straight line, or your shoulders straining.
sensation.firstCue: Fix your lean angle, brace the core. Curl with elbows only, squeeze at top.

wrongSpot.fix: Your hips are sagging out of line. Brace your core and straighten up your stance if needed.
You're leaning back too far for your current strength. Walk your feet closer to reduce the angle.
Your wrist is bending back at the top. Keep it straight, palm facing your forehead.

sensation.nextDay: A burn in the front of the upper arm for a day or two, similar to a standard curl.
sensation.stopIf: Numbness or tingling in the hands, or sharp low-back pain from the lean.

mistakes.wrong: Letting the hips sag or pike
mistakes.right: Brace your core and keep a rigid straight line from head to heels through every rep.
Walk your feet closer to the anchor to reduce the angle and the resistance.
Keep your body angle fixed — only your elbows should bend during the curl.

name: TRX Y-Fly
instructions: Set the TRX straps to roughly chest length. Hold a handle in each hand with palms facing each other, and walk your feet back until you're leaning away from the anchor at a light, comfortable angle, arms extended in front of you.
Brace your core to keep your body in a straight line from head to heels. This should feel light — the point of this exercise is control, not how much you can lean.
Exhale and sweep both arms up and out into a wide 'Y' shape overhead, keeping your arms fairly straight and thumbs turning slightly up as they rise.
Focus on drawing your shoulder blades down and together as your arms reach the top of the Y, rather than shrugging your shoulders toward your ears. Pause briefly at the top.
Inhale and lower your arms back down slowly to the starting position over 2–3 seconds, keeping the movement slow throughout — this exercise is meant to be light and controlled, never rushed.
cues: Move slowly and stay light — this is about the lower traps, not shoulder strength
Draw shoulder blades down and together, not up toward your ears
Keep your body in a straight line from head to heels throughout
modification: Walk your feet closer to the anchor to reduce the lean angle and make the sweep lighter.

sensation.feelHere: A light burn low between your shoulder blades, toward the bottom rather than the top.
sensation.notHere: Your upper traps or the top of your shoulders working hard.
sensation.firstCue: Sweep slow into a wide Y. Draw shoulder blades down and together, not up.

wrongSpot.fix: You're shrugging to raise your arms. Slow down and think 'blades down' before you reach the top.
Your hips are sagging out of the plank line. Brace your core and straighten your stance.
You've leaned back too far for a light exercise. Walk your feet closer to the anchor.

sensation.nextDay: A light, low ache between the shoulder blades for a day is normal; this exercise should stay gentle.
sensation.stopIf: Pain shooting down a leg, or sharp low-back pain from the plank lean.

mistakes.right: Draw your shoulder blades down and together as your arms rise, keeping shoulders away from your ears.
Walk your feet closer to the anchor — this move should feel light, not heavy.
Move slowly in both directions; speed defeats the purpose of this control-focused exercise.

name: Incline Push-Up
instructions: Place both hands on a sturdy elevated surface — a bench, a step, or a countertop — slightly wider than shoulder-width. Walk your feet back until your body forms a straight line from head to heels, angled up toward your hands.
Brace your core and squeeze your glutes so your hips don't sag or pike. The higher the surface, the easier the push-up — start with something waist-height if a standard push-up feels too hard.
Take a breath in. Bend your elbows to roughly 45 degrees away from your torso and lower your chest toward the surface with control, keeping your body rigid the whole way down.
Lower until your chest nears the surface, then press back up to full extension, exhaling as you push. Keep your neck neutral and your gaze slightly ahead of your hands throughout.
Reset at the top before the next rep. As this gets easy, move to a lower surface — that's how you progress toward a standard floor push-up.
cues: Lower surface height = harder exercise — pick a height where your last rep still has good form
Elbows at 45 degrees, not flared to a T
Keep hips and shoulders moving as one rigid unit
modification: Use a higher surface (kitchen counter, sturdy table) to make it easier, or reduce reps to 8.

sensation.feelHere: The middle of your chest and the back of your upper arms.
sensation.notHere: The front point of your shoulder or your lower back.
sensation.firstCue: Elbows at 45 degrees. Lower for a slow 3 count toward the surface.

wrongSpot.fix: Elbows are flaring out. Bring them to about 45 degrees from your ribs before you lower.
Your hips are sagging. Brace your core and keep a straight line from head to heels.

sensation.nextDay: A mild ache across the chest and upper arms for a day or so is normal. Sharp pain is not.
sensation.stopIf: Anything shoots down your arm, or your hand goes numb or tingly.

mistakes.wrong: Picking a surface too low too soon
mistakes.right: Start higher than you think you need — you can always lower it as you get stronger.
Brace your core so your body stays one straight line, not a bent one.

name: Decline Push-Up
instructions: Place your hands on the floor, shoulder-width apart, and rest the tops of your feet on a low sturdy surface — a step or a low couch cushion works. Your body should form a straight line, angled down toward your hands.
Brace your core hard before you start — the steeper angle puts more of your body weight through your arms and shoulders, and a sagging core will show up in your low back first.
Take a breath in. Bend your elbows to roughly 45 degrees and lower your chest toward the floor with control, keeping the line from feet to head unbroken.
Lower until your chest is a couple inches from the floor, then press back to full extension, exhaling as you push. Keep your neck neutral throughout.
Reset your plank before each rep. If your feet keep sliding off the step or your hips start to sag partway through the set, that's your cue to lower the step height rather than fight through it.
cues: Feet elevation controls difficulty — start low, raise it only once form is solid
Brace the core before every rep, not partway through
Elbows at 45 degrees, same as a standard push-up
modification: Use a lower step, or go back to a standard floor push-up until you build the core control this needs.

sensation.feelHere: The upper part of your chest, near the collarbone, plus the back of your upper arms and a strong core brace.
sensation.notHere: Your lower back working hard, or the front point of your shoulder.
sensation.firstCue: Brace your core hard first. Elbows at 45 degrees. Lower for a slow 3 count.

wrongSpot.fix: Your core isn't braced enough for the steeper angle. Squeeze your glutes and tighten your core before you lower.
Elbows are flaring wide. Bring them to about 45 degrees from your torso.

sensation.nextDay: A broad ache in the upper chest and arms for 1-2 days is normal. Low back soreness is not.
sensation.backNote: The steeper angle asks more of your core to keep your spine neutral. If your low back is doing the work instead of your core, lower the step and rebuild the brace first.
sensation.stopIf: Anything shoots down your arm or leg, or numbness or tingling anywhere.

mistakes.wrong: Letting the hips sag under the steeper load
mistakes.right: Brace your core hard before you start, not once you feel it slipping.

mistakes.wrong: Jumping to a high step too soon
mistakes.right: Build up the step height gradually as your core control improves.

name: Diamond Push-Up
instructions: Get into a high plank position and bring your hands together under your chest, touching thumbs and index fingers to form a diamond or triangle shape. Body in a straight line from head to heels.
Take a breath in. Bend your elbows and lower your chest toward your hands, keeping your elbows tracking back close to your ribs rather than flaring out.
Lower only until you feel a comfortable stretch — you do not need to touch your chest to your hands, and you should stop well short of your elbow's deepest bend.
Press back up to extension, exhaling as you push, but stop just short of locking your elbows out hard. The close hand position already asks a lot of the elbow joint.
Reset your plank before the next rep. If your elbows start to ache rather than your triceps burning, drop to your knees for the rest of the set.
cues: Stop short of full lockout — protect the elbow, don't grind into it
Elbows track back along your ribs, not out to the sides
Go easier and lighter than feels impressive — this one is about the joint, not ego
modification: Perform from your knees, or widen your hand position slightly if a true diamond is too much on the elbows.

sensation.feelHere: The back of your upper arm, right at the triceps, especially near the elbow.
sensation.notHere: A pinch or ache inside the elbow joint itself.
sensation.firstCue: Elbows track back, not out. Stop short of full lockout at the top.

wrongSpot.fix: That's the joint, not the muscle. Stop short of lockout and don't lower into the deepest stretch — widen your hands slightly if it continues.
You're letting your elbows flare out. Keep them tracking back along your ribs.

sensation.nextDay: A focused ache on the back of the upper arms for 1-2 days is normal. Elbow joint pain is not.
sensation.stopIf: Sharp or pinching pain at the elbow, or anything shooting down your arm.

mistakes.wrong: Locking out hard at the top every rep
mistakes.right: Stop just short of lockout and squeeze the triceps instead.

mistakes.wrong: Lowering into the deepest possible elbow bend
mistakes.right: Lower only to a comfortable stretch — you don't need to touch your hands.

name: Wide Push-Up
instructions: Start in a high plank with your hands noticeably wider than shoulder-width — roughly one and a half shoulder-widths apart. Body in a straight line from head to heels, core braced.

Take a breath in. Bend your elbows and lower your chest toward the floor. Your elbows will naturally point out more than in a standard push-up — that's expected with this hand width, but don't overdo it.
Lower until you feel a stretch across your chest, staying controlled rather than dropping. Keep your body moving as one rigid unit — no sagging hips.
Press back up to full extension, exhaling as you push, driving through your palms and squeezing your chest together as you rise. Move at a steady, controlled pace rather than rushing the lockout.
Reset your form before each rep. If your shoulders start to feel loaded instead of your chest, bring your hands in slightly narrower and keep watching how the elbows track as you lower.
cues: Hands about one and a half shoulder-widths apart — wide, not extreme
Let elbows flare more than usual, but keep it controlled
Squeeze your chest together as you press up
modification: Perform from your knees, or narrow your hand placement slightly if your shoulders feel it more than your chest.

sensation.feelHere: Across the outer edges of your chest, toward your armpits.
sensation.notHere: The front or top of your shoulder taking the load.
sensation.firstCue: Hands wide, elbows flared but controlled. Lower for a slow 3 count.

wrongSpot.fix: Your hands may be too wide for your current shoulder mobility. Bring them in an inch or two and keep the descent controlled.
Your hips are sagging. Brace your core to keep a straight line.

sensation.nextDay: A broad ache across the outer chest for 1-2 days is normal. Shoulder joint pain is not.
sensation.stopIf: Sharp or pinching pain at the shoulder, or anything shooting down your arm.

mistakes.right: Keep it to about one and a half shoulder-widths — extreme width just stresses the shoulder.

mistakes.wrong: Dropping fast into the bottom position
mistakes.right: Lower with control to a comfortable stretch, not a bounce.

name: Pike Push-Up
instructions: Start on hands and feet, hands slightly wider than shoulder-width, and walk your feet in toward your hands while pushing your hips up and back. You want an inverted-V shape, with your hips as the highest point.
The more vertical your torso, the more this shifts from chest to shoulders — that's the goal here. Let your head hang naturally between your arms, looking toward your feet or slightly behind you.
Take a breath in. Bend your elbows and lower the crown of your head toward the floor, keeping your hips high the whole time — don't let them drop toward a regular push-up position.
Lower until your head nears the floor, then press back up through your palms to the starting position, exhaling as you push. Your hips should stay lifted throughout the whole rep.

Reset your hips high before the next rep. This exercise is meant to build the shoulder strength and overhead pressing pattern you'll eventually use for standing presses, so treat the hip position as non-negotiable.
cues: Hips stay high the entire rep — that's what makes it shoulder work, not chest work
Let your head hang, don't shrug it up toward your ears
Walk feet closer to hands for a steeper, harder angle once this feels easy
modification: Keep your feet further from your hands for a shallower, less vertical angle, or elevate your hands on a step to reduce the load.

sensation.feelHere: The front and top of your shoulders, and the back of your upper arms.
sensation.notHere: Your neck or the top of your traps working hard.
sensation.firstCue: Hips high, head hangs loose. Lower for a slow 3 count.

wrongSpot.fix: You're shrugging your shoulders up toward your ears, or your hips have dropped so it's turned into a push-up. Reset your hips high and let your shoulders stay down and back.

wrongSpot.felt: Front of the shoulders, sharp or pinching
wrongSpot.fix: That's the joint, not the muscle. Shorten the range and don't lower all the way to the floor.

sensation.nextDay: A broad ache across the front of the shoulders for 1-2 days is normal. Sharp joint pain or neck strain is not.
sensation.stopIf: Sharp shoulder pain, or anything shooting down your arm.

mistakes.wrong: Letting the hips sink toward a push-up
mistakes.right: Keep your hips as the highest point of your body — that's what shifts load to the shoulders.

mistakes.wrong: Shrugging shoulders up toward your ears
mistakes.right: Let your head hang and keep your shoulders pulled down away from your ears.

name: Scapular Push-Up
instructions: Get into a high plank position, arms fully extended and locked, hands under your shoulders. This is a small-range drill — your elbows will not bend at all during the movement.
Brace your core to keep a straight line from head to heels. Keeping your arms straight, let your shoulder blades sink together and down, so your chest drops slightly between your arms.
From that lowered position, push the floor away — spread your shoulder blades apart and round your upper back slightly, without bending your elbows at all.
That short pinch-and-spread of the shoulder blades is the entire rep. Move slowly and deliberately — this is an activation drill, not a strength-builder, so control matters more than speed.
Repeat for the full set, keeping your arms locked straight throughout. If your elbows start bending, you've turned it into a tiny push-up — reset and shorten the range.
cues: Arms stay locked straight the entire time — only the shoulder blades move
Think 'push the floor away' at the top, not 'push my body up'
Small, slow, controlled — this is activation, not a strength rep
modification: Perform from your knees to reduce the load through your arms while you learn the movement.

sensation.feelHere: A wrapping feeling around your ribs, under your armpit, as your shoulder blade spreads.
sensation.notHere: Your chest or triceps working — if you feel those, your elbows are bending.
sensation.firstCue: Lock your elbows straight. Let your shoulder blades pinch together, then spread apart.

wrongSpot.fix: Your elbows are bending, turning this into a tiny push-up. Lock your arms straight and isolate the shoulder blade movement only.
You're shrugging instead of spreading. Keep your neck long and let the movement happen at your shoulder blades, not your neck.

sensation.nextDay: Little to no soreness is expected — this is a light activation drill.
sensation.stopIf: Any wrist pain, or anything shooting down your arm.

mistakes.wrong: Bending the elbows during the movement
mistakes.right: Keep your arms locked straight — this becomes a push-up only if the elbows bend.

name: Dumbbell Incline Press (Floor)
instructions: Stack a couple of firm cushions or a folded step against a wall or couch to create a shallow incline — aim for roughly 30 degrees, not much steeper. A steep incline is the single biggest reason this exercise ends up in the front shoulder instead of the chest.
Lie back on the incline with a dumbbell in each hand at chest level. Before you press a single rep, pull your shoulder blades back and down and pin them there — this is not optional on an incline.
Take a breath in and brace your core. Keep your elbows at roughly 45 degrees from your torso, not flared out wide — flared elbows load the front of the shoulder instead of the chest.
As you exhale, press both dumbbells up and slightly inward until your arms are nearly extended above your upper chest. Pause briefly, keeping your shoulder blades set the whole time.

Inhale and lower with control back to chest level over 2-3 seconds. If your shoulder is doing the work instead of your chest, the fix is usually the setup — flatten the incline, reset your shoulder blades, and tuck the elbows before you blame your execution.
cues: Keep the incline shallow — around 30 degrees, not steep — steeper by design shifts load to the front delt
Pin your shoulder blades back and down before every single rep
Elbows at 45 degrees, not flared wide
modification: Use 10 lb dumbbells, flatten the incline further, or drop to a flat dumbbell floor press if your shoulder is still loud.

sensation.feelHere: The upper part of your chest, near the collarbone, with some help from the back of your arms.
sensation.notHere: The front point of your shoulder doing most of the work.
sensation.firstCue: Set your shoulder blades back and down first. Elbows at 45 degrees. Lower for a slow 3 count.

wrongSpot.fix: This is usually the setup, not your execution. Check three things: is your incline steeper than about 30-45 degrees, are your shoulder blades set back and down, and are your elbows flared past 45 degrees? Fix those before adding weight.
That's the joint, not the muscle. Stop the set, flatten the incline, and drop the weight.

name: Dumbbell Floor Fly
instructions: Lie on your back on the floor with knees bent and feet flat. Hold a 10 lb dumbbell in each hand, arms extended straight up above your chest, palms facing each other with a slight bend in the elbows.
Press your lower back gently into the floor and brace your core. Keep that same slight elbow bend locked in place for the whole set — it does not change throughout the movement.

Take a breath in. Lower both arms out to the sides in a wide arc, like opening your arms for a hug, until your upper arms touch the floor. The floor stops you from lowering too far — that's the built-in safety limit.
Feel a stretch across your chest at the bottom, then reverse the arc and bring the dumbbells back together above your chest, exhaling as you rise. Squeeze your chest together at the top.
Keep the movement slow and controlled in both directions — this is not a heavy lift, it's a stretch-and-squeeze for the chest, so resist any urge to rush the reps or add more weight than you need.
cues: Keep a slight, fixed bend in the elbows the whole time — don't turn it into a press
Let the floor stop your arms at the bottom — don't force a deeper stretch
Squeeze your chest together at the top like closing a hug
modification: Use lighter weight or shorten the range of motion, stopping before your arms fully touch the floor.

sensation.notHere: The front of your shoulder or your elbows straining.
sensation.firstCue: Keep a slight elbow bend fixed throughout. Lower slowly to the floor.

sensation.stopIf: Anything shoots down your arm, or your hand goes numb or tingly.

mistakes.right: Lock in a slight bend at the start and keep it fixed for the whole set.

name: Dumbbell Arnold Press
instructions: Sit tall on a bench with back support if available, feet flat on the floor. Hold a 10 lb dumbbell in each hand at shoulder height, palms facing your body, elbows bent and tucked in front of your shoulders.
Brace your core before you move — a seated overhead press is exactly the kind of exercise where the low back tries to arch to help you press. Keep your ribs stacked over your hips, not flared up.
As you exhale, press the dumbbells overhead while simultaneously rotating your palms outward, so they face away from you by the top of the press. Arms extend without locking the elbows out hard.

Pause briefly at the top with the dumbbells over your shoulders, not out in front. Inhale and reverse the motion with control, rotating your palms back to face you as you lower to the starting position.
Keep your core braced through every rep. If you notice your low back arching as the weight gets overhead, that's your signal to drop the weight or shorten the range rather than push through it.
cues: Brace your core before you press — this is where a low back arch likes to sneak in
Rotate your palms out as you press up, and back in as you lower
Dumbbells finish over your shoulders, not out in front of your face
modification: Perform seated with back support, use lighter weight, or reduce the range by not pressing all the way to full extension.

sensation.notHere: Your lower back working, or a pinch at the top of the shoulder.

wrongSpot.fix: That's the joint, not the muscle. Stop just short of full overhead extension.

sensation.nextDay: A broad ache across the shoulders for 1-2 days is normal. Low back soreness is not — that means you arched.

sensation.stopIf: Anything shoots down your arm or into your low back, or numbness or tingling anywhere.

mistakes.right: Brace your core and keep your ribs down — if you're arching, the weight is too heavy.
Let the rotation happen smoothly through the whole press, not as a snap at the top.

name: Dumbbell Front Raise
instructions: Stand tall with feet hip-width apart, a 10 lb dumbbell in each hand, arms resting in front of your thighs with palms facing your body. Brace your core lightly to keep your torso still throughout.
Take a breath in. As you exhale, raise one or both arms straight out in front of you, keeping a slight bend in the elbow, until your arms reach about shoulder height — no higher.
Pause briefly at shoulder height. Do not let your torso lean back to help the weight up — if you feel yourself leaning, the weight is too heavy or you're moving too fast.
Inhale and lower with control back to the starting position over 2-3 seconds. Resist the urge to let the dumbbells drop — the lowering is where a lot of the work happens.
Keep your core braced and your torso upright for the whole set. Alternating one arm at a time can make it easier to control if lifting both together causes you to lean.
cues: Raise to shoulder height only — going higher shifts load to the traps, not the shoulder
Keep your torso still — no leaning back to help the weight up
Lower slowly — the control on the way down is half the exercise
modification: Raise one arm at a time instead of both together, or use a lighter weight if your torso wants to lean.

sensation.notHere: Your upper traps or neck shrugging up.

mistakes.wrong: Leaning back to swing the weight up
mistakes.right: Keep your torso upright and still; lighten the weight if you're leaning.

name: Dumbbell Close-Grip Floor Press
instructions: Lie on your back on the floor with knees bent, feet flat. Hold a dumbbell in each hand at chest level, but bring your elbows in closer to your ribs than a standard floor press — roughly 20-30 degrees from your torso instead of 45.
Press your lower back gently into the floor and brace your core. The dumbbells should be closer together than shoulder-width, nearly in line with the center of your chest.
Take a breath in. Lower the dumbbells until your elbows touch the floor — let the floor set your depth, don't reach for a deeper stretch than that.

Press back up, exhaling as you push, keeping your elbows tucked close the whole way. Stop just short of locking your elbows out hard at the top — the close grip already puts extra demand on the elbow joint.
Pause briefly at the top without a hard lockout, then lower again with control. If your elbows start to ache rather than the back of your arms burning, widen your grip slightly or lighten the weight.

Let the floor set your depth — don't chase a deeper stretch
Stop short of a hard lockout at the top to protect the elbow

name: Dumbbell Floor Skull Crusher
instructions: Lie on your back on the floor with knees bent, feet flat. Hold a 10 lb dumbbell in each hand with a neutral grip — palms facing each other — arms extended straight up above your shoulders.

Press your lower back gently into the floor and brace your core. This exercise is notorious for elbow pain, so use lighter weight than feels impressive and keep your grip neutral throughout, not rotating to palms-up.
Take a breath in. Keeping your upper arms completely still and vertical, bend only at the elbows to lower the dumbbells toward the floor beside your head — your elbows are the only joint that moves.
Let the floor stop your descent naturally near your ears. Do not force a deeper stretch — the floor's stopping point is the safe limit for this movement.
Reverse the motion by extending your elbows back to the starting position, exhaling as you press, keeping your upper arms fixed and your elbows from drifting outward or inward.
cues: Neutral grip, palms facing each other — this is easier on the elbow than a straight bar
Upper arms stay completely still — only the elbow bends
Lighter than feels impressive — this exercise is notorious for elbow pain

name: TRX Chest Press
instructions: Set the TRX straps to mid-length. Face away from the anchor, hold a handle in each hand, and lean forward with your body straight, arms extended in front of your chest. The further your feet are from the anchor, the harder this gets — start close and upright.
Brace your core to keep a rigid line from head to heels — the handles will sway slightly, and your core resists that movement throughout the set.
Take a breath in. Bend your elbows to roughly 45 degrees and lower your chest toward your hands, leaning further into the straps as you descend.
Lower until your chest nears the handles, then press back away to the starting position, exhaling as you push through your palms and squeezing your chest together.
Reset your rigid body line before each rep. Walk your feet forward, away from the anchor, to make it harder; walk them back, closer to the anchor, to make it easier.
cues: Feet further from the anchor = harder — that's your load dial, not the weight
Keep your body rigid — resist the strap sway with your core
Elbows at 45 degrees, same mechanics as a floor push-up

name: TRX Tricep Press
instructions: Set the TRX straps to mid-length. Face the anchor, hold a handle in each hand, and walk forward until you're leaning toward the anchor with arms extended overhead, body in a straight line. Start with feet closer to the anchor and more upright.
Brace your core before you move — leaning back with arms overhead is exactly the setup where a low back arch likes to sneak in. Keep your ribs stacked over your hips, not flared open.
Take a breath in. Keeping your upper arms fixed near your ears, bend your elbows and lower your head toward your hands, letting your body lean further into the straps.

Lower until your elbows reach roughly 90 degrees, then press back up to full extension by straightening your elbows, exhaling as you push. Your upper arms stay still throughout — only the elbows move.
Reset your braced, straight-line position before the next rep. Walk your feet further from the anchor to make it harder, or closer to make it easier — that's your load dial.

Brace your core the whole time — overhead work is where a back arch sneaks in
Upper arms stay fixed near your ears — only the elbows bend
modification: Walk your feet closer to the anchor for a more upright, easier angle, or reduce the range of motion.

sensation.feelHere: The back of your upper arms, and a core burn from bracing against the lean.
sensation.notHere: Your lower back working, or your shoulders straining at the top.
sensation.firstCue: Brace your core first. Upper arms fixed near your ears. Only elbows bend.

wrongSpot.fix: You're arching to manage the overhead lean. Brace your core harder and walk closer to the anchor to reduce the angle.
Your upper arms are drifting away from your ears. Keep them fixed and let only your elbows move.

sensation.nextDay: A focused ache on the back of the upper arms for 1-2 days is normal. Low back soreness is not.
sensation.backNote: Leaning back with arms overhead is a common spot for the low back to arch and assist. Keep your core braced and your ribs stacked over your hips; walk closer to the anchor if you feel your back working.
sensation.stopIf: Anything shoots down your arm or into your low back, or numbness or tingling anywhere.

mistakes.wrong: Arching the low back under the overhead lean
mistakes.right: Brace your core and walk closer to the anchor if your back starts working.

mistakes.wrong: Letting the upper arms drift away from the ears
mistakes.right: Keep them fixed in place; only the elbow joint should move.
